title: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation

questions.subtopic: Project Roles and Accountability. Project Manager Authority
questions.question: An IS auditor wants evidence that a new project's manager was formally given authority over project resources. Which document is MOST appropriate to examine?

options.A: The work breakdown structure and its task schedule
options.B: The project risk register with assigned response owners
options.C: The project charter approved by the sponsor
options.D: The business case signed by the sponsor and steering committee

questions.key_concept: The project charter formally authorizes a project, names its sponsor and grants the project manager authority over resources.
questions.pre_read: Separate documents that justify a project from the one that authorizes it and delegates authority.
questions.correct_explanation: The project charter is the document that formally authorizes the project, names the sponsor and grants the project manager authority to use organizational resources. The business case is the strongest alternative: it justifies the investment and supports the decision to proceed, but it does not delegate authority to a named project manager.

wrong_explanations.A: The work breakdown structure is a planning artifact produced after authorization. It decomposes deliverables but grants no one authority.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk register records threats and responses during planning and execution. It does not authorize the project or its manager.
wrong_explanations.D: The business case justifies the investment and feeds the go decision, but authority over resources is delegated in the charter.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are planning artifacts created after the project is authorized, so neither can grant authority.
Final two: C beats D because the business case justifies funding, while the charter actually delegates authority to the project manager.
Exam cue: when the stem asks who authorized a project or its manager, look for the sponsor-approved charter.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that developers began coding a new application before user requirements were signed off. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Test cases will be written against unconfirmed assumptions
options.B: Design documents will be produced after the code they describe
options.C: Later rework will push project costs over budget
options.D: The delivered system may not meet business needs

questions.key_concept: Approved requirements are the baseline every later SDLC phase builds on; skipping them risks a system that misses business needs.
questions.pre_read: Recall the SDLC order and ask what each phase hands to the next. Then weigh outcome risk against symptom risk.
questions.correct_explanation: In a linear SDLC each phase produces artifacts that feed the next, and approved requirements are the baseline for design, build and testing. Coding without them means the system may be built to the wrong target and fail to deliver business value. Cost overrun from rework comes closest: it is real, but it is a symptom of the larger risk of not meeting business needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tests built on unconfirmed assumptions are one technical effect; they inherit the same wrong target rather than being the main risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Documentation out of sequence is a process weakness, but the business impact is a system that misses what users need.
wrong_explanations.C: Rework and overruns are likely, but they follow from the core problem: building something the business did not agree to.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are technical side effects inside the project, test design and documentation order, not the business impact of building without agreed requirements.
Final two: D beats C because failing to meet business needs is the root risk; cost overrun is one consequence of it.
Exam cue: when a phase is skipped, pick the option about the business outcome over its cost or schedule symptoms.

questions.question: Before go-live, an IS auditor must confirm that a new payroll system passes data correctly to the general ledger and bank interfaces. Which testing evidence is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Integration test results tracing records across each connection
options.B: Acceptance test results signed off by the payroll business owners
options.C: Unit test results logged by the individual developers
options.D: Code coverage reports produced by the build pipeline

questions.key_concept: Each test level has its own scope: unit for modules, integration for interfaces between components, system for the whole, UAT for business acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Match the audit objective in the stem to the test level whose scope covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Integration testing is the level designed to verify that data passes correctly between connected components and systems, so its results directly evidence the payroll-to-ledger and bank flows. Business acceptance sign-off comes closest: it shows users accept the workflows, but users judge business outcomes on selected scenarios and do not systematically verify every interface record.

wrong_explanations.B: Acceptance confirms the system meets user needs. It is not designed to verify each interface's data transfer systematically.
wrong_explanations.C: Unit tests verify single modules in isolation. They cannot show that data moves correctly between systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Coverage reports measure how much code the tests exercised. They say nothing about interface data accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: C tests modules in isolation and D measures code exercised; neither examines data passing between systems.
Final two: A beats B because integration testing is designed to verify interface data flows, while UAT confirms business acceptance.
Exam cue: match the objective to the test level: interfaces point to integration testing, business fit to UAT.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a release's source code is baselined, but its approved design specifications can be edited freely. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Specification edits are traceable through the tool's version history
options.B: The specifications should be configuration items in the baseline
options.C: The specifications should be locked against editing by the design lead
options.D: Specification edits are acceptable if rebaselined at the next release review

questions.key_concept: Configuration items include code, designs, requirements and builds; all must be under formal change control as part of the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Ask what belongs in a product baseline. Then ask how approved changes to it should happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A configuration item is any identified artifact placed under formal change control as part of the product baseline, including requirements, designs, code and build files. Uncontrolled specifications mean the baseline cannot be trusted. A read-only lock is the tempting option: it stops unauthorized edits, but it gives approved changes no controlled path and rests on one person instead of a change process.

wrong_explanations.A: Version history shows who edited what, but no one authorizes the edit; traceability after the fact is not change control.
wrong_explanations.C: A lock stops edits, but it offers no way to authorize, record and baseline the changes the project will still need, and it relies on one person.
wrong_explanations.D: Rebaselining later records edits after they happen; configuration management requires authorization before a baselined item changes.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an edit history as control although nothing authorizes the edits, and D reviews edits after the fact, which detects rather than prevents.
Final two: B beats C because configuration management blocks unauthorized edits and gives approved changes a controlled path; a lock only blocks.
Exam cue: a configuration item is any controlled artifact in the baseline, not just code, and not just hardware.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a project's risk register. Which condition BEST justifies the project manager escalating a risk to the sponsor?

options.A: The risk was re-rated higher in the most recent risk assessment
options.B: The risk would delay a critical-path deliverable by two weeks
options.C: The planned response draws on the project's contingency reserve
options.D: Residual exposure exceeds the manager's delegated tolerance

questions.key_concept: Project risks are escalated when residual exposure exceeds delegated tolerance or the response needs authority beyond the manager's mandate.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the decision for this risk, and what would move it to someone else.
questions.correct_explanation: Escalation is driven by authority: when residual exposure exceeds the tolerance the project manager was delegated, or a response needs authority beyond that mandate, the decision belongs to the sponsor. A higher re-rating nearly wins: it signals a worsening risk, but the manager may still be able to treat it within existing tolerance.

wrong_explanations.A: A higher rating is a useful signal, but if exposure stays within the manager's tolerance it can be handled without escalating.
wrong_explanations.B: A critical-path delay is serious, but escalation follows delegated tolerance; if the delay stays within the manager's limits, the manager treats it.
wrong_explanations.C: Contingency reserve for identified risks is within the project manager's authority; drawing on it is not a reason to escalate. Management reserve is the sponsor's.

tips: Eliminate: B measures severity rather than authority, and C uses contingency reserve, which the project manager controls for identified risks.
Final two: D beats A because escalation follows delegated tolerance and authority; a re-rating alone may still sit within the manager's limits.
Exam cue: escalate when a risk exceeds the tolerance or authority delegated to the current level, not merely when it changes.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the business case for a seven-year platform investment whose largest benefits arrive after year three. Which measure should the auditor expect as the PRIMARY basis for choosing among options?

options.A: Payback period, showing how quickly the cost is recovered
options.B: Total undiscounted return over the seven-year life
options.C: Net present value of the discounted cash flows
options.D: Accounting rate of return on the average investment

questions.key_concept: NPV suits long-horizon investments with material later cash flows; payback suits decisions dominated by liquidity and quick recovery.
questions.pre_read: Notice the time horizon and when the benefits arrive. Ask which metric counts cash flows after cost is recovered.
questions.correct_explanation: Net present value discounts every expected cash flow over the investment's whole life, so it reflects both the time value of money and the large benefits arriving after year three. Payback period is the tempting option: it is useful when quick recovery dominates, but it stops counting once the cost is recovered, so it ignores the late cash flows that carry most of the value here.

wrong_explanations.A: Payback does measure how long capital stays at risk, a real liquidity concern, but a liquidity measure answers when, never how much.
wrong_explanations.B: Adding seven years of cash flows without discounting treats a year-seven benefit as worth the same as one today, overstating late returns.
wrong_explanations.D: Accounting rate of return uses accounting profit, not cash flows, and ignores when the returns arrive.

tips: Eliminate: B adds cash flows without discounting them, and D uses accounting profit rather than cash flows; neither values money by when it arrives.
Final two: C beats A because NPV captures late benefits and the time value of money; payback stops counting once cost is recovered.
Exam cue: long horizon and late benefits point to NPV; tight cash and fast recovery point to payback.

questions.subtopic: Test Types and Techniques. Requirements Coverage
questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that every approved requirement for a new system was built and tested. Which evidence is MOST useful?

options.A: A traceability matrix linking requirements to test results
options.B: Business sign-off on the final acceptance test cycle
options.C: Code review records showing coding standards were met
options.D: A map linking each requirement to its design, with version history

questions.key_concept: A requirements traceability matrix links each requirement to design, code and tests, proving completeness and supporting change impact analysis.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence follows each requirement all the way to a test result.
questions.correct_explanation: A requirements traceability matrix links each approved requirement forward to its design, code and test cases, so the auditor can spot any requirement with no test or no result. Acceptance sign-off is the most tempting alternative: it shows users accepted what they tested, but it cannot show that every requirement was covered by a test.

wrong_explanations.B: Sign-off confirms acceptance of the tests that were run. Without traceability, untested requirements would go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Code reviews check how code was written. They do not map code back to approved requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: A requirements-to-design map shows each requirement was designed, but it stops short of code and tests, so it cannot show each was built and tested.

tips: Eliminate: C checks how code was written, and D traces requirements only as far as design; neither shows each one was built and tested.
Final two: A beats B because completeness needs a requirement-by-requirement link; sign-off covers only what was actually tested.
Exam cue: 'every requirement built and tested' is a completeness question; look for traceability, not approval.

questions.question: A steering committee commits release dates based on a newly formed Scrum team's velocity after only two sprints. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Convert story points into hours to fix sprint commitments
options.B: Forecast dates only once the team's own velocity has stabilized
options.C: Have the product owner assign story points alone
options.D: Borrow a mature team's velocity on similar work for forecasting

questions.key_concept: Agile velocity forecasts become reliable when the team sizes work relatively and velocity has stabilized over several sprints.
questions.pre_read: Remember that velocity is empirical and belongs to one team. Ask what data a committed date should rest on.
questions.correct_explanation: Velocity is an empirical, team-specific measure: it becomes a reliable basis for committed dates only after the same team has sized work against its own past stories for several sprints. Converting points to hours is the tempting option because it sounds precise, but it abandons relative sizing and turns two sprints of unstable data into time commitments the team cannot yet support.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would welcome tying commitments to effort, but a unit change adds no evidence. Forecasts earn trust from a team's own settled history.
wrong_explanations.C: Sizing by one person loses the team's shared judgment. Points stop reflecting the effort of those doing the work.
wrong_explanations.D: Story points are relative to each team, so another team's velocity does not translate; it gives a precise-looking but invalid forecast.

tips: Eliminate: C removes the team's ownership of estimates, and D borrows velocity from a team whose points mean something different.
Final two: B beats A because committed dates need this team's stabilized empirical velocity; converting to hours adds false precision.
Exam cue: in agile, reliability comes from team-owned estimates and observed history, not from fixed-hour commitments.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to production several times a day. Which control provides the GREATEST assurance over build quality?

options.A: Developer attestation that known defects have been resolved
options.B: Quarterly penetration testing of the current production release
options.C: Automated nightly regression test runs against the main code branch
options.D: Automated gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans

questions.key_concept: In CI/CD, automated quality gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans give consistent preventive assurance for every build.
questions.pre_read: Note the deployment frequency. Ask which control acts on every build before production rather than afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: With several deployments a day, only an enforced control in the pipeline can act on every build before it reaches production. Gates that fail the build on test or scan failures are preventive and consistent. Nightly automated regression runs are the strongest alternative: they are consistent, but they are detective and run after many builds have already been deployed.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-attestation is unverified and not independent. It gives little assurance that defects were really fixed.
wrong_explanations.B: Quarterly testing examines a tiny fraction of releases. Hundreds of builds would reach production untested in between.
wrong_explanations.C: Nightly regression runs suffice for daily releases; when code ships several times a day, the check sits where every build must pass.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on unverified self-attestation, and B tests far too rarely for daily deployments.
Final two: D beats C because an enforced gate stops every bad build before release; a nightly run only finds problems afterward.
Exam cue: in high-frequency pipelines, prefer preventive gates in the deployment flow over checks that run after release, automated or not.

questions.subtopic: Test Data Management. Using Live Data
questions.question: Developers request production customer data to populate a new test environment. Which control should the IS auditor MOST expect to see?

options.A: Encryption of the test database at rest
options.B: Signed confidentiality agreements from each requesting developer
options.C: Masking of personal data before it is extracted
options.D: Access to the test environment limited to named staff and logged

questions.key_concept: Production-derived test data should be masked or pseudonymized before extraction, so non-production environments never hold real personal data.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can see the data once it is in test. Prefer controls that remove exposure over controls that guard it.
questions.correct_explanation: Masking or pseudonymizing personal data before extraction means the test environment never holds recoverable personal data, which applies data protection by design. Encryption at rest nearly wins: it protects stored data from theft of the media, but anyone using the test system still sees real identifiers.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption at rest protects against stolen media, but authorized test users still see real personal data in clear text.
wrong_explanations.B: Agreements deter misuse but do not reduce exposure. Real personal data still sits in a less controlled environment.
wrong_explanations.D: Restricting and logging access narrows who sees the data, but every named user still sees real personal data in test.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on signatures and D on limiting who enters; neither changes the personal data the developers see.
Final two: C beats A because masking removes personal data from test entirely; encryption still exposes it to every test user.
Exam cue: for test data, remove the sensitive content at the source rather than protecting it after it has been copied.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default); ISO/IEC 29100 (Privacy Framework); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.33 (Test Information)

Round 2 (Oct 2026, quality-gate fixes from the standards audit, pedagogy check and strong and weak blind tests): weak blind test: the runner-up admitted its own flaw ('with identifiers left intact'); A is now plain encryption at rest.

questions.question: A development manager asks an IS auditor where static application security testing adds the MOST value. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Scan each pull request and fail builds on high-severity findings
options.B: Scan each release candidate before the change board reviews it
options.C: Scan the production code base quarterly to track long-term trends
options.D: Route findings to the security team to forward critical items

questions.key_concept: SAST adds most value when run on every pull request, with builds failing on high-severity findings: shift left, fast feedback.
questions.pre_read: Think about when a flaw is cheapest to fix. Compare an early enforced check with a later one.
questions.correct_explanation: Static testing is most effective early and often: scanning each pull request gives developers fast feedback while the code is fresh, and failing builds on high-severity findings stops flaws from progressing. Scanning release candidates is the closest choice: it still finds flaws before production, but late in the cycle, when fixes are slower and costlier and may delay the release.

wrong_explanations.B: Both release-candidate and pull-request scans apply the same rules to the same code; feedback teaches most, though, while the author still has the change open.
wrong_explanations.C: Quarterly scans of production find flaws only after they are live. They measure trends rather than prevent defects.
wrong_explanations.D: Filtering findings through another team slows feedback and leaves most issues unfixed. Developers lose ownership of secure code.

tips: Eliminate: C tracks trends in released code, which measures posture but stops no flaw from shipping, and D delays and filters feedback away from developers.
Final two: A beats B because shifting scans left to each pull request fixes flaws earliest and cheapest; release-time scans come late.
Exam cue: for security testing in development, choose the earliest enforced point that gives developers fast feedback.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that customer balances migrated completely and accurately to a new core platform. Which evidence is BEST?

options.A: User acceptance test results for the main workflows
options.B: Record counts and control totals reconciled source to target
options.C: A sample of accounts compared on screen in both systems
options.D: Conversion logs showing each record was read and written

questions.key_concept: Data conversion integrity is evidenced by source-to-target reconciliation of record counts and control totals, with variances investigated.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the words completely and accurately. Ask which evidence compares the data itself, not the system's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness and accuracy of converted data are proven by reconciling source and target in full: matching record counts, control totals and hash totals, with every variance investigated. Comparing a sample of accounts on screen is the tempting option because it examines the data itself, but a sample cannot prove that every balance arrived, so missing or altered records outside it go undetected.

wrong_explanations.A: Acceptance testing checks that workflows function. It does not prove that every migrated record and amount matches the source.
wrong_explanations.C: A sample checks some accounts in detail but cannot show that every record and balance transferred.
wrong_explanations.D: The conversion program's logs report its own activity; they count records handled but cannot show balances arrived unaltered, which needs reconciled control totals.

tips: Eliminate: A tests workflows rather than the migrated data, and D relies on the conversion program's own record counts, which say nothing about amounts.
Final two: B beats C because full reconciliation covers every record and total; a sample cannot prove completeness.
Exam cue: for data conversion, completeness and accuracy evidence means counts and control totals matched between source and target.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI07 (Managed IT Change Acceptance and Transitioning); COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls); ISO/IEC 12207 (Software Life Cycle Processes)

Round 2 (Oct 2026, quality-gate fixes from the standards audit, pedagogy check and strong and weak blind tests): audit: the runner-up loses on completeness, so the tag is evidence-quality; self-check after the weak blind test: D is now the conversion program's own logs of every record. questions.question: An IS auditor finds that several failed production changes were approved by a change advisory board (CAB) that checks only each change's description and timing. What should the auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Route standard, normal and emergency changes to the full board
options.B: Require each change to name a business owner who confirms its timing
options.C: Have the board judge readiness from test and backout evidence
options.D: Hold a post-implementation review of each failed change

questions.key_concept: A change advisory board assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes before authorization; it neither plans nor executes them.
questions.pre_read: Separate who sits on a board from what it checks. Then ask whether each fix acts before or after a change.
questions.correct_explanation: A CAB adds value by assessing the risk, test evidence and backout plan of significant changes before authorizing them; approving on description and timing alone lets untested or unrecoverable changes through. A post-implementation review of failures is the tempting option: it captures lessons, but it acts after the damage and does not stop the next weak change from being approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard changes are pre-authorized and emergency changes follow an expedited path reviewed soon after; routing them all to the full board adds volume without deepening the check on risky ones.
wrong_explanations.B: A business owner confirming timing adds accountability for when a change runs, but the board would still not assess its risk, testing or backout plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing failures afterward supports learning, but it is detective; the board's main value is assessment before authorization.

tips: Eliminate: A floods the full board with pre-authorized standard and urgent emergency changes, and B adds an owner who confirms timing, which the board already checks.
Final two: C beats D because a CAB adds most assurance by assessing risk before authorization; reviewing failures afterward is detective.
Exam cue: change governance assures by checking risk, testing and backout before approval; pick the fix that strengthens the pre-approval check.

questions.question: A QA manager reports that defect density per thousand lines of code doubled after a new test team joined. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Compare density with the previous team's results on the last release
options.B: Report that density still sits below the industry benchmark
options.C: Recommend delaying the release until the new defects are fixed
options.D: Analyze root causes to separate better detection from worse code

questions.key_concept: Rising defect density can reflect better testing or worse code; root-cause analysis must come before any conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed at the same time as the metric. Ask whether a conclusion is justified yet.
questions.correct_explanation: A rise in defect density can mean more thorough testing finds more defects, or that the code itself got worse. A new test team makes both plausible, so the auditor must analyze root causes before concluding. Comparing with the previous team's results is the tempting option because it looks like analysis, but that comparison is what showed the doubling; it cannot say whether detection or the code changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Comparing teams is a standard trend check, though a metric that moves when its measurer changes is explained before it is compared.
wrong_explanations.B: An outside benchmark assumes comparable measurement, but the way defects are found has just changed; the comparison proves nothing yet.
wrong_explanations.C: Recommending a delay acts on the number before its cause is known; the rise may reflect better testing rather than worse code.

tips: Eliminate: B leans on an outside benchmark although the measurement itself changed, and C acts on the number before its cause is known.
Final two: D beats A because comparing results again only restates the rise; root-cause analysis shows whether detection or the code changed.
Exam cue: when a metric moves after a change in how it is measured, investigate the cause before drawing conclusions.

questions.question: An organization is buying business-critical custom software from a small start-up vendor. Which contract provision should the IS auditor MOST recommend?

options.A: Source code escrow with defined release conditions
options.B: A right-to-audit clause over the vendor's development process
options.C: A performance bond payable if the vendor fails to deliver
options.D: Financial backing from the vendor's parent company if the vendor defaults

questions.key_concept: Source code escrow protects continuity of business-critical custom software when the vendor may fail or stop supporting it.
questions.pre_read: Identify the main risk: the vendor might not survive. Ask which provision still works after the vendor is gone.
questions.correct_explanation: Escrow places the source code with an independent agent and releases it if defined events occur, such as vendor failure. For business-critical custom software from a vendor whose survival is uncertain, that protects continuity. A right-to-audit clause is the strongest alternative: it gives visibility into how the vendor builds software, but it does nothing if the vendor stops trading.

wrong_explanations.B: Audit rights help assess development quality while the vendor operates. They provide no access to source code if it fails.
wrong_explanations.C: A bond pays compensation, but money does not keep critical software supported once the vendor is gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Parent backing compensates for a default, but it neither supplies the source code nor keeps the software maintainable.

tips: Eliminate: C and D compensate in money, a bond or parent backing, rather than preserving the software itself.
Final two: A beats B because escrow secures source code if the vendor fails; audit rights only give visibility while it operates.
Exam cue: critical custom software plus a fragile single vendor points to escrow with clear release triggers.

questions.question: Six months after a customer relationship management (CRM) system went live, an IS auditor performs a post-implementation review. Which finding should the auditor report as MOST significant?

options.A: The project closed 4 percent over its approved budget
options.B: Realized benefits have not been measured against the business case
options.C: Acceptance test sign-off is missing for two low-use reports
options.D: User surveys rate the new screens as harder to learn

questions.key_concept: A post-implementation review primarily compares realized benefits with the approved business case to confirm value delivery.
questions.pre_read: Remember why the project was approved. Ask which option tests whether that promise was kept.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-implementation review exists to confirm the investment delivered the value promised in the business case. If realized benefits have not been measured, nobody knows whether the CRM succeeded, so the review's main purpose is unmet. The 4 percent overrun is the tempting option: it is a real variance, but a project can finish on budget and still fail to deliver its benefits.

wrong_explanations.A: A small cost overrun is reported at closure, but it says nothing about whether the system delivers its promised value.
wrong_explanations.C: Missing sign-off for two low-use reports is a documentation gap in a pre-go-live control, not the review's main question.
wrong_explanations.D: Learning-curve complaints are one input to benefits, not evidence of whether the business case targets were met.

tips: Eliminate: C is a minor gap in a pre-go-live control, and D is one user-experience input rather than the value the investment promised.
Final two: B beats A because MOST significant ranks findings by the review's purpose, which is value delivered against the business case; budget performance is secondary.
Exam cue: post-implementation reviews look back to the business case: did the promised benefits actually arrive?

questions.subtopic: SDLC Methodology Selection. Regulated vs Agile
questions.question: A health insurer's CIO wants Scrum-only delivery for a regulated claims platform that undergoes annual SOC 1 audits. Which approach should the IS auditor MOST recommend?

options.A: Pure Scrum, using sprint reviews as the audit evidence
options.B: Waterfall, with signed phase deliverables as audit evidence
options.C: Scrum, with a single compliance sign-off before final release
options.D: Hybrid agile with stage gates and signed, traceable requirements

questions.key_concept: Regulated projects can use agile delivery when stage gates, signed baselines and traceability give auditors the evidence they need.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the regulator and auditor need to see. Then look for the option that provides it without discarding agility.
questions.correct_explanation: A hybrid keeps agile delivery while adding the controls regulators and auditors rely on: stage gates, signed requirements baselines, traceability and controlled scope changes. Strict waterfall nearly wins: it produces strong evidence, but it assumes agile cannot be controlled and gives up delivery flexibility the organization values, when a hybrid can satisfy both needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Sprint reviews show working increments but leave no signed baselines or traceability. Auditors would lack evidence over requirements and changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Waterfall yields strong evidence but gives up the delivery flexibility the CIO wants, when agile with gates and baselines can satisfy regulators too.
wrong_explanations.C: One sign-off at the end gives no stage gates or traceability during delivery, so gaps surface when they are costliest to fix.

tips: Eliminate: A drops the traceability that regulated audits need, and C checks compliance once, at the end, when gaps are costliest to fix.
Final two: D beats B because a controlled hybrid meets evidence needs and keeps agility; waterfall needlessly sacrifices delivery flexibility.
Exam cue: in regulated agile projects, recommend adding gates and traceability to agile rather than abandoning agile.

questions.question: Four weeks before an ERP go-live, only 47% of user acceptance testing (UAT) cases have passed against agreed exit criteria. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate recommendation to the steering committee?

options.A: Ask the project manager to set revised exit criteria for go-live
options.B: Have the audit team re-execute the failed cases independently
options.C: Defer go-live until a further UAT cycle meets the exit criteria
options.D: Go live on schedule, moving failed cases to Phase 2

questions.key_concept: UAT exit criteria decide go-live readiness; the auditor recommends meeting them rather than moving failures to a later phase.
questions.pre_read: Compare the pass rate with the agreed criteria. Ask which option keeps the criteria meaningful and the auditor independent.
questions.correct_explanation: Agreed exit criteria are the control that decides readiness. With fewer than half the cases passed, the auditor should recommend deferring go-live until a further cycle meets them. Moving failed cases to Phase 2 is the tempting option: it meets the date, but it accepts large untested risk without meeting the agreed criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: Revising criteria can be legitimate, but the project manager owns the schedule, not acceptance; criteria reset by the delivery side mid-test no longer measure the business's agreed standard.
wrong_explanations.B: Executing tests is management's job. Audit performing them would impair independence and not fix the defects.
wrong_explanations.D: Carrying a few defects forward is normal with formal sign-off, but here the date is deciding; a deadline is a constraint, not evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because A lets the project manager reset criteria the business agreed, which defeats them, and B has the auditor perform testing that belongs to management.
Final two: C beats D because agreed exit criteria should decide readiness; going live on schedule accepts major untested risk.
Exam cue: when testing fails its exit criteria, the auditor recommends holding to the criteria, not shifting failures to a later phase.

questions.question: Hours before branches open, a core-banking cutover shows an unexplained $4.7M deposit variance; a tested fallback plan exists. What is the IS auditor's BEST advice?

options.A: Invoke the fallback plan and revert to the legacy system
options.B: Lock the affected accounts and open on the new platform
options.C: Post the variance to suspense and reconcile at month-end
options.D: Open on the new platform and investigate using live data

questions.key_concept: When cutover reconciliation shows an unexplained material variance, invoking the tested fallback plan protects data integrity and customers.
questions.pre_read: Note that the cause is unknown. Ask which option avoids relying on any data from the new platform.
questions.correct_explanation: A material variance with an unknown cause means the integrity of the new platform's balances cannot be trusted. The documented, tested fallback exists for exactly this situation. Locking affected accounts is the most tempting alternative: it contains part of the exposure, but with the root cause unknown the auditor cannot be sure other accounts are correct.

wrong_explanations.B: Locking only the visibly affected accounts assumes the problem is contained. With the root cause unknown, other balances may also be wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Clearing an unexplained variance to suspense hides an integrity failure. It also delays resolution until month-end.
wrong_explanations.D: Investigating with live transactions compounds bad balances and puts customers' funds at risk while the cause is unknown.

tips: Eliminate: C defers an unexplained variance to month-end, after customers have transacted on it, and D lets customers transact on data whose integrity is unproven.
Final two: A beats B because with the root cause unknown, only fallback protects all balances; locking assumes the problem is contained.
Exam cue: an unexplained material variance, no time left to diagnose and a tested fallback mean revert; with time and a known issue, assess at the gate first.

questions.subtopic: Major Release Governance Under Regulatory Deadline
questions.question: A release must meet a fixed regulatory deadline in five weeks, but two of nine new reports, neither required by the regulation, remain blocked in UAT. What should the IS auditor MOST appropriately recommend?

options.A: Deploy everything, excluding the blocked reports from UAT scope
options.B: Ship tested reports now, deferring blocked ones under risk acceptance
options.C: Adopt manual workarounds for the blocked reports as permanent controls
options.D: Halt the entire release until both blocked reports pass UAT

questions.key_concept: Under fixed deadlines, ship a fully tested scope subset and defer blocked items with documented risk acceptance; never skip testing silently.
questions.pre_read: Notice the deadline is fixed and only part of the scope is blocked. Ask which option keeps testing intact and still meets the date.
questions.correct_explanation: Splitting scope lets the organization meet the regulatory deadline with a subset that has fully passed UAT, while the blocked reports follow in a later release under formally documented risk acceptance. Halting everything comes closest: it protects quality, but it guarantees a missed fixed deadline when a fully tested subset could ship safely.

wrong_explanations.A: Silently dropping blocked items from test scope ships untested code and hides the gap from decision-makers.
wrong_explanations.C: Workarounds can bridge a short gap, but making them permanent replaces a designed control with an informal one.
wrong_explanations.D: Holding the whole release would win if the blocked reports were required by the regulation; optional scope should never hold a mandated date hostage.

tips: Eliminate: A ships untested code without disclosure, and C turns a temporary workaround into a permanent control.
Final two: B beats D because a fully tested subset meets the deadline with documented risk; halting everything misses it needlessly.
Exam cue: under a fixed deadline, reduce scope to what is fully tested and formally accept the residual risk, rather than skip testing.

questions.subtopic: Project Management Structures. Projectized vs Functional vs Matrix
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that, in a projectized organization, moving a developer to a critical project task waits weeks for approval. Who should the auditor expect to hold PRIMARY authority for this reassignment?

options.A: The developer's functional department manager
options.B: The resource manager in the project management office
options.C: The project manager leading the project team
options.D: The project sponsor who signed the project charter

questions.key_concept: In a projectized structure, team members report to the project manager, who has full authority over project resources.
questions.pre_read: Recall how authority differs across functional, matrix and projectized structures. Then separate sponsor duties from day-to-day control.
questions.correct_explanation: In a projectized structure, team members report to the project manager for the life of the project, so the auditor should expect the project manager to reassign them without outside approval. The sponsor is the tempting option: the sponsor authorizes the project and resolves escalations, but day-to-day assignment of team members is delegated to the project manager.

wrong_explanations.A: Functional managers control staff in functional and matrix structures. In a projectized structure, staff report to the project manager.
wrong_explanations.B: A central resource manager allocates pooled staff in matrix settings; in a projectized structure the project manager already controls the team.
wrong_explanations.D: A sponsor's mandate covers funding, scope and escalation, but the organization's structure, not seniority, decides who directs a project's people.

tips: Eliminate: A describes functional or matrix authority, and B describes a shared resource pool; in a projectized structure the team reports to the project manager.
Final two: C beats D because projectized structures give the project manager full resource authority; the sponsor handles escalations, not assignments.
Exam cue: projectized means the project manager controls resources; functional means department managers do; matrix splits authority.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds orders reaching processing with customer numbers that match no customer on file. Which control is MOST likely missing?

options.A: A range check on each customer number at entry
options.B: A check digit verified on each customer number at entry
options.C: A format check on each customer number's length and characters
options.D: An existence check against the customer master records

questions.key_concept: Each input edit catches a different defect: check digits catch keying errors, while existence checks confirm a referenced record actually exists.
questions.pre_read: Ask what exactly is wrong with the customer numbers. Then pick the edit that tests that defect.
questions.correct_explanation: A customer number can be in range and carry a valid check digit yet belong to no customer. Only an existence check, a lookup against the customer master records, rejects numbers that match no real customer before processing. The check digit is the tempting option: it catches keying errors such as transposed digits, but a well-formed number that was never issued still passes it.

wrong_explanations.A: A range check confirms the number falls within allowed limits; a number inside the range can still belong to no customer.
wrong_explanations.B: Check digits do stop most mistyped numbers at entry, yet form and existence are separate questions, and each input edit answers only one.
wrong_explanations.C: A format check confirms the number is well formed; a well-formed number can still match no customer on file.

tips: Eliminate: A tests the number's limits and C its format; neither confirms the customer exists.
Final two: D beats B because only a lookup against the master records proves the customer exists; a check digit tests the number's form.
Exam cue: match the edit to the defect: keying errors point to check digits, references to nothing point to existence checks.

questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing how quickly a software vendor can tell customers which products contain a newly disclosed library vulnerability. Which vendor artifact BEST supports this?

options.A: The vendor's vulnerability disclosure policy with its response time targets
options.B: A software bill of materials listing each component and version
options.C: An annual third-party penetration test of the vendor's products
options.D: Quarterly vulnerability scan reports for the vendor's hosting servers

questions.key_concept: An SBOM records each product's components, versions and dependencies so a vulnerable component can be traced to affected products quickly.
questions.pre_read: Ask which artifact links a component to the products that contain it, not which one finds weaknesses on servers.
questions.correct_explanation: An SBOM is a formal, machine-readable record of the components and versions in each product, so the vendor can query it and name affected releases within hours. A disclosure policy is the tempting option because it sets response-time targets, but it cannot tell the vendor which products contain the library, so the targets cannot be met.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would expect a disclosure policy as a vendor commitment, but a response promise is only as good as the inventory behind it.
wrong_explanations.C: An annual penetration test probes products for exploitable flaws at one point in time; it does not inventory the components inside each one.
wrong_explanations.D: Host scans assess the vendor's own infrastructure. They do not inventory libraries compiled into products shipped to customers.

tips: Eliminate: C tests products once a year without listing their components, and D scans the vendor's own servers, not the products it ships.
Final two: B beats A because a disclosure policy promises response times, but only an SBOM tells the vendor which products contain the library.
Exam cue: 'which products contain component X' is exactly the question an SBOM exists to answer.

questions.question: A threat model for a payment system flags repudiation: approvers could later deny approving a payment. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Encrypt stored approval records with keys held by the security team
options.B: Require stronger multi-factor authentication when approvers sign in
options.C: Keep tamper-evident logs tying each approval to its approver
options.D: Require a second approver for each payment above a set amount

questions.key_concept: STRIDE's Repudiation covers actions users can deny; tamper-evident logs tied to authenticated identities provide non-repudiation.
questions.pre_read: Name the property repudiation threatens. Ask which control leaves proof of who did what.
questions.correct_explanation: Repudiation is the threat that a user denies an action and the system cannot prove otherwise. The control that answers it is a tamper-evident record tying each approval to the individual who made it. Stronger sign-in authentication is the tempting option: it proves who opened the session, but without a protected record of each action the approver can still dispute the payment.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects the confidentiality of the records; it does not prove which individual approved a payment.
wrong_explanations.B: Sign-in strength answers spoofing, a different STRIDE threat; match each STRIDE threat to its own control family.
wrong_explanations.D: Dual approval reduces the chance of a fraudulent payment, but either approver could still deny acting; it creates no proof of who approved.

tips: Eliminate: A protects confidentiality, but repudiation is an accountability threat that secrecy cannot answer. D is dual control, which guards against one person's fraud rather than a later denial.
Final two: C beats B because the gap is evidence of the action, which logging supplies; authentication alone proves only who signed in.
Exam cue: in STRIDE, repudiation is answered by tamper-evident action records tied to individuals; spoofing is answered by authentication.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the feasibility study for a major enterprise resource planning (ERP) investment assesses technical fit and cost-benefit in depth. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add a sensitivity analysis of the cost and benefit estimates
options.B: Have the ERP vendor confirm the study's technical findings
options.C: Add vendor stability, licensing and ongoing support costs to the study
options.D: Extend the study to operational, legal and schedule feasibility

questions.key_concept: A complete feasibility study covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule dimensions before the go/no-go decision.
questions.pre_read: List the feasibility dimensions a go/no-go decision needs. Then check which ones this study covers.
questions.correct_explanation: A go/no-go decision needs every feasibility dimension: technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule. Any one can sink a technically sound, profitable project, so the missing dimensions should be studied before approval. A sensitivity analysis is the tempting option because it makes the economic case more rigorous, but it deepens a dimension already covered and leaves operational, legal and schedule risks unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: Sensitivity analysis stress-tests the cost and benefit estimates, a dimension already covered; operational, legal and schedule risks stay unexamined.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's confirmation is not independent, and technical fit is the dimension the study already covers in depth.
wrong_explanations.C: Licensing and support costs belong to the economic dimension the study already covers, and vendor stability is a supplier-selection check; operational, legal and schedule feasibility stay unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor to confirm a dimension already covered, and C adds costs the economic study covers plus a supplier-selection check, not a missing dimension.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is missing dimensions; a sensitivity analysis only stress-tests the economic case already studied.
Exam cue: close feasibility gaps before approval, and remember TELOS: technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how a PMO compares development productivity across teams using Java, COBOL and a low-code platform. Which sizing measure is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Function points counted from user-visible functional requirements
options.B: Story points estimated by each team during sprint planning
options.C: Lines of code delivered per developer each month
options.D: Number of source files committed in each release

questions.key_concept: Function point analysis sizes software by delivered functionality, making it language-independent and usable for cross-platform comparison and early estimates.
questions.pre_read: Note the mixed technologies. Ask which measure stays comparable when languages and teams differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Function points measure functional size from what users see, independent of language, so Java, COBOL and low-code teams can be compared on the same scale. Story points are useful for a team's own planning, but each team calibrates them differently, so they cannot support cross-team productivity comparisons.

wrong_explanations.B: Story points do size work within one team, but comparing teams needs a unit no team defines for itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Lines of code depend on language; COBOL and low-code platforms produce very different counts for the same function.
wrong_explanations.D: File counts reflect how code is organized, not delivered functionality, and vary widely across languages and platforms.

tips: Eliminate: C and D count code artifacts, which vary by language and platform for the same function.
Final two: A beats B because function points follow a standard counting method, while story points are calibrated differently by each team.
Exam cue: comparing across languages, or sizing before code exists, points to function point analysis.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a support team's urgent fixes either wait for the next two-week sprint or skip sprint planning. Which delivery method should the auditor consider the MOST suitable fit?

options.A: Scrum, adding each urgent fix to the current sprint on arrival
options.B: Kanban, with work-in-progress limits and pull-based flow
options.C: Scrum, with shorter one-week sprints and sprint commitments
options.D: Waterfall releases, with an emergency change path for urgent fixes

questions.key_concept: Kanban fits continuous, variable-priority work through pull-based flow and WIP limits; Scrum fits time-boxed iterative product development.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the work arrives and what happens to urgent items. Ask which method keeps them inside the process.
questions.correct_explanation: Kanban suits work that arrives continuously: items are pulled when capacity frees up, so urgent fixes enter the process instead of waiting or going around it, and work-in-progress limits keep the flow controlled. Shorter sprints are the tempting option, but they still batch work into fixed commitments, so an urgent fix must still wait days or break the sprint.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding fixes mid-sprint breaks the sprint commitment each time and turns the current bypass of sprint planning into policy.
wrong_explanations.C: Shorter sprints would win if urgent fixes could wait a few days; a delivery method follows the shape of demand, not the planning calendar.
wrong_explanations.D: Emergency change is meant for genuine emergencies; sending routine support work through it overloads that path and weakens control, while releases still batch other work.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks the sprint commitment whenever a fix arrives, and D sends routine support work through the emergency path meant for true emergencies.
Final two: B beats C because pull-based flow lets urgent work enter the process; shorter sprints still batch work into commitments.
Exam cue: continuous, interrupt-driven work points to Kanban; when urgent work goes around a process, fix the fit so it stays inside the control.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that pipeline scan findings sit unresolved for months, although the security team logs and triages each one. Which change BEST reflects DevSecOps practice?

options.A: Have the security team fix findings in a central queue
options.B: Add open findings to the monthly security report to management
options.C: Feed findings into team backlogs with severity-based fix deadlines
options.D: Commission an annual penetration test to confirm which findings matter

questions.key_concept: DevSecOps makes security a shared responsibility: scan findings go into delivery teams' backlogs with severity-based fix deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns a security finding in DevSecOps, and how it reaches the people who can fix it.
questions.correct_explanation: DevSecOps makes security a shared responsibility: findings flow into the delivery team's own backlog, are prioritized like other work and must be fixed within severity-based deadlines, so the people who wrote the code fix it. Central fixing by the security team is the strongest alternative: it gets findings addressed, but it keeps security outside the team, creates a bottleneck and leaves developers repeating the same flaws.

wrong_explanations.A: A central remediation team is a recognized stopgap when findings pile up, but in DevSecOps each delivery team owns the flaws its code creates.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting raises visibility, but findings still sit outside the teams who must fix them, so the delay continues.
wrong_explanations.D: An annual test is periodic and late. It does not change who owns findings or how quickly they are fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B reports findings to management without changing who fixes them, and D adds a late, periodic test that does not change ownership.
Final two: C beats A because DevSecOps makes the delivery team own and fix its flaws, rather than routing them to a central bottleneck.
Exam cue: in DevSecOps questions, prefer the option that puts security work inside the team's normal workflow.

questions.question: Before UAT starts on a new billing system, an IS auditor reviews the acceptance criteria. Which attribute provides the MOST assurance that the criteria are well formed?

options.A: Measurable criteria agreed by the business owner before testing
options.B: Criteria approved by the QA owner and traced to technical design
options.C: Criteria drafted by developers from their own build decisions
options.D: Code-coverage and unit-test pass rates used as exit thresholds

questions.key_concept: Well-formed UAT criteria are measurable, tied to business requirements, agreed by the business owner and fixed before testing starts.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns acceptance and what the system is being tested against: business requirements or the technical build.
questions.correct_explanation: UAT confirms the system meets business needs, so its criteria must be measurable, agreed by the business owner and fixed before testing begins. QA approval with traceability to the technical design nearly wins: it shows rigor, but it validates against how the system was built rather than what the business required, and the business owner has not accepted the criteria.

wrong_explanations.B: Tracing to the technical design tests what was built, not what the business needs. Without business-owner agreement, acceptance lacks its proper owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Developers defining criteria from their own build choices removes independence; the system is judged against itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Coverage and unit-test rates measure developer testing. They say nothing about whether business requirements are met.

tips: Eliminate: C lets the builders judge their own work, and D applies developer-testing metrics to a business test.
Final two: A beats B because acceptance belongs to the business owner against requirements; QA tracing to design checks what was built.
Exam cue: UAT criteria are business-owned, testable and set before execution; design- or code-based criteria are the wrong test level.

questions.question: A QA manager reports 95 percent code coverage on a payments module, yet defects keep reaching production. Which evidence would BEST show the IS auditor how effective the test suite is?

options.A: A coverage report showing 100 percent of statements executed by tests
options.B: A count of automated tests passing on each build
options.C: A count of defects found in system testing before release
options.D: A mutation score showing how many seeded faults the tests detect

questions.key_concept: Mutation testing measures test-suite effectiveness by checking whether tests catch deliberately injected faults; coverage only shows what code ran.
questions.pre_read: Separate 'code was executed' from 'a fault would be detected'. Ask which technique measures the second.
questions.correct_explanation: A mutation score measures effectiveness directly: small faults are seeded into the code, and the share the tests catch shows whether they check results. Full statement coverage is the tempting option, but coverage only shows which lines ran; tests can execute every line with weak assertions, which is exactly why defects escape despite 95 percent coverage.

wrong_explanations.A: More coverage shows more lines executed, not that tests check results; high coverage with weak assertions already explains the escapes.
wrong_explanations.B: A passing count shows activity, not strength; weak tests pass easily, so green builds can coexist with escaping defects.
wrong_explanations.C: Defect counts depend on code quality and tester effort; a low count cannot show whether the automated suite would catch faults.

tips: Eliminate: B counts tests that pass, which weak tests do easily, and C counts defects, which depends on code quality, not test strength.
Final two: D beats A because mutation scores show whether tests catch faults, while coverage only shows which lines ran.
Exam cue: high coverage plus escaped defects signals weak assertions; mutation testing measures what the tests actually verify.

questions.question: A bank's customer web application passes its pre-release security testing, yet attackers keep exploiting new flaws in production before patches ship. Which control should the IS auditor recommend adding in the next release as BEST?

options.A: Static application security testing of source code at each commit
options.B: Runtime application self-protection within the live application
options.C: Interactive application security testing during QA test runs
options.D: Quarterly penetration tests of the production application

questions.key_concept: SAST reads code, DAST and IAST test running apps before release, and RASP protects the app from inside in production.
questions.pre_read: Note when the attacks happen. Ask which control blocks attacks in production rather than only finding weaknesses.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap is protection while flaws are exploited in production. Runtime application self-protection (RASP) runs inside the live application, sees how each request is handled and can block an attack before a patch ships. Interactive testing (IAST) is the tempting option because it also instruments running code, but it runs during QA to find flaws before release; it cannot stop live attacks.

wrong_explanations.A: SAST analyzes code before it runs. It finds coding flaws early but cannot see or block attacks in production.
wrong_explanations.C: IAST instruments the application during QA testing to find vulnerabilities. It is a pre-release testing tool, not production protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Periodic penetration tests find weaknesses at a point in time; they report flaws but block nothing between tests.

tips: Eliminate: A reads code that is not running, and D tests periodically; both find weaknesses, but neither blocks an attack in production.
Final two: B beats C because RASP protects live traffic in production, while IAST instruments the code only during testing.
Exam cue: SAST and IAST find flaws before release; RASP protects from inside in production.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that teams release to production every week, but long-lived feature branches are merged into the main branch only once a quarter. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Integration defects surface late, in large batches hard to trace
options.B: Quarterly merges create review backlogs that delay approval of changes
options.C: Weekly releases leave too little time for user acceptance testing
options.D: Code on long-lived branches is not scanned until it merges

questions.key_concept: Long-lived branches defer integration, so defects surface late and in large batches; trunk-based development merges small changes at least daily.
questions.pre_read: Ask how often the work is integrated. Then separate the root risk from its symptoms.
questions.correct_explanation: Deferring integration for a quarter lets months of changes collide at once, so conflicts and integration defects surface late, in large batches whose cause is hard to trace. The review backlog is the tempting option, but it is a symptom of the same practice; the root risk to release quality is the late, large-batch integration.

wrong_explanations.B: Review backlogs and late defects share one cause, the quarterly merge, though risks rank by harm to production, not by process friction.
wrong_explanations.C: Weekly releases are common with automated testing; the risk comes from how rarely work is integrated, not how often it ships.
wrong_explanations.D: Late scanning is a real gap, but branch code is still scanned when it merges, before release; the larger risk is how rarely the branches integrate.

tips: Eliminate: C blames release frequency, which automated pipelines support safely, and D worries about scan timing, though branch code is still scanned at merge, before release.
Final two: A beats B because late, large-batch integration is the root risk; the review backlog is one symptom of it.
Exam cue: the longer code waits to integrate, the larger and later the defects; continuous integration merges small changes at least daily.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that only container images built by the organization's own pipeline run in production. Which control provides the BEST assurance?

options.A: Weekly antivirus scans of images running in production
options.B: TLS encryption on each connection to the image registry
options.C: Deployments restricted to a single approved private registry
options.D: Image signing at build, with signature checks before deployment

questions.key_concept: Signing images at build and verifying signatures before deployment proves an image's origin and that it was not altered.
questions.pre_read: Ask which control proves who built the image, rather than where it is stored or how it travels.
questions.correct_explanation: Signing each image in the build pipeline and having the cluster verify the signature before scheduling proves both who built the image and that it has not changed since. Restricting pulls to one approved registry is the closest choice: it narrows the source, but anyone able to push to that registry could place an altered image there.

wrong_explanations.A: Antivirus finds known malware. It cannot show where an image was built or detect subtle unauthorized changes.
wrong_explanations.B: TLS protects images in transit. It does not prove who built the image or that it was unaltered at the source.
wrong_explanations.C: A single registry narrows the source, but an image pushed there through a compromised account would still deploy unverified.

tips: Eliminate: A detects only known malware, and B protects the connection, not the image itself.
Final two: D beats C because a verified signature proves origin and integrity, while a trusted registry only trusts a storage location.
Exam cue: provenance questions want cryptographic signing at build plus verification at deployment.

questions.question: A team will deploy new cloud servers next month to host a migrated claims system. What should the IS auditor verify FIRST before production data is loaded?

options.A: That monitoring and alerting are configured for the new servers
options.B: That the new servers are tagged in the asset inventory
options.C: That the servers are configured to the approved security baseline
options.D: That load testing has confirmed enough capacity for peak claims volume

questions.key_concept: Verify target infrastructure against its approved security baseline before production data is migrated into it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what is put at risk the moment real data lands in the new environment.
questions.correct_explanation: Once production data is loaded, any misconfiguration exposes real customer information, so the target infrastructure must first be verified against the approved security baseline, covering hardening, access and network rules. Load testing comes closest: capacity matters before go-live, but it can be proven with test data, while an insecure environment puts claims data at risk the moment it arrives.

wrong_explanations.A: Monitoring detects problems once the system runs; it does not stop a misconfigured server from exposing data loaded into it.
wrong_explanations.B: Inventory tagging supports asset management and can be completed before go-live; it does not protect the data being loaded.
wrong_explanations.D: Capacity must be proven before go-live, but load tests can use test data. Security must be in place before real data arrives.

tips: Eliminate: A sets up detection rather than secure configuration, and B is asset record-keeping; neither protects data the moment it lands.
Final two: C beats D because real data must not land in an unverified environment; capacity can be proven with test data.
Exam cue: before real data enters any new environment, verify its security configuration first; capacity, monitoring and records can follow.

questions.question: Halfway through the quarter, a customer-facing service with an agreed error-budget policy has used its entire error budget. Which release response should the IS auditor expect management to take FIRST?

options.A: Re-measure the SLO over a longer window before changing releases
options.B: Freeze non-essential releases and prioritize reliability work
options.C: Keep releasing, using canary rollouts and extra production monitoring
options.D: Add on-call engineers and continue the planned release schedule

questions.key_concept: When an error budget is exhausted, non-essential releases stop and reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an error budget is for: it decides when the team may keep shipping features and when it must stop.
questions.correct_explanation: An exhausted error budget means users have already absorbed the agreed amount of unreliability. The agreed policy response is to freeze non-essential changes and spend engineering effort on reliability until the budget recovers. Canary rollouts with extra monitoring reduce the risk of each release, but they still spend reliability the service no longer has and sidestep the agreed policy.

wrong_explanations.A: A longer window can look like better analysis, but changing how the SLO is measured after the budget runs out delays the agreed response and hides the reliability problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Safer rollout methods reduce per-release risk but still add change to a service that has used up its tolerance for failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra on-call staff speed recovery from failures, but the agreed policy pauses non-essential change once the budget is spent; releasing on schedule keeps spending reliability already used up.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because A changes how the SLO is measured after the budget runs out, and D keeps the release schedule that the agreed policy pauses.
Final two: B beats C because the policy for an exhausted budget is to stop non-essential change, not to release more carefully.
Exam cue: once the error budget is spent, feature releases pause and reliability work takes priority until it recovers.

questions.question: A bank will replace its core platform across six business units with very different processes. Which cutover approach should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Phased rollout by business unit, one wave at a time
options.B: Big-bang cutover over one weekend, avoiding temporary interfaces
options.C: Module-by-module cutover applied to the six units at once
options.D: Pilot in the smallest unit, then big-bang the remaining five together

questions.key_concept: Phased cutover suits complex, multi-unit replacements because staged waves limit blast radius and allow mid-course correction.
questions.pre_read: Weigh complexity and impact. Ask how many units a single failure would hit under each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: With six units and very different processes, a phased rollout limits the blast radius of any failure to one unit and lets lessons from early waves correct later ones. A pilot followed by a single cutover limits early risk, but the remaining five units, each with different processes, would still go live together, so one failure would hit most of the bank.

wrong_explanations.B: Big-bang suits simpler, lower-risk replacements. Here a single failure would hit all six units at once with no chance to adjust.
wrong_explanations.C: Phasing by module still moves all six very different units together for each module, so one module's failure hits the whole bank.
wrong_explanations.D: A pilot reduces early risk, but moving the other five very different units in one step still exposes most of the bank to a single failure.

tips: Eliminate: B exposes all six units to one weekend's failure, and C phases by module but still moves all six different units at once.
Final two: A beats D because a pilot tests only one unit; the five very different remaining units would still fail together.
Exam cue: complex, multi-unit, high-impact replacements point to phased cutover; small, low-risk systems suit big-bang.

questions.question: At month 8 of a 14-month ERP project, the PMO reports a cumulative CPI of 0.78 and SPI of 0.85; the team says recent rebaselining will fix this. What should the IS auditor conclude FIRST?

options.A: Performance is within tolerance for a complex ERP rollout
options.B: A conclusion should wait until rebaselined figures mature
options.C: Earned value analysis cannot yet predict outcomes at this stage
options.D: Cost and schedule are materially behind and need corrective action

questions.key_concept: Cumulative CPI and SPI well below 1.0 at mid-project signal material variance that rarely self-corrects and needs corrective action.
questions.pre_read: CPI (cost performance index) and SPI (schedule performance index) compare earned value with actual cost and planned value; below 1.0 means behind.
questions.correct_explanation: Cumulative indices of 0.78 and 0.85 at month 8 mean the project earns 78 cents of value per dollar spent and is 15% behind plan; cumulative CPI rarely recovers much after mid-project. The auditor should report a material variance needing action. Waiting for rebaselined data sounds prudent, but rebaselining resets the yardstick without fixing performance and delays the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: A CPI of 0.78 is well below accepted tolerance. Calling it normal for ERP hides a material overrun.
wrong_explanations.B: Rebaselining changes the plan, not the performance. Waiting delays corrective action while costs keep overrunning.
wrong_explanations.C: By mid-project, cumulative earned value indices are reliable predictors; cumulative CPI tends to stabilize early.

tips: Eliminate: A treats earning only 78 cents of value per dollar spent as normal, and C wrongly claims earned value analysis cannot predict at mid-project.
Final two: D beats B because rebaselining resets the yardstick but does not fix performance; waiting only delays corrective action.
Exam cue: CPI or SPI well below 1.0 past the midpoint signals real variance; a rebaseline resets the plan, never the performance, so it cannot explain variance away.

questions.question: A fraud-detection model's false-positive rate has risen from 4% to 11% in eight months; its go-live plan did not cover monitoring. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Retrain the model on the most recent eight months of data
options.B: Raise the alert threshold and monitor false positives weekly
options.C: Put the model under lifecycle governance with drift thresholds
options.D: Assign an independent validation team to revalidate the model now

questions.key_concept: Production ML needs lifecycle governance: an accountable owner, drift monitoring, retraining triggers and performance gates.
questions.pre_read: Separate the symptom (rising errors) from the cause. Ask why the decline went unmanaged for eight months.
questions.correct_explanation: The rising false-positive rate is a symptom; the root cause is that monitoring was never planned, so drift (accuracy falling as real data changes) went unaddressed for eight months. Lifecycle governance, with an accountable owner, drift thresholds and retraining triggers, keeps the model reliable over time. An independent revalidation is the tempting option, but it checks only today's model; revalidation belongs inside the lifecycle.

wrong_explanations.A: Retraining may correct today's drift, but an unvalidated retrained model is an uncontrolled change, and with no monitoring in place the next drift goes unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: A higher threshold cuts false positives but lets more fraud through; watching the rate weekly does not address why the model drifts.
wrong_explanations.D: Revalidation checks today's model, but without ongoing monitoring, drift thresholds or retraining triggers, the next degradation would again go unmanaged.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains and redeploys without validation, itself an uncontrolled model change, and B trades false positives for missed fraud.
Final two: C beats D because governance keeps catching drift as it happens, while a one-time revalidation only checks today's model.
Exam cue: when a symptom comes with a missing control framework, recommend the framework, not the one-time fix.
