questions.subtopic: Open-Source License Risk. Strong Copyleft (GPL) in SaaS
questions.question: Before investor due diligence, an IS auditor finds core SaaS modules import an AGPL-licensed library, which counsel warns may force source disclosure. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Isolate or replace the AGPL code and scan licenses before merging
options.B: Commission a second legal opinion on the AGPL exposure
options.C: Add the AGPL notice to the product's third-party license file
options.D: Disclose the AGPL use in the data room and defer remediation

questions.key_concept: Open-source license risk is managed by tracking licenses, scanning before merge and isolating strong-copyleft components.
questions.pre_read: Notice counsel has already flagged the risk. Ask which option reduces exposure now and keeps new copyleft code out.
questions.correct_explanation: Counsel has already flagged a real disclosure risk, so the sound response reduces exposure now: isolate the copyleft component behind a service boundary or replace it, and scan licenses before code is merged, which also stops new issues entering. A second legal opinion nearly wins: it may refine the legal view, but it reduces no exposure and adds no ongoing control, whatever it concludes.

wrong_explanations.B: A second opinion would win if counsel's advice were in doubt; once a credible warning stands, treatment begins while analysis continues.
wrong_explanations.C: License notices satisfy attribution terms, but the AGPL's obligation is to offer source to network users; a notice reduces no exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Disclosure is transparent and may be expected, but deferring remediation leaves the exposure in place and new copyleft code can still enter.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a notice, which meets attribution terms but not the AGPL's source obligation, and D discloses the risk but defers reducing it.
Final two: A beats B because counsel has already flagged the risk; reducing exposure and blocking new copyleft code beats refining the legal view.
Exam cue: once a qualified expert has flagged a risk, prefer a control that reduces it over seeking yet another opinion.

questions.question: Twelve weeks before a payments-platform cutover, the CIO plans one technical-only mock conversion three weeks before go-live. What should the IS auditor recommend to the cutover risk committee as BEST?

options.A: One full end-to-end rehearsal in the final week before go-live
options.B: Staged rehearsals adding business steps, each reviewed before the next
options.C: Rely on the documented playbook, since rehearsal repeats steps already known
options.D: Run the technical rehearsal and test business steps after go-live

questions.key_concept: High-stakes cutovers need staged rehearsals covering technical and business steps, each reviewed, with time left to fix issues.
questions.pre_read: Check two things: does the rehearsal cover business steps, and is there time to fix what it finds?
questions.correct_explanation: A high-volume payments cutover needs rehearsals that cover technical and business procedures and leave time to fix what they reveal. Staged cycles, technical first, then end-to-end with business teams, then a dry run, each followed by a review, achieve that. One full rehearsal a week out is realistic, but any serious issue it finds leaves no time to correct.

wrong_explanations.A: A single late rehearsal tests the right scope, but leaves no time to fix problems before go-live.
wrong_explanations.C: A playbook that has never been exercised is unproven. Rehearsals find gaps in timing, hand-offs and procedures that documents hide.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing business procedures after go-live exposes live payments to untested operational steps during the riskiest period.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts an unexercised playbook, and D leaves business procedures untested until after go-live.
Final two: B beats A because staged cycles leave time to fix what each rehearsal finds; one late rehearsal leaves none.
Exam cue: for high-stakes cutovers, rehearse early, rehearse more than once, and include business processes.

questions.subtopic: Project Lifecycle Phases. PMBOK Process Groups
questions.question: A project plan maps the five PMI process groups one-to-one onto five sequential SDLC phases. What should the IS auditor identify as the MOST significant control weakness?

options.A: Monitoring and controlling would run once, not across every phase
options.B: Planning would not be revisited as later phases add detail
options.C: Executing could not begin until planning had fully finished
options.D: Initiating would happen before requirements are fully known

questions.key_concept: PMI process groups are not SDLC phases; they repeat within each phase, and monitoring and controlling runs throughout the project.
questions.pre_read: Distinguish project management process groups from SDLC phases, and ask which group must operate continuously.
questions.correct_explanation: Process groups are not phases: they interact and repeat within every phase, and monitoring and controlling runs throughout to catch cost, schedule and scope variances. Confining it to one phase leaves the rest of the project without oversight. Revisiting planning is the closest concern: progressive elaboration matters, but missing oversight is the greater control gap because variances would go undetected.

wrong_explanations.B: Planning does recur as detail emerges, but uncontrolled variance across most phases is the larger governance risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for planning to finish slows delivery, but it is an efficiency issue; it does not leave the project without oversight.
wrong_explanations.D: Initiating is meant to come first, authorizing the project before detailed requirements are elaborated; that is normal, not a weakness.

tips: Eliminate: C is a delivery-speed issue rather than a control gap, and D describes initiating doing its normal job before detailed requirements exist.
Final two: A beats B because oversight that runs only once lets variances go undetected, a greater gap than a stale plan.
Exam cue: process groups overlap and repeat within phases; monitoring and controlling never stops until closure.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that batch totals for payroll records differ between the input file and the processed output. Which control objective is MOST directly at risk?

options.A: Authorization of payroll changes before they are entered
options.B: Validity of payroll records as entered at input
options.C: Completeness and accuracy of data through processing
options.D: Integrity of the payroll master file between pay runs

questions.key_concept: Data integrity controls keep data complete, accurate, valid and unaltered from input through processing to output.
questions.pre_read: Ask where between input and output the totals stopped matching.
questions.correct_explanation: Batch totals are an integrity control: when input and output totals differ, records were lost, duplicated or altered during processing, so completeness and accuracy through processing are at risk. Validity at input is the tempting option because the stem mentions the input file, but the input total is the reference point; the difference arose after it, during processing.

wrong_explanations.A: Authorization concerns whether a change was approved before entry; unapproved records would sit in both totals, so a mismatch does not point to it.
wrong_explanations.B: Input validity is a genuine control objective, yet a mismatch belongs between the last point where totals agree and the first where they part.
wrong_explanations.D: Standing master data between runs is a separate concern; the mismatch is between this run's input file and its output, so the loss arose in processing.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns approval before entry and D concerns standing data between runs; batch totals compare this run's input with its output.
Final two: C beats B because the input total is the baseline; a difference between input and output arises during processing.
Exam cue: control totals, hash totals and record counts protect integrity: complete, accurate, valid data from input to output.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the closure plan for a project whose new system is live and formally accepted by the sponsor. Which planned activity BEST belongs in formal project closure?

options.A: Run a final penetration test before declaring the project closed
options.B: Release resources, close project accounts and archive records
options.C: Measure realized business benefits before closing the project
options.D: Keep the project open to fix defects during the warranty period

questions.key_concept: Project closure releases resources, completes financial closeout, archives records and captures lessons after formal acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Separate what ends the project now from what can only be measured after months of live operation.
questions.correct_explanation: Formal closure follows acceptance: the project releases staff and contracts, completes financial closeout and archives records so it stops consuming resources. Closure schedules the post-implementation review and records lessons learned; the review itself comes later. Measuring benefits before closing is the tempting option, but benefits take months of live operation to appear, so measuring them is not a closure step.

wrong_explanations.A: Security testing belongs before go-live and acceptance; testing after acceptance is an operational activity, not a closure step.
wrong_explanations.C: Benefit measurement shares closure's aim of accounting for what was delivered, though projects close on outputs while the business owns and measures outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Warranty defects are handled through the support or vendor contract; holding the project open keeps consuming its budget and team.

tips: Eliminate: A places security testing after acceptance, when it belongs before go-live, and D treats warranty support as project work instead of an operational or contract activity.
Final two: B beats C because closure releases resources and schedules the benefits review; benefits can only be measured months after closure.
Exam cue: closure means release, close out, archive and learn; benefits realization is measured later, after operations stabilize.

questions.question: Three closed projects each held a lessons-learned workshop, yet all repeated the same vendor-onboarding delays. Which practice should the IS auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Keep a searchable lessons repository reviewed at project start
options.B: Hold a detailed lessons workshop when each project ends
options.C: Add a lessons-learned sign-off step to the project closure checklist
options.D: Invite the vendor to each lessons-learned workshop

questions.key_concept: Lessons learned capture what worked and what did not, and add value only when future projects can find and apply them.
questions.pre_read: The same problem recurring is the clue. Ask whether the gap is capturing lessons or reusing them.
questions.correct_explanation: The same delay recurring across three projects shows lessons are being captured but not reused. Value comes when lessons are stored where others can find them and consulted at initiation and planning. More thorough end-of-project workshops come closest, but better capture alone does not change what the next project does if no one reads the lessons.

wrong_explanations.B: Workshops capture lessons, which appears to happen already. The repeated delays show the gap is reuse at project start.
wrong_explanations.C: A sign-off proves lessons were captured at closure, which already happens; it does not make the next project consult them.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor input may sharpen the onboarding lessons, but they are still captured at closure and not reused at the next start.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a sign-off and D adds a participant at closure; neither puts lessons in front of the next project.
Final two: A beats B because the repeated problem shows lessons are not reused; a more detailed workshop is still only capture.
Exam cue: lessons learned only count when future projects consult them; look for the option that feeds them forward.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a regulator learned of a rollout's reporting change from a press release, although executives and end users were briefed. What should the auditor recommend as the MOST important communication control?

options.A: Add the regulator to the steering committee's weekly status report
options.B: Brief the regulator directly before each future release
options.C: Analyze stakeholders by influence and interest, then tailor updates
options.D: Publish status, risks and decisions on a self-service dashboard

questions.key_concept: Effective project communication starts with stakeholder analysis by influence and interest, then tailors content, format and frequency to each group.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the regulator was missed, not only who was missed. Then look for the fix that would have caught it.
questions.correct_explanation: Stakeholder analysis comes first: groups differ in influence and interest, so content, format and frequency should be planned for each, and a high-influence regulator should have been identified and informed directly. Briefing the regulator before each release is the tempting option because it fixes the gap found, but without analysis the next high-influence group can be missed the same way.

wrong_explanations.A: The committee's report is written for governance decisions; the regulator needs different content and timing, and other high-influence groups may still be missed.
wrong_explanations.B: Briefing the regulator fixes this one gap, but without stakeholder analysis other high-influence groups can still be missed.
wrong_explanations.D: A dashboard is passive. It cannot confirm that high-influence stakeholders saw, understood or acted on the information relevant to them.

tips: Eliminate: A sends the regulator a report built for the committee, though groups need different content and frequency, and D is passive, so no one confirms key groups received it.
Final two: C beats B because briefing the regulator fixes the one gap found; stakeholder analysis finds every high-influence group before another is missed.
Exam cue: when one stakeholder was missed, fix the process that identifies stakeholders, not only the one gap.

questions.question: A program's business case was approved two years ago; costs have since risen 40% while expected benefits have fallen. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Continue as approved and track costs and benefits monthly
options.B: Cancel the program now to stop further cost overruns
options.C: Commission an independent estimate of the remaining cost to complete
options.D: Resubmit the updated business case for an investment decision

questions.key_concept: A business case is a living document: when costs or benefits change materially, update it and have sponsors re-approve the investment.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decision makers need before choosing to continue or stop, and who makes that choice.
questions.correct_explanation: A business case is a living document: when costs and benefits shift materially, it should be updated and put back to the sponsors so they judge continued investment on current facts. An independent cost-to-complete estimate is a tempting check, but benefits have fallen too, and an estimate refines one input without putting the decision back to the sponsors.

wrong_explanations.A: Monitoring shows the gap widening, but spending continues on a two-year-old approval; no one re-decides whether to continue.
wrong_explanations.B: The case may no longer hold, but canceling before updating it acts on incomplete analysis, and sponsors make that call.
wrong_explanations.C: An auditor would value an independent estimate as stronger evidence, but evidence feeds a decision and never stands in for one.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps spending on a two-year-old approval that no longer reflects the facts, and B cancels before the case is updated, a call that belongs to the sponsors.
Final two: D beats C because costs and benefits have both moved; a cost estimate refines one input but does not put the decision back to the sponsors.
Exam cue: when costs or benefits change materially, revisit the business case and have sponsors re-approve before more is spent.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a Scrum team keeps no design documentation, saying working software is its documentation. What should the auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Record design and control decisions well enough for maintenance
options.B: Produce full design documents before each sprint begins
options.C: Accept the practice, since agile values working software
options.D: Rely on code comments in place of separate design documents

questions.key_concept: Agile favors just-enough documentation, not none: design and control decisions must be recorded well enough for maintenance and audit.
questions.pre_read: Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation. Ask whether that means no documentation.
questions.correct_explanation: Agile favors working software over comprehensive documentation, but not over none: the team should record design decisions, control-relevant logic and interfaces at the level needed for maintenance, support and audit. Relying on code comments is the most tempting alternative: comments help developers, but they rarely explain architecture, control decisions or why choices were made, and non-developers cannot use them.

wrong_explanations.B: Heavy design documents every sprint undermine agile delivery and quickly go stale. The need is proportionate, not exhaustive.
wrong_explanations.C: Agile values documentation less, not at nothing. Unrecorded design decisions hurt maintenance and control assurance.
wrong_explanations.D: Comments explain lines of code, but not architecture or control decisions, and non-developers cannot use them.

tips: Eliminate: B imposes heavy upfront documents that defeat agile delivery, and C reads less documentation as none.
Final two: A beats D because design and control decisions need a recorded home; code comments explain code, not decisions.
Exam cue: in agile audits, expect just-enough documentation that still supports maintenance, control and audit.

questions.question: API releases repeatedly break partner integrations. Which practice should the IS auditor recommend as BEST to prevent this?

options.A: Emailing partners a week before deploying any breaking change
options.B: Running consumer contract tests in the provider's pipeline before deploying
options.C: A shared staging environment where partners can test before each release
options.D: Full regression of the provider's own test suite before each release

questions.key_concept: API breaking changes are prevented by running consumer contract tests in the provider's pipeline before deployment, with versioning as a migration path.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word prevent. Separate options that stop the break before release from those that warn about or react to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Consumer-driven contract tests run in the provider's pipeline check each change against what partners actually rely on, so a breaking change is caught before it is deployed. A shared staging environment helps partners find breaks early, but it depends on every partner testing every release; nothing in the provider's pipeline blocks a breaking change.

wrong_explanations.A: Notice informs but does not prevent. Partners who miss the email or cannot migrate in time still break on release day.
wrong_explanations.C: Staging and contract tests both aim to catch breaks before release; preventing one, though, is the job of whoever makes the change.
wrong_explanations.D: The provider's own tests check its intended behavior, not what each partner relies on, so changes that break consumers still pass.

tips: Eliminate: A only warns partners, and D tests the provider's own expectations rather than what consumers rely on.
Final two: B beats C because contract tests in the provider's pipeline block a breaking change, while staging depends on every partner testing every release.
Exam cue: to PREVENT a failure, prefer a control that tests before release over one that communicates or reacts.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the reconciliation tolerances proposed to decide cutover after a parallel run. Which basis for the tolerances should the auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Zero tolerance, investigating every variance before cutover proceeds
options.B: One materiality threshold for balances, rates and reference data
options.C: Tolerances the migration vendor used on its past projects
options.D: Per-category thresholds based on materiality and business impact

questions.key_concept: Parallel-run reconciliation tolerances should be set per data category by materiality and business impact, with documented investigation rules.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks for a basis for tolerances. Ask which option ties acceptable variance to the impact of the error.
questions.correct_explanation: Tolerances should be risk-based: financial balances may need near-zero variance, while descriptive reference fields can tolerate more, each with documented investigation rules. This focuses effort where an error would matter. Zero tolerance sounds rigorous, but it treats a trivial formatting difference like a misstated balance, consumes investigation effort on immaterial items and can delay cutover without reducing meaningful risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Zero tolerance is defensible for cash balances, yet a threshold exists to sort errors that matter from noise, and one that sorts nothing is no threshold.
wrong_explanations.B: One threshold for every category treats balances and reference fields alike, though materiality differs by data category and business impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Another project's tolerances reflect different data and risks; they are not tied to the materiality of this organization's categories.

tips: Eliminate: B applies one threshold across categories whose materiality differs, and C borrows tolerances set for other organizations' data.
Final two: D beats A because materiality-based thresholds focus scrutiny where errors matter, while zero tolerance spends it everywhere equally.
Exam cue: when a threshold must be set, prefer risk-based and materiality-driven over uniform or absolute rules.

questions.subtopic: Test Types and Techniques. Limited Test Time
questions.question: Time is limited to test a new loan system before go-live. Which test strategy should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Spreading test effort evenly across the modules so no area is missed
options.B: Testing the most frequently used transactions first
options.C: Focusing test effort where failure impact and likelihood are highest
options.D: Risk-ranking transactions by loan value, largest first

questions.key_concept: Risk-based testing concentrates effort on areas with the highest failure impact and likelihood, maximizing assurance when time is limited.
questions.pre_read: Notice the constraint: limited time. Ask which strategy uses that time where a failure would hurt most.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based testing allocates effort by the product of failure impact and likelihood, so interest calculation, payments and access control get deep coverage while low-risk screens get lighter checks. With limited time, this delivers the most assurance per hour. Even coverage sounds thorough and fair, but it gives a cosmetic report the same attention as the interest engine and runs out of time before the riskiest areas are tested deeply.

wrong_explanations.A: Even coverage holds up only when time allows every module deep testing; under a squeeze, depth goes where failure is likeliest and costliest.
wrong_explanations.B: Usage volume is only part of risk; a rarely run but high-impact function, such as interest calculation, would be tested late.
wrong_explanations.D: Loan value is one part of impact; ranking by it misses high-risk functions such as interest calculation or access control whatever a transaction's value.

tips: Eliminate: B ranks by usage alone and D by loan value alone; risk combines failure impact and likelihood.
Final two: C beats A because risk-based allocation tests critical functions deeply, while even spreading dilutes effort across trivial areas.
Exam cue: limited time or budget plus a choice of focus usually points to a risk-based answer.

questions.subtopic: Performance Testing Types. Load vs Stress vs Soak
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the test plan for a replacement portal, whose predecessor slowed down until restarted each week, includes one-hour peak load tests and a stress test. What is the MOST significant gap?

options.A: No endurance (soak) test at expected load
options.B: No spike test of sudden traffic surges
options.C: No failover test of the portal's load balancer
options.D: No volume test of a year's projected data growth

questions.key_concept: Load tests confirm expected volume, stress tests find breaking points, and soak tests reveal degradation and leaks over extended duration.
questions.pre_read: Notice what cured the old portal's slowdown. Ask which test runs long enough to reveal that kind of fault.
questions.correct_explanation: A slowdown that a restart clears points to leaks: a soak (endurance) test holds expected load for days and exposes memory leaks, resource exhaustion and gradual slowdown that a one-hour test ends before revealing. A failover test is the tempting option because it also concerns availability, but it proves recovery from a component failure, not that the portal avoids slow degradation.

wrong_explanations.B: A spike test checks sudden bursts, a short-term limit; a portal that slows until restarted is degrading gradually at normal volume.
wrong_explanations.C: Failover proves recovery when a component fails; it does not reveal the gradual leaks that force restarts.
wrong_explanations.D: Data growth slows a system steadily, but a restart does not undo it; slowdowns that a restart clears point to leaks, which soak testing finds.

tips: Eliminate: B tests sudden bursts, a short-term limit, and D tests data growth, which a restart would not cure.
Final two: A beats C because only an extended run reveals gradual degradation; failover proves recovery from a sudden fault.
Exam cue: match the test to the objective. Duration points to soak, normal volume to load, beyond limits to stress.

questions.question: An application team pulls hundreds of open-source libraries into each build. Which control should the IS auditor expect as the PRIMARY safeguard against using flawed components?

options.A: Annual penetration testing of the production application
options.B: Dependency scanning at every build for known vulnerabilities
options.C: An approved library list enforced at each build
options.D: One-time manual developer review of each new library

questions.key_concept: Software composition analysis at every build is the primary control for known vulnerabilities in open-source dependencies.
questions.pre_read: Notice the scale (hundreds of libraries) and frequency (each build). Ask which control keeps pace with both.
questions.correct_explanation: Software composition analysis inventories every dependency at each build and matches it against vulnerability databases, so newly disclosed vulnerabilities (CVEs) are flagged and routed for remediation quickly. It scales to hundreds of libraries and runs continuously. An annual penetration test is a valuable independent check, but it samples exploitable paths once a year, while new dependency vulnerabilities are published daily and can sit unpatched for months.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor values a penetration test for what attackers can reach, but controls must keep pace with their risk.
wrong_explanations.C: An approved list is enforced at each build but vetted once; it goes stale as new vulnerabilities are disclosed in libraries already on it.
wrong_explanations.D: A single review at adoption cannot track vulnerabilities disclosed later and does not scale to hundreds of libraries.

tips: Eliminate: C and D vet libraries once, at approval or adoption, so neither catches vulnerabilities disclosed later.
Final two: B beats A because continuous scanning at every build keeps pace with new disclosures, while an annual test leaves months of exposure.
Exam cue: for third-party code pulled into each build, composition analysis at every build is the primary control; tests of the finished application sample too little, too late.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds database administrators applying schema changes directly in production during business hours. Which control would BEST address this?

options.A: Restricting direct schema changes to approved, scheduled and logged windows
options.B: Letting developers alter the schema through their code commit rights
options.C: Logging each schema change in a register after it is applied
options.D: Deploying reviewed, versioned migration scripts through change management

questions.key_concept: Database schema changes should flow through versioned, reviewed and tested migration scripts within the change-management process.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the real exposure is: the hour of the change, or the lack of review, testing and traceability.
questions.correct_explanation: The core risk is unreviewed, untested and untraceable change, not its timing. Versioned migration scripts are peer reviewed, tested in lower environments and deployed through the change-management workflow, giving an audit trail and a rollback path. Moving the same direct changes to a maintenance window reduces user impact, but administrators would still alter production without review, testing or version history.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval authorizes the change, and scheduling and logging set when and how visibly it happens, but administrators still alter production by hand, with no reviewed, tested script or rollback path.
wrong_explanations.B: Giving developers production schema access worsens segregation of duties and still bypasses review and testing.
wrong_explanations.C: An after-the-fact register records changes but does not review or test them before they reach production.

tips: Eliminate: B widens uncontrolled production access, and C records changes only after they reach production.
Final two: D beats A because reviewed, tested, versioned scripts address the real risk; approving, scheduling and logging direct changes still leaves them untested and untraceable to code.
Exam cue: when a finding is uncontrolled change, the BEST fix routes it through change management, not just a different time slot.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the rollback plan a change advisory board approved for a high-risk release that also changes the database schema. Which feature should the auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Prior build, database backup and config snapshot kept on hand
options.B: A detailed rollback runbook reviewed and approved by the owner
options.C: A tested, time-bound procedure restoring code, data and configuration
options.D: A rollback rehearsed in a test environment last year

questions.key_concept: A robust rollback plan is tested, time-bound and restores data and configuration consistency, not just the previous code version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would give confidence that the rollback will actually work on the night.
questions.correct_explanation: A rollback plan provides assurance only if it has been exercised, can be completed within a defined window, and restores data and configuration as well as code. Many failed rollbacks happen because a schema or configuration change was not reversible. An approved runbook shows the steps were reviewed, but until it is rehearsed nobody knows whether it restores code, data and configuration within the window.

wrong_explanations.A: The pieces exist, but nobody has shown they restore together, or how long that takes, so the plan is unproven.
wrong_explanations.B: A reviewed runbook would do for a code-only change; with a schema change in play, approval records intent, not capability.
wrong_explanations.D: Last year's rehearsal tested a different release; this release's data and configuration changes have never been rolled back.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the pieces without proving they restore together, and D rehearsed an earlier release, not this one's data and configuration changes.
Final two: C beats B because only a rehearsed procedure proves restoration within the window; an approved runbook is still untested.
Exam cue: a rollback plan must reverse every layer the release changes, code, data and configuration, and be proven within the window.

questions.question: An organization is splitting its monolithic billing application into dozens of microservices. Which governance addition should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Letting each service team choose its own interfaces and standards
options.B: Service contracts and end-to-end observability across service calls
options.C: Container orchestration security in place of application-level controls
options.D: Unit test coverage targets enforced in each service's pipeline

questions.key_concept: Microservices shift risk into service interactions, so governance must add service contracts and end-to-end observability.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changes when one application becomes many. Look for the control aimed at that new risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Splitting a monolith moves risk into the interactions between services. Explicit service contracts govern how services change without breaking each other, and end-to-end observability, such as distributed tracing and correlated logs, lets teams follow a billing transaction across many services. Per-service unit coverage is good engineering, but each service can pass its own tests while the transaction still fails between them.

wrong_explanations.A: Uncoordinated interfaces make services incompatible and create inconsistent security, which is the main distributed-system risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Platform security does not replace application controls. Input validation, authorization and processing controls still sit in each service.
wrong_explanations.D: Unit tests verify each service alone. They cannot detect failures in the calls and data flows between services.

tips: Eliminate: A invites incompatible services, and C trades application controls for platform security, though validation and authorization still run inside each service.
Final two: B beats D because the new risk lives between services, and unit tests only check each service in isolation.
Exam cue: when architecture becomes distributed, look for controls over interfaces and end-to-end visibility.

questions.question: A project team designing an internet-facing customer portal specifies username-and-password sign-in. Which security requirement should the IS auditor recommend adding as MOST important before development proceeds?

options.A: A phishing-resistant second factor required at every customer sign-in
options.B: Password changes forced every 30 days for every user
options.C: Account lockout after three failed attempts until a help desk reset
options.D: Sixteen-character passwords with mixed case and symbols

questions.key_concept: Build phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication into the requirements during design, so stolen passwords alone never give access and no costly retrofit is needed.
questions.pre_read: Notice the portal is still being designed. Ask which requirement still protects accounts after a password is stolen.
questions.correct_explanation: Specifying a phishing-resistant second factor, such as a FIDO2 security key, in the design means a stolen or guessed password alone no longer grants access, and building it in now costs far less than retrofitting after release. Longer, complex passwords resist guessing, but they remain a single factor: a phished or reused password still works, and strict rules push users toward predictable patterns.

wrong_explanations.B: Forced periodic rotation without signs of compromise yields weaker, predictable passwords, and current NIST guidance discourages it.
wrong_explanations.C: A low lockout threshold lets attackers lock out customers at will and floods the help desk, without stopping phished credentials.
wrong_explanations.D: Stronger passwords resist guessing but are still one factor. Phishing and credential reuse defeat them.

tips: Eliminate: B is discouraged by current NIST guidance, and C creates a denial-of-service risk for customers.
Final two: A beats D because a second factor stops stolen passwords, while a stronger password is still one factor.
Exam cue: set security requirements during design, when they are cheapest; to strengthen authentication, add an independent factor rather than tighten the existing one.

questions.subtopic: Build vs Buy vs SaaS. Multi-Factor Decision
questions.question: The CIO favors a custom-built warehouse system, citing unique processes; the COO favors SaaS for speed. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to the steering committee?

options.A: Pilot the SaaS product in one warehouse before deciding
options.B: Score both options against the CIO's documented unique processes
options.C: Compare both options in one business case against agreed requirements
options.D: Run vendor demonstrations to see which product best fits current processes

questions.key_concept: Build, buy or SaaS decisions should follow a business case comparing lifetime cost, requirements fit and risk, with assumptions challenged.
questions.pre_read: Notice both executives already favor an answer. Ask what analysis should come before any solution is chosen.
questions.correct_explanation: Each executive is asserting a conclusion. The committee first needs a structured comparison: lifetime cost, fit against documented requirements, and delivery and lock-in risk, with the uniqueness claim tested rather than assumed. Vendor demonstrations are a normal later step, but running them first assumes a purchase, judges products against current processes instead of agreed requirements, and lets vendors frame the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: A pilot tests one product in practice before requirements and alternatives are compared, so it assumes SaaS and skips the business case.
wrong_explanations.B: Scoring both options compares them, but on one executive's framing and one factor; lifetime cost and delivery risk are left out.
wrong_explanations.D: Requirements are the yardstick for build and buy alike. Demos show how a product handles real work, yet yardsticks are fixed before anything is measured.

tips: Eliminate: A trials one product before the options are compared, and B compares both but only on fit to processes one executive defined.
Final two: C beats D because the business case and requirements comparison comes before product evaluation, not after vendor demos.
Exam cue: in build-or-buy decisions, agreed requirements and a business case come before demonstrations, pilots or any favored solution.

questions.question: A business case for a new document management system presents only the vendor's proposed system and its benefits. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a sensitivity analysis of the vendor's benefit estimates
options.B: Benchmark the proposed price against similar systems elsewhere
options.C: Have IT approve the technical design before the case proceeds
options.D: Weigh the proposal against other options, including doing nothing

questions.key_concept: A sound business case compares realistic alternatives, including the do-nothing option, so approvers can judge the best use of funds.
questions.pre_read: Ask how approvers can know this solution is the best choice if nothing else was considered.
questions.correct_explanation: A business case justifies an investment by showing the chosen option is better than the alternatives, including continuing as is. With one solution presented, approvers cannot judge whether it is the best use of funds. A sensitivity analysis is the tempting option because it makes the case more rigorous, but it still examines only the one option on offer.

wrong_explanations.A: Sensitivity analysis tests how far the vendor's benefit estimates can move, but it still examines one option; approvers cannot see whether another serves better.
wrong_explanations.B: A price benchmark tests what this solution costs, not whether a different approach, or no change, would serve the business better.
wrong_explanations.C: Technical design approval comes later. It confirms feasibility, not that this investment beats the alternatives.

tips: Eliminate: B tests the price of the one option offered, and C moves to design approval before the investment choice is justified.
Final two: D beats A because a sound case compares options; a sensitivity analysis only stress-tests the one option presented.
Exam cue: a sound business case compares alternatives, including the do-nothing option, before approval.

questions.subtopic: Failed Deployment with Bad Rollback. Incident Governance
questions.question: A failed release wrote orders the rollback script cannot read, so rolling back would strand them; the CTO wants it now. What should the IS auditor expect the release's recovery procedure to require FIRST?

options.A: Execute the rollback now and repair the affected orders afterward
options.B: Preserve the affected orders before restoring service another way
options.C: Invoke the disaster recovery plan and fail over to the standby site
options.D: Restore the database from last night's backup and replay the orders

questions.key_concept: When a rollback would strand or lose data written by the failed release, preserve that data first, then restore service by hotfix or roll forward.
questions.pre_read: Notice the rollback script cannot read the new data. Ask what is lost if the rollback runs anyway.
questions.correct_explanation: The known rollback path cannot read orders written in the new format, so running it would leave them unreadable or lost; the first priority is preserving that data in a safe staging area. Only then should service be restored by a hotfix or roll forward, followed by reconciliation. Rolling back follows the usual recovery playbook, but it knowingly strands customer transactions that may not be recoverable.

wrong_explanations.A: Rollback is the standard recovery path, but data that cannot be recreated is protected before service is restored.
wrong_explanations.C: Failover suits loss of a site; the standby replicates the same failed release and new-format orders, so the problem moves with it.
wrong_explanations.D: Restoring last night's backup discards every order written since, and replaying new-format orders may fail or corrupt them.

tips: Eliminate: C invokes disaster recovery, which suits site loss, though the standby carries the same faulty release, and D restores a backup that loses every order since.
Final two: B beats A because protecting the data comes before restoring service by a path known to strand it.
Exam cue: when recovery would destroy data, preserve the data first, then restore service by another route.

questions.question: After acquiring a regional bank, the acquirer plans a 24-month core-platform migration. Which governance principle should the IS auditor recommend to the audit committee as MOST important?

options.A: Discover dependencies, then sequence migrations by risk
options.B: Run both core platforms in parallel until migration completes
options.C: Migrate shared infrastructure first, then customer-facing systems
options.D: Migrate the highest-risk systems first to retire risk early

questions.key_concept: M&A IT integration should discover the acquired systems and dependencies first, then sequence migrations by risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the acquirer does not yet know about the acquired bank, and what must happen before migrations are ordered.
questions.correct_explanation: An acquired bank's real environment rarely matches its documentation: integrations, custom rules and in-flight projects must be discovered before migration is planned. Sequencing by risk, informed by those dependencies, avoids breaking hidden links and protects customers. Moving shared infrastructure first sounds dependency-aware, but it fixes the order before the acquired bank's real links are known.

wrong_explanations.B: Running both platforms for the whole program doubles operating cost and reconciliation effort, and it does not decide what moves when.
wrong_explanations.C: An infrastructure-first order is a common migration pattern, but patterns from other estates stay hypotheses until this estate's dependencies are mapped.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the riskiest systems first sounds prudent, but risk cannot be ranked before dependencies are discovered, and failures would hit the most critical systems first.

tips: Eliminate: B runs two platforms for the whole program without ordering the moves, and D sends the highest-risk systems through a migration process not yet proven on anything.
Final two: A beats C because the order must follow dependencies discovered in the acquired bank, not a fixed rule set before discovery.
Exam cue: in M&A integration, discovery of the acquired environment comes before any migration sequencing.

questions.subtopic: Control Design. Segregation of Duties in Roles
questions.question: During design of a new purchasing application, an IS auditor finds that one role can create a supplier and approve its payments. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Review a monthly log of new suppliers after go-live
options.B: Rely on managers to assign roles carefully to their own staff
options.C: Show a warning when one user performs both tasks
options.D: Have the system prevent every conflicting task combination

questions.key_concept: Build segregation of duties into the role design so the application prevents conflicting combinations, rather than detecting misuse later.
questions.pre_read: The system is still being designed. Ask which option stops the conflict rather than spotting it afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: Design is the cheapest point to fix segregation of duties: defining the conflicting tasks in the role model and having the application prevent one user from holding both builds the control in, consistent and testable. A monthly log review nearly wins: it is a reasonable compensating control where separation is impossible, but here the conflict can be prevented outright.

wrong_explanations.A: A log review detects misuse weeks after payments are made. It is a compensating control, not a substitute for preventable separation.
wrong_explanations.B: Manual care in assigning roles is inconsistent, and nothing in the system stops a conflicting combination.
wrong_explanations.C: A warning can be clicked through. It records the conflict but does not prevent one user completing both steps.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on manual care with no system enforcement, and C flags the conflict but still lets one user complete both steps.
Final two: D beats A because preventing a conflict in the design beats detecting misuse after payment.
Exam cue: when a control gap is found at design, recommend building a preventive control in rather than adding detection later.

questions.question: A pre-go-live penetration test of a new customer portal finds two high-risk vulnerabilities, and the sponsor wants to launch on schedule. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Launch on project manager risk approval, fixing them in the next release
options.B: Launch with monitoring that the CISO approves as adequate
options.C: Fix them first, or have the risk owner formally accept them
options.D: Launch with firewall rules blocking the findings' attack patterns

questions.key_concept: High-risk findings from pre-production testing are fixed before go-live or formally accepted by the accountable risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should decide to carry a known high risk into production, and how that decision is recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: High-risk findings from pre-production security testing should be fixed before go-live or, if the business must launch, formally accepted by the accountable risk owner with compensating controls and a fix date. Launching with the project manager's approval is the strongest alternative: it may match the business choice, but the project manager is not the risk owner, so known high risks would reach customers without accountable acceptance.

wrong_explanations.A: Project managers weigh delivery risks daily as a core duty, but the person under schedule pressure is the wrong one to waive a risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Monitoring detects exploitation rather than preventing it, and the CISO advises on security risk; residual business risk must be accepted by the accountable business risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Firewall rules may reduce exposure, but they are an unproven compensating control, and no accountable risk owner has accepted the residual risk.

tips: Eliminate: B adds detective monitoring approved by the CISO, who advises on risk but does not own it, and D relies on firewall rules no risk owner accepted.
Final two: C beats A because known high risks need fixing or acceptance by the risk owner; a project manager's approval is not that.
Exam cue: before go-live, open high risks are fixed or formally accepted by the risk owner, never quietly deferred.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a GitOps deployment model. Which feature MOST supports assurance that production matches approved changes?

options.A: Drift reports generated weekly by comparing clusters to Git
options.B: An agent continuously reconciling clusters to the reviewed Git state
options.C: Pull-request approvals recorded in Git for each production change
options.D: A CI pipeline pushing each approved build to the cluster

questions.key_concept: GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth, with an agent continuously reconciling actual cluster state to the approved declared state.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks about matching approved changes over time. Ask which option keeps checking after deployment.
questions.correct_explanation: In GitOps, Git holds the reviewed, declared state, and an in-cluster agent continuously compares actual state to it and corrects drift. Any manual change is reverted or flagged, so production keeps matching what was approved. A weekly drift report is the tempting option because it also compares clusters to Git, but it runs days apart and corrects nothing, so production can run unapproved changes in between.

wrong_explanations.A: Drift reports and the agent check against the same reviewed Git state, but assurance comes from enforcing the approved state, not from reporting departures.
wrong_explanations.C: Recorded approvals prove what was authorized, but they say nothing about whether production still matches that state.
wrong_explanations.D: Push deployment controls what goes in, but nothing detects later manual drift, so ongoing alignment is not assured.

tips: Eliminate: C proves changes were approved but not that production still matches them, and D deploys once with nothing checking for later drift.
Final two: B beats A because continuous reconciliation detects and corrects drift as it occurs; a weekly report finds it days later and corrects nothing.
Exam cue: assurance that state stays as approved needs continuous comparison, not just a controlled one-time deployment.

questions.subtopic: Code Review Effectiveness. Pull Request Patterns
questions.question: Management wants pull-request reviews to catch more defects. Which practice should the IS auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Small, focused changes reviewed by at least one independent peer
options.B: Approving merges whenever the automated CI build passes
options.C: Unanimous approval from every team member before merging
options.D: One designated reviewer approving the changes submitted by each author

questions.key_concept: Pull-request reviews catch most defects when changes are small and focused and an independent peer reviews them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes a reviewer actually find a defect: the size of the change and the freshness of the reviewer's view.
questions.correct_explanation: Reviewers find far more defects in small, focused changes than in large ones, and an independent peer brings a fresh view of logic and design. Keeping changes small also keeps review fast enough that it is not rubber-stamped. A designated reviewer per author offers consistency, but it encourages familiarity and routine approval, and does nothing about large changes that overwhelm any reviewer.

wrong_explanations.B: A passing build shows the code compiles and tests pass. It does not review logic, design or security.
wrong_explanations.C: Requiring every team member creates bottlenecks and diffuses responsibility, so each reviewer looks less carefully.
wrong_explanations.D: A named reviewer gives each merge clear accountability. Review quality, though, depends on fresh eyes and on how much one reader can hold in mind.

tips: Eliminate: B skips human review, and C slows merging while diluting accountability.
Final two: A beats D because small changes with a fresh independent reviewer find more defects than a fixed, familiar pairing.
Exam cue: review quality depends on manageable scope and real independence, not on more approvers or automation alone.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a nine-hour regression suite, made up mostly of end-to-end UI tests, is often skipped before urgent releases. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rebalance to equal numbers of unit, integration and end-to-end tests
options.B: Run the suite in parallel across more build agents
options.C: Run the full suite weekly instead of before each release
options.D: Rebalance toward many fast unit tests and few end-to-end tests

questions.key_concept: The test pyramid favors many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and the fewest end-to-end tests for cost-effective coverage.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the suite is skipped. Then pick the change that removes that cause without leaving releases untested.
questions.correct_explanation: The suite is skipped because it is slow, so the fix is its composition: the test pyramid puts many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests and few end-to-end tests, kept for critical business flows so coverage is kept. That gives quick feedback teams will not bypass. Running the suite in parallel is the tempting option because it cuts run time quickly, but the slow, brittle tests remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Equal counts keep many slow end-to-end tests, so run times stay long and the pressure to skip the suite remains.
wrong_explanations.B: More agents shorten the run at extra cost, but the suite stays dominated by slow end-to-end tests, so run times and cost grow again as it expands.
wrong_explanations.C: A weekly run avoids the delay but lets urgent releases ship without regression testing, which is the risk itself.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps many slow end-to-end tests by counting layers equally, and C removes the delay by leaving releases untested.
Final two: D beats B because a pyramid shortens the suite at its root; more agents buy speed with cost while the slow tests remain.
Exam cue: when a control is skipped because it is slow, fix its design so it fits the process; for regression suites, think pyramid.

questions.question: Management schedules the post-implementation review of a new loan origination system for one week after go-live. What should the IS auditor MOST appropriately recommend?

options.A: Keep the one-week date while project staff remember the details
options.B: Fold the review into next month's project closure report
options.C: Reschedule it for a date after operations have stabilized
options.D: Replace it with a user satisfaction survey after the first week

questions.key_concept: Schedule a post-implementation review after a period of stable operation, so benefits and control performance can be measured on real data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a post-implementation review measures, then ask whether one week of live operation can produce that evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-implementation review judges whether the system delivers its intended benefits and operates stably, so it should follow a period of normal operation, often several months, long enough for real performance data to build up. Keeping the one-week date comes closest: fresh memories help capture lessons, but one week of start-up issues cannot show benefits, and lessons can be recorded separately at project closure.

wrong_explanations.A: Early timing preserves memories, but one week of live data reflects start-up issues and cannot show whether benefits were achieved.
wrong_explanations.B: Project closure looks back on delivery a month in; benefits need longer stable operation before they can be measured.
wrong_explanations.D: A satisfaction survey after one week captures early impressions, not measured benefits or control performance.

tips: Eliminate: B folds the review into project closure, which looks back on delivery rather than on benefits, and D swaps measured benefits for early user opinion.
Final two: C beats A because benefits need stable operation to show; lessons can be captured at closure without rushing the review.
Exam cue: a post-implementation review needs enough live operation to produce evidence, typically months, not days, after go-live.

questions.question: A project team is defining security controls for a new patient-records application. Which basis should the IS auditor expect as MOST appropriate for deriving the control requirements?

options.B: The full control catalog of a recognized security framework
options.C: A risk assessment informed by the data's classification
options.D: The controls the development team can build within budget

questions.key_concept: Control requirements come from a risk assessment informed by data classification; frameworks help select controls, not decide what is needed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes this system's controls proportionate to its own risks.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls should be proportionate to risk, so requirements are derived from a risk assessment that considers the classification of patient data, threats and business impact, with a framework then used to select and check controls. Applying a full framework catalog is the most tempting alternative: it looks thorough, but it ignores this system's specific risks, adding unneeded controls and possibly missing context-specific ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Another client's controls reflect that client's risks. They may not fit this application's data, users or threats.
wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would check coverage against a recognized framework, but a catalog lists what is possible; risk decides what is required.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget shapes choices, but letting it define the requirements leaves high risks uncontrolled without a deliberate decision.

tips: Eliminate: A copies another client's risk profile, and D lets cost, not risk, set the requirements.
Final two: C beats B because control requirements come from this system's risks; a framework is a menu, not a decision.
Exam cue: when asked what should drive control design, choose the risk assessment, informed by data classification.

questions.subtopic: Application Logging. Security Monitoring & Audit Traceability
questions.question: An IS auditor evaluates logging for a new payments application. Which design BEST supports both security monitoring and audit traceability?

options.A: Security events logged centrally with synced clocks and tamper protection
options.B: Every user input, including failed password values, logged to local files
options.C: One percent of application events sampled to control storage costs
options.D: Full transaction detail logged and retained on each application server

questions.key_concept: Useful logs capture security-relevant events centrally, with synchronized time and integrity protection, so they serve as reliable evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which logs could still be trusted and correlated after an incident.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring and traceability both need logs that can be correlated and trusted. Central collection with synchronized clocks lets events from different systems be lined up, and tamper protection keeps them usable as evidence. Detailed logs kept on each server look thorough, but anyone with server access can alter them, and events cannot easily be correlated across systems.

wrong_explanations.B: Recording password values turns the log into a credential store and a new breach target; logs should record outcomes, not secrets.
wrong_explanations.C: Sampling discards most events, so a rare malicious request is likely to be missed and the audit trail is incomplete.
wrong_explanations.D: Detail without integrity is weak evidence: local logs can be changed by server administrators and are hard to correlate across systems.

tips: Eliminate: B logs credentials, creating a new exposure, and C samples away the rare events that matter most.
Final two: A beats D because evidence must be trustworthy and correlatable, not just detailed.
Exam cue: for audit logs, look for integrity, time synchronization and central retention before volume of detail.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a data conversion in which developers wrote the rules mapping legacy customer fields to the new system. Who is the MOST appropriate approver of these rules?

options.A: The developers who wrote and unit-tested the rules
options.B: The data owner accountable for the migrated records
options.C: The business analyst who gathered the conversion requirements
options.D: The project manager accountable for the conversion

questions.key_concept: Data mapping rules decide what converted data means, so the accountable data owner approves them before conversion runs.
questions.pre_read: Ask who is accountable for what the customer data means and how it may be used.
questions.correct_explanation: Mapping rules decide what customer data means in the new system, so the data owner, who is accountable for that information and understands its business meaning, should approve them before conversion runs. The business analyst is the tempting option: they understand the requirements, but understanding is not accountability; the data owner answers for the data's meaning and use.

wrong_explanations.A: Developers approving their own rules is self-review. Technical testing does not confirm the business meaning of each field.
wrong_explanations.C: The analyst understands the requirements but is not accountable for the data; approval belongs to the person who answers for its meaning and use.
wrong_explanations.D: The project manager coordinates the conversion but is not accountable for the meaning of the data, and may favor the schedule.

tips: Eliminate: A lets developers approve their own work, and D owns the schedule rather than the meaning of the data.
Final two: B beats C because approval follows accountability; the analyst understands the requirements but does not answer for the data.
Exam cue: decisions about what data means or who may use it belong to the data owner, not IT or the project.

questions.question: A new claims system will process 50,000 payments a day, and duplicate payment is the key risk. Which control design should the IS auditor consider MOST effective?

options.A: A monthly review of a sample of payments by finance staff
options.B: A daily report of possible duplicates for clerks to investigate
options.C: A policy telling staff to check for duplicates before entry
options.D: An automated check that holds payments matching earlier ones

questions.key_concept: For high-volume, well-defined risks, automated preventive controls built into the application beat manual or detective controls.
questions.pre_read: Compare when each control acts: before the money leaves, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: At 50,000 payments a day, an automated preventive control is most effective: a system check that holds payments matching earlier ones stops duplicates before money leaves, consistently and at volume. The daily duplicates report nearly wins: it is a useful detective control, but it finds duplicates after payment and depends on clerks keeping up with a high-volume queue.

wrong_explanations.A: Monthly sampling detects problems weeks later and examines a fraction of payments. Duplicates paid meanwhile must be recovered.
wrong_explanations.B: A duplicates report earns its place when matches are too fuzzy to block; where a rule can be coded, prevention outranks detection.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy relies on every clerk checking by hand. At high volume it is inconsistent and leaves no reliable evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A samples too little too late, and C relies on manual effort at high volume.
Final two: D beats B because preventing a duplicate beats detecting it after the money has gone.
Exam cue: for high-volume, well-defined risks, prefer automated preventive controls built into the application.

questions.question: A project manager asks the IS auditor to design the application controls for a new billing system. What is the auditor's MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Design the controls, then have management formally approve them
options.B: Decline any involvement until the system has gone live
options.C: Advise on control requirements while management designs them
options.D: Design the controls and have another auditor audit them later

questions.key_concept: During development the auditor advises on control requirements; management designs, implements and owns the controls.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose job it is to design controls, and what the auditor's role is during a project.
questions.correct_explanation: Early auditor involvement is valuable, but control design is a management responsibility. The auditor can advise on control requirements under agreed advisory terms, while management designs, implements and owns the controls, which keeps the auditor objective for later audits. Having a colleague audit auditor-designed controls is the strongest alternative: it reduces the self-review threat, but audit would still have taken on a management role.

wrong_explanations.A: Management's approval does not change who designed the controls; audit would still be reviewing its own work in later audits.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting until go-live means gaps are found when they are costliest to fix. Advisory involvement during design is appropriate.
wrong_explanations.D: Rotating auditors reduces self-review, but audit has still performed a management function, impairing its objectivity.

tips: Eliminate: A still has audit design the controls, which management's approval does not cure, and B gives up the value of early involvement.
Final two: C beats D because the auditor should advise rather than design; a different reviewer does not undo audit doing management's job.
Exam cue: the auditor recommends and advises under agreed terms; management designs, implements and owns controls.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a DevOps delivery scorecard that reports deployment frequency and lead time for changes, and nothing else. What is the MOST significant gap?

options.A: No count of story points or commits completed per developer
options.B: No measure of failed changes or of time to restore service
options.C: No defect density or automated test coverage figures for each release
options.D: No cycle time per story or sprint burndown for each team

questions.key_concept: The DORA four key metrics pair throughput (deployment frequency, lead time) with stability (change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time, formerly time to restore).
questions.pre_read: Sort the reported measures into speed and stability. Ask which side the scorecard leaves blank.
questions.correct_explanation: Delivery performance must balance speed with stability. The scorecard already covers throughput, so the gap is stability: how often deployments cause failures and how quickly service is restored. Defect density and test coverage are the tempting option, but they are internal quality proxies that can look healthy while production releases still fail; only outcome measures show whether changes reach users reliably.

wrong_explanations.A: Activity counts reward output, are easy to game and say nothing about whether changes reach production safely.
wrong_explanations.C: Defect density and coverage describe code inside the pipeline; they can look good while production deployments still fail.
wrong_explanations.D: Cycle time and burndown measure speed again, the dimension the scorecard already covers, so the stability gap remains.

tips: Eliminate: A tracks developer activity rather than delivery outcomes, and D adds more speed measures to a scorecard that already measures speed.
Final two: B beats C because delivery performance is judged by stability in production, not by internal quality proxies.
Exam cue: a balanced delivery scorecard pairs throughput with stability; find which side is missing.

questions.question: A business case for a new self-service portal assumes 90% of customers adopt it within a year, and the projected return rests on that figure. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Benchmark the 90% target against peer portal adoption
options.B: Require a post-implementation review to confirm adoption after a year
options.C: Add a contingency reserve to the budget in case adoption lags
options.D: Test how the return changes if adoption falls short of 90%

questions.key_concept: When a business case rests on one key assumption, approvers need sensitivity analysis showing how results change if it falls short.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much of the decision rests on one number.
questions.correct_explanation: The whole return rests on one optimistic assumption, so approvers need a sensitivity analysis showing how the result changes at lower adoption rates before committing funds. Benchmarking against peer portals is the tempting option: it tests whether 90% is plausible, but not how far the return falls if adoption misses it.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer benchmarking is a valid check on an assumption's realism, but realism and resilience differ: a case must survive its assumption being wrong.
wrong_explanations.B: A review after a year confirms adoption too late; approvers need to see the risk in the assumption before funds are committed.
wrong_explanations.C: A reserve adds cost to absorb a shortfall, but approvers still cannot see how far the return falls if adoption misses.

tips: Eliminate: B checks adoption a year after the money is spent, and C adds cost to cushion a shortfall without showing its effect on the return.
Final two: D beats A because a benchmark tests whether 90% is plausible, but approvers must see what the return becomes if adoption falls short.
Exam cue: when a business case depends on one key assumption, recommend sensitivity analysis before approval.

questions.question: Six months after rolling out an AI coding assistant, an IS auditor finds unverified licenses in generated code and secrets pasted into prompts. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Set usage rules with automated checks on assistant inputs and outputs
options.B: Peer-review AI code and remind staff not to paste secrets
options.C: Let each team set its own assistant policy based on local risk
options.D: Block the assistant until every generated file passes license review

questions.key_concept: AI coding assistant governance targets its specific risks: license scanning of output, data-handling rules for prompts and user training.
questions.pre_read: List the two findings. Then ask which option enforces a control on every use rather than relying on people.
questions.correct_explanation: The findings are license contamination in generated code and sensitive data leaking into prompts. Usage rules backed by automated checks, license scanning of output and secret detection on prompts, target both while keeping the tool. Peer review with reminders is the tempting option because it covers both findings, but it relies on people: reviewers cannot spot copied licensed code, and a reminder does not stop a secret being pasted.

wrong_explanations.B: Peer review does catch logic flaws in AI output, but a risk raised by every use needs a control on every use.
wrong_explanations.C: Team-level policies produce inconsistent controls; the license and data-handling risks are enterprise-wide and need one policy.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking until license review treats one finding at the cost of the tool, and does nothing about secrets pasted into prompts.

tips: Eliminate: C splits an enterprise-wide risk across team policies, and D treats only the license finding while halting the tool.
Final two: A beats B because automated checks act on every use; review and reminders depend on people and cannot see license origin.
Exam cue: when a risk recurs with every use of a tool, prefer automated, enforced controls over review and reminders.

questions.question: Midway through a staged four-region release, the first two regions show sharply elevated error rates, and the release manager wants to continue. What should the IS auditor expect the release procedure to require FIRST?

options.A: Halt the remaining regions and roll back the affected ones
options.B: Pause the remaining regions and widen monitoring before deciding
options.C: Convene the incident bridge to find root cause before acting
options.D: Skip the final region but keep the release live elsewhere

questions.key_concept: During a failing staged rollout, halt propagation and roll back per the playbook first, then investigate root cause.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the staged rollout was designed to achieve once a failure appears.
questions.correct_explanation: A staged rollout exists so early failures stop the release before it spreads. With clear failure in two regions, the first step is containment: stop further deployment and restore service using the rollback playbook. Root-cause analysis is essential, but delaying action until it finishes leaves customers on a failing release while the cause is investigated.

wrong_explanations.B: Pausing stops the spread, but the two failing regions stay live while monitoring gathers data; customers there keep meeting the errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Diagnosis matters, but it should follow containment; waiting for root cause prolongs customer impact.
wrong_explanations.D: Sparing one region still leaves the failing regions live and customers exposed to elevated errors.

tips: Eliminate: B pauses the spread but leaves the failing regions live, and D spares one region while customers stay on the failing release.
Final two: A beats C because containment and service restoration come before root-cause analysis.
Exam cue: in a live failure, contain and restore first, then investigate the root cause.

questions.question: A CTO wants to rewrite a 35-year-old COBOL policy system as microservices, and three key maintainers retire within 18 months. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Approve the rewrite but start with the lowest-risk policy modules first
options.B: Capture retiring staff knowledge and compare modernization options
options.C: Keep the system unchanged, since mainframe rewrites usually fail
options.D: Outsource the mainframe so the risk moves to a provider

questions.key_concept: Legacy modernization starts by securing at-risk knowledge and comparing options in a business case before committing to a build approach.
questions.pre_read: Notice the retirement deadline and that the CTO already has a favored option.
questions.correct_explanation: Two risks dominate: undocumented business rules held by people about to leave, and a target chosen before options are compared. Capturing knowledge now and running a fit-gap analysis of re-host, re-platform, replace and rewrite builds the business case before committing. Starting with low-risk modules is sensible phasing, but it commits to the CTO's preferred option without evidence it fits.

wrong_explanations.A: Phasing reduces execution risk, but it skips the comparison that should justify the rewrite in the first place.
wrong_explanations.C: Doing nothing still loses the retiring knowledge and leaves the firm dependent on an aging platform.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves operations, not accountability; the firm still owns the business rules and the policy processing that depend on them.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the knowledge-loss deadline unaddressed, and D assumes accountability moves with outsourcing, though the organization keeps it.
Final two: B beats A because the business case and options analysis must come before committing to a build approach.
Exam cue: when a stem names a preferred solution, look for the option that tests it against alternatives first.
