questions.question: A vendor will stop security patches for a critical check-processing component in 90 days, and replacements take 12 to 18 months to integrate. What should the IS auditor recommend that management do FIRST?

options.A: Keep the component and patch it internally when needed
options.B: Select the replacement vendor with the fastest integration time
options.C: Launch a transition program with interim compensating controls
options.D: Begin a replacement RFP and accept the unpatched risk meanwhile

questions.key_concept: Vendor abandonment of a critical component needs a transition program: interim compensating controls, proper evaluation and a planned migration.
questions.pre_read: Compare the 90-day patch deadline with the 12 to 18 month replacement time.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap is clear: patches stop in 90 days, but a replacement needs a year or more. Management should start a structured transition now, with compensating controls such as isolation and monitoring for the unpatched period, owner acceptance of what remains, and a formal evaluation of replacements. Choosing on integration speed alone skips due diligence and still leaves months of unpatched exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal teams rarely have the vendor's source code or expertise, so reliable patching is unlikely and security risk grows after 90 days.
wrong_explanations.B: Speed is one criterion, not the selection basis; it skips due diligence and leaves the interim gap uncontrolled.
wrong_explanations.D: Starting procurement helps, but accepting a year or more of unpatched exposure without compensating controls leaves the largest risk untreated; acceptance should cover only what remains after controls.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes patching ability the firm lacks, and D accepts a long unpatched gap instead of controlling it.
Final two: C beats B because a risk-based transition covers the interim exposure and a proper evaluation, not just speed.
Exam cue: when support ends before a replacement can land, look for interim compensating controls and a planned transition, with the owner accepting what remains.

questions.question: A health-tech team ships two-week sprints, and its privacy team is consulted only after features are built. Which change should the IS auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: A quarterly privacy review of features already released
options.B: A privacy sign-off on each new feature just before its release
options.C: Annual privacy training for sprint team members
options.D: Privacy checks on data flows and consent at sprint planning

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design in agile belongs at sprint planning: data flows, minimization and consent are checked before stories are committed.
questions.pre_read: Ask at which point in the sprint the design can still be changed cheaply.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy by design means privacy shapes the feature before it is built. Checking data flows, minimization and consent when stories are planned lets the team change the design at low cost. A sign-off before release adds an independent gate, but it arrives after the design is fixed, so problems mean costly rework or pressure to release anyway.

wrong_explanations.A: A quarterly review finds problems after features with privacy defects have already reached users.
wrong_explanations.B: A pre-release gate is better than nothing, but it comes after design, when fixing privacy problems is costly.
wrong_explanations.C: Training builds awareness, but privacy is still assessed only after features are built, so design flaws still need costly rework.

tips: Eliminate: A reviews features after release, and C trains people without changing when privacy is assessed.
Final two: D beats B because controls designed in at planning beat a gate applied after the design is fixed.
Exam cue: in agile, privacy needs enter as acceptance criteria when stories are planned, not as a sign-off after the feature is built.

questions.question: A query passed load testing on a 12,000-row test table but overloaded production, which holds 180 million rows. Which recommendation should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Requiring senior DBA code review of query performance before each release
options.B: Staging with production-scale data volumes and matching database tiers
options.C: Raising the load test's concurrent users to production peak levels
options.D: Load testing against a 1% sample of production data

questions.key_concept: Performance tests are valid evidence only when staging matches production data volume, infrastructure tier and load patterns.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test table size with production, then ask what the test result really proved.
questions.correct_explanation: The test passed because the environment did not resemble production: a tiny data set produced misleading query behavior. Testing is valid evidence only when conditions represent production, so staging needs realistic data volumes and a matching database tier. Expert code review helps, but query performance depends on data volume and execution plans (how the database chooses to run a query) that a reviewer cannot predict from code alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Review can spot obvious inefficiency, but query behavior at scale depends on data volume, which only representative testing reveals.
wrong_explanations.C: More concurrent users tests concurrency, but the failure came from data volume; a 12,000-row table stays unrepresentative.
wrong_explanations.D: A 1% sample is far closer to production than 12,000 rows, but at about 1.8 million rows it still understates the volume that broke the query.

tips: Eliminate: C fixes concurrency when the failure came from data volume, and D scales the data up but still far below production.
Final two: B beats A because test evidence is valid only when conditions match production; review cannot reproduce scale.
Exam cue: when a test passed but production failed, question how representative the test environment was.

questions.subtopic: Continuous Compliance Evidence. Regulated High-Deploy DevOps
questions.question: A bank deploys to production over 30 times a day, and its external auditor says manual change evidence no longer scales. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Generating tamper-evident records linking each deploy to its approval
options.B: Reconciling deploy logs, tickets and approvals each quarter
options.C: Holding a monthly change-board review of a sample of deployments
options.D: Accepting the pipeline's branch-protection settings as evidence of approval

questions.key_concept: High-frequency delivery is auditable when the pipeline generates tamper-evident change evidence linking every deployment to its approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option produces reliable evidence for every change at the moment it happens.
questions.correct_explanation: At this volume, evidence must be produced by the pipeline itself. Automated, tamper-evident records that tie each deployment to its approval, build and approver give complete, reliable evidence the external auditor can test. A quarterly reconciliation of every deployment is the tempting option because it is complete, but it is manual and finds unapproved changes months after release.

wrong_explanations.B: A full reconciliation covers every change, but it is manual and quarterly; unapproved deployments run for months, and the manual effort is what no longer scales.
wrong_explanations.C: Sampling after the fact cannot evidence every change, and unauthorized deployments may go undetected for weeks.
wrong_explanations.D: Branch-protection settings show a control is configured, not that every deployment actually went through an approval.

tips: Eliminate: C samples part of the changes weeks later, and D accepts a configured setting as proof that approvals happened.
Final two: A beats B because evidence created as each change deploys is complete and timely; a quarterly reconciliation finds problems months later.
Exam cue: when volume outgrows manual evidence, look for evidence the pipeline creates as each change deploys, not later manual checks.

questions.question: Management wants to use code-coverage metrics to improve software quality. Which approach should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: One 80 percent coverage gate applied to every repository
options.B: Risk-based gates on new code, leaving older code unmeasured
options.C: Risk-based coverage targets that focus on critical code paths
options.D: Raising the coverage gate each year until repositories reach 90%

questions.key_concept: Code coverage is a necessary but not sufficient signal; set risk-based targets and focus on critical paths.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether every line of code carries the same risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Coverage shows which code tests exercise, not whether the tests are good, so it is most useful when directed by risk. Higher targets for critical paths, such as authentication or calculations, put testing effort where failure matters most. A single uniform gate is simple to enforce, but it treats trivial code like critical code and encourages padding tests to hit the number.

wrong_explanations.A: Both a uniform gate and risk-based targets make coverage a release condition, though a measure turned into a target soon stops measuring anything.
wrong_explanations.B: Gating new code is common, but risk does not follow code age; critical existing paths stay untested.
wrong_explanations.D: A rising blanket target still treats all code alike and pushes teams to pad tests; coverage shows which code ran, not whether tests are good.

tips: Eliminate: B weighs risk only in new code, leaving critical older paths unmeasured, and D raises a blanket target, which rewards padded tests.
Final two: C beats A because effort should follow risk; a uniform threshold treats all code as equally important.
Exam cue: when a metric drives behavior, prefer the risk-based use over a single blanket target.

questions.subtopic: Test Types and Techniques. Input Field Testing
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that testers of a loan system rule accepting applicant ages 18 to 65 used one representative value from each age range. What is the MOST significant gap?

options.A: No random ages generated across the full range of numbers
options.B: No values chosen by business users from real loan applications
options.C: Too few values were tested inside each valid age range
options.D: No tests on and either side of each age limit

questions.key_concept: Boundary-value analysis tests values on and either side of each limit, where off-by-one defects cluster.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in a valid range an off-by-one error would show up, and whether the evidence reaches it.
questions.correct_explanation: Defects in range rules cluster at the edges, such as using greater-than where greater-than-or-equal was meant. Boundary-value analysis tests on and either side of each limit, here at least 17, 18, 65 and 66, which one mid-range value per partition never reaches. Adding more values inside each range is the tempting fix, but more mid-range values still miss the edges.

wrong_explanations.A: Random values rarely land exactly on a limit, so many tests would be needed to hit an edge defect by chance.
wrong_explanations.B: Real applicants' ages mostly fall mid-range, so business-chosen values seldom test the limits where defects occur.
wrong_explanations.C: Extra in-range values do raise confidence that each class behaves alike, yet partitioning chooses the classes and boundary analysis chooses where to probe them.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on chance to hit a limit, and B uses realistic mid-range ages that seldom reach the edges.
Final two: D beats C because off-by-one errors live at the limits, and more mid-range values still miss them.
Exam cue: for range rules, test on and either side of each limit; partitioning alone sets the classes, not the edges.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing a behavior-driven development (BDD) project wants assurance that delivered features meet business requirements. Which evidence is MOST useful?

options.A: Given-When-Then scenarios agreed with the business, run as tests
options.B: A unit-test coverage report showing most code paths are exercised
options.C: Developers' test logs showing builds passed before each release
options.D: Business sign-off emails sent after each release has gone live

questions.key_concept: In BDD, business-agreed Given-When-Then scenarios run as automated acceptance tests, so they show each requirement was both specified and verified.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence links each delivered feature back to a requirement the business agreed.
questions.correct_explanation: In behavior-driven development, business, developers and testers agree plain-language Given-When-Then scenarios before coding, and those scenarios run as automated acceptance tests. Passing scenarios therefore show, requirement by requirement, that delivered behavior matches what the business agreed. Post-release sign-off emails are the tempting option: they show business approval, but they are informal, come after go-live and do not tie approval to specific tested behavior.

wrong_explanations.B: Coverage shows how much code the unit tests exercise, not whether features do what the business asked for.
wrong_explanations.C: Developer test logs show builds passed the developers' own tests; they say nothing about business requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would keep the emails as corroboration of business satisfaction, but satisfaction is not conformance: requirements are proven criterion by criterion.

tips: Eliminate: B and C measure developers' code testing, not whether features meet business requirements.
Final two: A beats D because agreed scenarios run as tests prove each requirement; sign-off emails after go-live are informal and untied to tests.
Exam cue: for assurance that requirements are met, look for evidence that links business-agreed criteria to executed tests.

questions.question: An IS auditor must rely on data lineage for a regulatory report fed by several application pipelines. Which control provides the MOST reliable lineage?

options.A: An owner-maintained lineage register, reviewed and signed off each quarter
options.B: A data catalog populated by stewards at onboarding
options.C: Pipelines emitting lineage metadata automatically to a central store
options.D: Lineage diagrams produced by the project at design time

questions.key_concept: Reliable lineage is captured automatically at runtime and stored centrally, rather than documented by hand.
questions.pre_read: Ask which lineage records would still be accurate the day after a pipeline change.
questions.correct_explanation: Lineage evidence is reliable only if it reflects how data actually moves today. Pipelines that emit source, transformation and destination metadata at runtime keep a central repository current without depending on people to remember changes. An owner-maintained register adds accountability, but manual records drift between reviews, so the auditor could rely on lineage that no longer matches the pipelines.

wrong_explanations.A: A signed register is fine for lineage that rarely changes; for live pipelines, evidence the system emits outranks records people keep.
wrong_explanations.B: A catalog filled in at onboarding records lineage once; it drifts as pipelines change unless something keeps it current.
wrong_explanations.D: Design-time diagrams show intended flows, which drift as pipelines change; they are not evidence of how data moves today.

tips: Eliminate: B records lineage once, at onboarding, and D documents intended flows that drift once pipelines change.
Final two: C beats A because system-generated evidence is more reliable than manually maintained records.
Exam cue: for evidence reliability, prefer system-generated, current records over manually maintained documentation.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the steering committee for a new ERP program. Which characteristic BEST indicates the committee can govern the program effectively?

options.A: It meets every week to review detailed task-level progress
options.B: Its members have authority to commit resources and decide
options.C: It is chaired by the project manager running the program
options.D: It is made up mostly of senior technical architects

questions.key_concept: A steering committee governs through decisions, so its members need authority to commit resources and resolve issues.
questions.pre_read: Separate governing (deciding and committing resources) from managing (tracking tasks).
questions.correct_explanation: A steering committee governs by making decisions on scope, funding and priorities, so its members must be senior business and IT stakeholders with authority to commit resources and resolve issues. Weekly task-level reviews come closest: they show engagement, but they pull the committee into management detail, which belongs to the project manager, and do not give it power to decide.

wrong_explanations.A: Task-level tracking is project management. A committee absorbed in detail may still lack the authority to decide.
wrong_explanations.C: The project manager reports to the committee. Chairing it would leave the manager overseeing their own performance.
wrong_explanations.D: Architects contribute expertise, but a committee without business decision makers cannot set priorities or commit funding.

tips: Eliminate: C has the manager oversee themselves, and D leaves out the business decision makers.
Final two: B beats A because governance needs decision authority; frequent detailed reviews are management, not governance.
Exam cue: effective project governance bodies have senior members with authority to decide and commit resources.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds hundreds of production feature flags whose purpose no one can explain, some toggled outside the release process. Which control is MOST important?

options.A: Require a change ticket for every production flag toggle
options.B: Run a yearly cleanup assigning owners, expiry dates and purposes
options.C: Restrict production flag toggles to the operations team
options.D: Govern flags as code with owners, expiry and change logs

questions.key_concept: Feature flags need lifecycle governance: versioned definitions, named owners, retirement dates and logged, authorized changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether flipping a production flag is any different from deploying a change.
questions.correct_explanation: Changing a production flag changes production behavior, so it needs the same discipline as code: an accountable owner, a planned expiry and a logged, authorized change trail. That addresses both findings, flags nobody can explain and toggling outside the release process. A yearly cleanup that assigns owners is the tempting option, but it acts once a year and leaves toggles changing production without a logged, authorized trail in between.

wrong_explanations.A: Change tickets bring toggles into change control, but hundreds of flags still have no owner, purpose or expiry.
wrong_explanations.B: A cleanup drive sensibly clears a flag backlog, yet an ongoing gap is not one-off debt: recurring risks need standing controls.
wrong_explanations.C: Restricting who toggles adds access control, but flags still lack owners, expiry and an authorized, logged change trail.

tips: Eliminate: A and C control only how flags change, by ticket or by restricted access, while hundreds of flags still have no owner, purpose or expiry.
Final two: D beats B because ownership and change control must be continuous; a yearly cleanup assigns owners once and leaves toggles unlogged between cleanups.
Exam cue: a production toggle is a production change; expect ownership, authorization and an audit trail.

questions.question: After a defective release disrupted payments, management proposes blue-green deployment, with both environments built from one template, for a payment app. Which risk should the IS auditor raise as GREATEST?

options.A: A defect reaches every customer at once before switch-back
options.B: Change approvals relaxed because switching back looks easy
options.C: The idle environment drifting out of step with live settings
options.D: Customers facing long downtime while traffic switches between environments

questions.key_concept: Blue-green deployment moves all users at once; it limits downtime, not exposure, so a defect reaches every customer until switch-back.
questions.pre_read: Recall what blue-green deployment limits and what it does not. Then picture the next faulty release.
questions.correct_explanation: Blue-green deployment keeps two identical environments and switches all traffic to the new one at once. It allows a fast switch back and near-zero downtime, but every customer meets a defect before anyone reverses it, repeating the failed release's harm. Relaxed approvals are the tempting option: they are a real behavior risk, but change management can control them, while all-at-once exposure is built into blue-green and happens on every release.

wrong_explanations.B: Complacent approvals are a genuine hazard when rollback seems cheap, but risks are ranked by what remains once existing controls have acted.
wrong_explanations.C: Both environments are built from one template, which controls drift; all-at-once exposure is built into blue-green and no template removes it.
wrong_explanations.D: Blue-green switches traffic almost instantly, so long downtime is the problem it solves, not one it creates.

tips: Eliminate: C is controlled by building both environments from one template, and D gets blue-green backwards, since it avoids downtime.
Final two: A beats B because all-at-once exposure is built into blue-green and recurs on every release, while relaxed approvals are behavior change management can control.
Exam cue: blue-green limits downtime, canary limits exposure; match the deployment strategy to the risk the stem names.

questions.question: An IS auditor's post-implementation review shows a new procurement system has delivered half its promised savings. Who should MOST appropriately own the corrective action plan?

options.A: The business sponsor of the project
options.B: The project manager who delivered the new system
options.C: The PMO that tracks benefits across the portfolio
options.D: The finance director accountable for the savings budget

questions.key_concept: Benefits realization is a business responsibility: the sponsor who committed to the benefits owns the plan to close a shortfall.
questions.pre_read: Ask who promised the savings in the business case, and whose role continues after the project closes.
questions.correct_explanation: Benefits belong to the business: the sponsor who committed to the savings in the business case is accountable for realizing them, including process changes, adoption and any further investment. The PMO is the tempting option because it tracks benefits across the portfolio, but tracking is not ownership; it cannot change the business processes and adoption that drive the savings.

wrong_explanations.B: The project manager's role ends at delivery and closure. Shortfalls often stem from business adoption and processes beyond their authority.
wrong_explanations.C: The PMO tracks and reports benefits across projects, but it does not own the business processes or adoption that deliver them.
wrong_explanations.D: Finance tracks the savings in the budget, but it does not own the processes and adoption that deliver them; the sponsor committed to the benefits.

tips: Eliminate: B's mandate ends at delivery and closure, before benefits are realized, and D accounts for savings without owning how the business delivers them.
Final two: A beats C because the sponsor who committed to the savings owns realizing them; the PMO tracks benefits but cannot change how the business works.
Exam cue: benefits realization is a business responsibility; look for the sponsor or business owner, not IT, the PMO or audit.

questions.question: Because the business owner is already measuring benefits in the post-implementation review of a new trade settlement system, which question should the IS auditor's own work MOST directly answer?

options.A: Whether the designed controls operate and meet their objectives
options.B: Whether the project finished within its approved budget and schedule
options.C: Whether users find the new screens easier than the old ones
options.D: Whether developers followed the coding standard during the build

questions.key_concept: In a post-implementation review, the IS auditor adds assurance on whether designed controls work in live operation and meet their objectives.
questions.pre_read: Benefits remain central, and the business owner is already measuring them. Ask what assurance only the auditor is placed to add.
questions.correct_explanation: Benefits remain the review's central question, and here the business owner is measuring them, so the auditor adds most value by testing whether the controls designed into the system work in live operation and meet their objectives, such as complete and accurate settlement. Budget and schedule performance comes closest: it is reviewed at closure, but on-time delivery can still leave settlement risks uncontrolled.

wrong_explanations.B: Budget and schedule are the usual measures of a finished project; once a system is live, the audit question moves from project to product.
wrong_explanations.C: Usability matters for adoption, but a preference for screens is not an assurance question about controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Coding standard compliance is a build-phase quality check. After go-live, the question is whether controls work in operation.

tips: Eliminate: C measures user preference, an adoption input the business owner tracks, and D checks build practice rather than live results.
Final two: A beats B because the auditor's value is assurance over live controls; on-budget delivery does not show risk is controlled.
Exam cue: in a post-implementation review, the IS auditor asks whether controls met their objectives in live operation.

questions.question: A new lending application approves loans using configurable limit tables instead of hard-coded rules. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST important in the design?

options.A: Hard-coding the limits so changes require a software release
options.B: Letting business users edit limits to respond quickly
options.C: Requiring logged, authorized approval for every limit change
options.D: Reviewing the limit tables once a year during the audit

questions.key_concept: Configurable parameters change system behavior like code does; design them with restricted access, approval and change logging.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changes the way loans are approved without any code change, and who should control it.
questions.correct_explanation: Configurable limit tables change how the application approves loans without any code change, so the design should restrict who can change them and require approval and a logged record of every change. Hard-coding the limits nearly wins: changes would pass through release management, but it removes the flexibility the business needs and pushes simple limit updates through a slow development cycle.

wrong_explanations.A: Hard-coding forces change control but makes every limit update a software release, defeating the design's purpose and inviting workarounds.
wrong_explanations.B: Open editing lets anyone change lending limits without approval or a record, which is the risk the control should address.
wrong_explanations.D: An annual audit review is not a management control. Unauthorized changes could operate for months before anyone notices.

tips: Eliminate: B removes authorization over limits, and D relies on an annual audit instead of a built-in control.
Final two: C beats A because controlled, logged changes keep both flexibility and accountability; hard-coding gives up flexibility.
Exam cue: configurable parameters are as powerful as code; design them with access restriction, approval and change logging.

questions.question: A migration team plans to convert three years of transaction history and discard the older 12 years. What should the IS auditor confirm FIRST?

options.A: That the new system has storage for the full history
options.B: That retention requirements for the older records are met
options.C: That users agree three years is enough for their daily work
options.D: That the discarded records are encrypted before deletion

questions.key_concept: Before any irreversible migration step, confirm legal, regulatory and contractual retention requirements are met, for example by archiving.
questions.pre_read: Discarding records cannot be undone. Ask what obligation applies to those records regardless of daily use.
questions.correct_explanation: Discarding records is irreversible, so before conversion the auditor should confirm that legal, regulatory and contractual retention requirements for the older 12 years are satisfied, for example by archiving them in a retrievable form. User agreement is the closest choice: business need decides what goes into the live system, but users cannot waive retention obligations that apply regardless of daily use.

wrong_explanations.A: Storage capacity is a technical question. Whether records may be discarded is decided by retention obligations, not by available space.
wrong_explanations.C: Users can say what they need day to day, but they cannot waive legal or regulatory retention obligations.
wrong_explanations.D: Encrypting records about to be deleted does not address whether deletion is allowed at all.

tips: Eliminate: A answers a capacity question, and D protects records whose deletion may itself be the problem.
Final two: B beats C because retention obligations bind regardless of what users need day to day.
Exam cue: before any irreversible data step in a migration, confirm legal and regulatory requirements are satisfied.

questions.question: The project manager who delivered a new HR system proposes to lead its post-implementation review. What is the IS auditor's PRIMARY concern?

options.A: The review may focus on delivery process rather than business outcomes
options.B: The review may rely on project status reports rather than operating data
options.C: The project manager may lack the business knowledge to judge benefits
options.D: The reviewer would be judging the results of their own work

questions.key_concept: A post-implementation review needs an objective reviewer; the person who delivered the system faces a self-review threat.
questions.pre_read: Ask who benefits if the review finds the project a success, then ask whether that person should write the verdict.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-implementation review must give the sponsor an objective view of whether the system delivered what was promised. A project manager reviewing their own delivery faces a self-review threat and an incentive to present results favorably, so an independent party should lead it. A process-heavy focus is the closest concern: it is a real scoping risk, but it is a symptom of the missing independence, not the root concern.

wrong_explanations.A: A narrow focus on delivery process is a scoping weakness, but it stems from the reviewer's conflict of interest, which is the root concern.
wrong_explanations.B: Relying on status reports is a real evidence weakness, but it follows from who leads the review; the root concern is self-review.
wrong_explanations.C: Business knowledge can be added through sponsors and users; a competence gap is fixable, while judging one's own work undermines every conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: B is an evidence choice an independent reviewer would correct, and C is a competence gap that business participants can fill.
Final two: D beats A because a self-review threat undermines every conclusion; drift toward process is only a symptom of it.
Exam cue: whoever built it should not be the one to judge it; look for the independence problem before the scope problem.

questions.question: A CIO plans to promote a successful machine-learning proof of concept straight into production, although it has no error handling, monitoring or rollback. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Run a code review and penetration test before promotion
options.B: Rebuild the solution from scratch as a separate production project
options.C: Run the model in shadow mode for a quarter before release
options.D: Require production-readiness criteria and a staged rollout

questions.key_concept: A proof of concept must pass production-readiness criteria, including resilience, monitoring, rollback and ownership, before staged release.
questions.pre_read: Name the kind of gaps in the stem, security or operational. Then ask what must be true before any release.
questions.correct_explanation: A proof of concept shows value in a controlled setting; it is not built for live data, scale or support. Production-readiness criteria covering error handling, monitoring, rollback and ownership, followed by a staged rollout, close every gap before release. Shadow running is the tempting option because it gathers live evidence safely, but it sets no readiness gate, so the missing controls are still missing when the model goes live.

wrong_explanations.A: Code review and penetration testing check security, but the stated gaps are error handling, monitoring and rollback, which neither adds.
wrong_explanations.B: A rebuild may prove right, but committing to it first skips the readiness criteria that show what is actually missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Shadow mode gathers evidence without customer impact, but it defines no readiness gate, so error handling, monitoring and rollback remain missing.

tips: Eliminate: A tests security, though the gaps are operational resilience, and B commits to a rebuild before readiness criteria show what is missing.
Final two: D beats C because readiness criteria close every gap before release; shadow running gathers evidence but sets no gate.
Exam cue: a proof of concept is not production. Expect readiness gates and staged rollout before release.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a waterfall plan, with requirements fixed before design starts, for a novel control system whose technical feasibility is unproven. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep waterfall and add a risk review at each phase gate
options.B: Adopt a spiral model that resolves the biggest risks first
options.C: Switch to rapid application development with minimal design reviews
options.D: Switch to Kanban, pulling small work items as capacity allows

questions.key_concept: The spiral model suits large, high-risk developments: each cycle identifies and resolves the biggest risks before more effort is committed.
questions.pre_read: Match the method to the uncertainty. Ask which method deals with the biggest risks first.
questions.correct_explanation: The spiral model fits large, high-risk developments: each cycle identifies and resolves the biggest risks, often with prototypes, before more effort is committed, so an infeasible approach surfaces early and cheaply. Risk reviews at waterfall gates are the tempting option because they add control, but the plan still fixes requirements before feasibility is proven, so the critical problem surfaces late.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk reviews at gates spot problems, but a plan that fixes requirements first still learns about feasibility late, when change is costly.
wrong_explanations.C: Rapid development speeds delivery, but cutting design review is a poor fit for a high-risk control system.
wrong_explanations.D: Kanban suits a flow of small, independent work items; it does not structure risk reduction for a novel build.

tips: Eliminate: C cuts review where risk is highest, and D manages a stream of small tasks without structuring risk reduction for a novel build.
Final two: B beats A because spiral attacks the biggest risks first; gate reviews in a fixed waterfall plan still learn about feasibility late.
Exam cue: match the method to the uncertainty; high technical risk points to risk-driven, iterative methods.

questions.question: A project is required to meet a new regulation and shows no financial return. How should the IS auditor expect the business case to MOST appropriately justify it?

options.A: By the obligation and its most cost-effective compliance option
options.B: By a projected return estimated from possible efficiency gains
options.C: By its alignment with the IT strategic plan
options.D: By a compliance risk score in a weighted model

questions.key_concept: Mandatory projects are justified by the obligation itself; the business case compares options to comply at the lowest cost and risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask why this investment is being made at all, then ask what a business case should compare when doing nothing is not allowed.
questions.correct_explanation: Mandatory projects are justified by the obligation itself: the business case should state the regulatory requirement and the consequences of non-compliance, then compare options to meet it at the lowest cost and risk. Estimating efficiency gains is the strongest alternative: genuine side benefits can be noted, but inventing a return to fit a financial template misstates why the investment is being made.

wrong_explanations.B: A projected return decides discretionary spending; once regulation rules out doing nothing, the case compares ways to comply.
wrong_explanations.C: Every investment should align with strategy, but alignment does not state why this one is required or compare ways to comply.
wrong_explanations.D: A weighted score ranks discretionary investments against each other; a mandatory project is not competing for approval, so the case should state the obligation and compare ways to comply.

tips: Eliminate: C cites strategic fit, which neither states the obligation nor compares ways to comply, and D ranks the project against others, though it is not competing for approval.
Final two: A beats B because a mandatory project is justified by the obligation and the most cost-effective compliant option, not a manufactured return.
Exam cue: when doing nothing is not allowed, the business case states the obligation and compares compliant options; it never invents a return.

questions.question: A business case lists benefits such as improved efficiency and better customer experience, stated only in general terms. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before approval?

options.A: Convert every benefit into a financial value before approval
options.B: Ask IT to measure the benefits once the system is live
options.C: Define measurable targets with a business owner for each benefit
options.D: Approve now and have each benefit owner set targets after go-live

questions.key_concept: Every promised benefit needs a measurable target, a baseline and a named business owner before the investment is approved.
questions.pre_read: Ask how anyone could later prove these benefits arrived, and who would answer if they did not.
questions.correct_explanation: Benefits stated in general terms cannot be measured or managed, so the case should give each benefit a measurable target, a baseline and a named business owner accountable for realizing it. Converting every benefit into money is the tempting option: it looks rigorous, but non-financial benefits can be measured without a price, and a valuation with no owner leaves no one accountable for delivering it.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would accept money values where conversion is reliable, but a figure's precision never substitutes for someone answering for it.
wrong_explanations.B: IT can supply measurements, but business owners are accountable for benefits, and undefined benefits give nothing to measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Setting targets after go-live lets the review measure whatever happened; even with named owners, targets must be set before approval.

tips: Eliminate: B hands benefits to IT after go-live, and D sets targets after the results are known.
Final two: C beats A because measurable targets need not be financial, and only a named business owner makes someone accountable.
Exam cue: before approval, every benefit needs a measurable target, a baseline and a named business owner; a price tag alone is not a target.

questions.subtopic: Post-Implementation Review. Which Changes to Review
questions.question: Management wants a full post-implementation review after every system change, including minor screen fixes. Which basis should the IS auditor recommend as BEST for deciding when a review is needed?

options.A: A yearly risk review of each system, whatever has changed
options.B: Reviews triggered when users complain about a change
options.C: Full reviews of every change, so that nothing is missed
options.D: The significance and risk of the change, set in policy

questions.key_concept: Post-implementation review effort should be scaled to the significance and risk of the change, defined in policy.
questions.pre_read: Reviews cost effort. Ask which basis puts that effort where failure would matter most.
questions.correct_explanation: Reviews cost effort, so policy should scale them to the significance and risk of the change: major systems and high-risk changes get a full review, while minor fixes are covered by change management and lighter checks. A yearly review cycle nearly wins: it is predictable, but it follows the calendar, so a major change may wait a year while stable systems are reviewed.

wrong_explanations.A: A yearly cycle is predictable but not tied to change; a major change could wait months while stable systems consume effort.
wrong_explanations.B: Complaint-driven reviews are reactive. Control failures and missed benefits often go unnoticed by users.
wrong_explanations.C: Fully reviewing every change wastes effort on trivial fixes and dilutes attention from the changes that matter.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for complaints, though users rarely notice failed controls or missed benefits, and C spends full review effort on trivial and major changes alike.
Final two: D beats A because review effort should follow risk and significance, not the calendar.
Exam cue: when a choice is about where to spend review or audit effort, the risk-based option usually wins.

questions.question: Four months after go-live, a post-implementation review finds that 35% of sales staff use the new CRM while the rest keep personal spreadsheets. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Recommend that management mandate CRM use through policy
options.B: Determine why staff are not using the new system
options.C: Recommend refresher CRM training for the sales staff
options.D: Report that the project failed to deliver its benefits

questions.key_concept: Low adoption is a symptom; establish its root cause before recommending a remedy.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing a fix, ask whether you yet know why staff avoid the system.
questions.correct_explanation: Low adoption is a symptom. Before recommending anything, the auditor should establish the cause, such as missing functions, poor training, slow performance or data quality, because the right remedy depends on it. Mandating use is the most tempting alternative: it may raise usage figures, but if the system does not fit how staff work, forced use can produce poor data and hide the real problem.

wrong_explanations.A: A mandate and a cause analysis share the goal of getting sales data into the CRM. A remedy chosen before diagnosis is a guess, though.
wrong_explanations.C: Training assumes the cause is skill; if the system lacks functions staff need, more training will not change their behavior.
wrong_explanations.D: Concluding failure before understanding the cause is premature. The cause shapes what the report should say.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the cause is a lack of skill, and D concludes before the facts are known.
Final two: B beats A because the remedy depends on the cause; a mandate may force usage without fixing why staff avoid the system.
Exam cue: when a review finds a symptom, the FIRST step is to find its root cause before recommending a fix.

questions.question: At hour 28 of a 48-hour ERP cutover, 12,000 supplier records are found with inconsistent country codes, a case the playbook does not cover. What is the IS auditor's BEST advice?

options.A: Pause at the gate and size the fix before going further
options.B: Proceed with the cutover and clean the supplier data after go-live
options.C: Roll back now, since the cutover plan is fundamentally flawed
options.D: Take the go/no-go decision on management's behalf to save time

questions.key_concept: Unexpected cutover issues should be assessed at a decision gate, then management proceeds or falls back based on evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice the issue is outside the playbook. Ask which option assesses impact before committing, and who decides.
questions.correct_explanation: A sound cutover uses decision gates so that unexpected issues are assessed before commitment. Pausing to size the fix and judge whether it fits the window lets management proceed or invoke fallback on evidence. Proceeding and cleaning up later keeps the schedule, but it loads known-bad master data into production without assessing the effect on supplier transactions.

wrong_explanations.B: Proceeding does protect a hard-to-rebook 48-hour window, yet it accepts a risk nobody has sized, and only sized risk can be accepted.
wrong_explanations.C: One unforeseen data issue does not prove the whole plan is flawed. Rollback should follow an assessment, not replace it.
wrong_explanations.D: The auditor advises but must not make management's operational decisions; doing so impairs independence.

tips: Eliminate: C reverts over one issue before its size is known, and D has the auditor take a decision that belongs to management.
Final two: A beats B because a risk-based decision at the gate assesses impact before committing bad data to production.
Exam cue: when a surprise arises mid-cutover and time remains, assess at the decision gate; revert at once only when integrity is unknown and time has run out.

questions.question: After $14M and four months, a new CRM module has won 23 of its 150 target customers. Which advice from the IS auditor to the board is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Stop the module, because the $14M already spent makes recovery uneconomic
options.B: Continue, but rebaseline the target at 50 customers
options.C: Weigh forward costs and benefits against the alternatives
options.D: Weigh total cost to date and future benefits against alternatives

questions.key_concept: Investment continue-or-stop decisions compare forward costs and benefits against alternatives and exclude sunk cost.
questions.pre_read: Notice the $14M already spent. Ask which options let it into the decision, openly or inside a total.
questions.correct_explanation: Money already spent cannot be recovered whichever way the board decides, so it must not drive the choice. The decision should compare the remaining cost and expected benefits of continuing against alternatives, such as other products or a sale of the technology. Weighing total cost to date is the tempting option because it looks complete, but it brings the sunk $14M back into the comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: The conclusion may be right, but the stated reason is sunk cost. Past spend is irrelevant to whether future spend is worthwhile.
wrong_explanations.B: Rebaselining lowers the target to fit results without asking whether further spend is worthwhile; it is escalation of commitment to a failing course.
wrong_explanations.D: Both weighings set the module's future benefits beside the alternatives, yet a decision weighs only what the decision itself can still change.

tips: Eliminate: A justifies stopping by money already spent, and B moves the target instead of assessing whether further spend is worthwhile.
Final two: C beats D because only future costs and benefits differ between the choices; cost to date is sunk whichever way the board decides.
Exam cue: decide on future costs and benefits only; money already spent is the same whichever way you choose.

questions.question: Eleven months into a 24-month integration, 70% of the budget is spent but 32% of milestones are done, and the CIO requests $20M more. What should the IS auditor recommend to the board FIRST?

options.A: Approve the request, as integrations commonly need extra funding
options.B: Cancel the integration and run both firms separately
options.C: Release the funds in tranches tied to the CIO's own revised milestones
options.D: Commission an independent review and rebaseline before releasing funds

questions.key_concept: A troubled program needs an independent review and rebaselined plan before more funding is committed.
questions.pre_read: Notice the gap between spend and progress. Ask which option tests the plan before money is released.
questions.correct_explanation: Spend running well ahead of delivery means the current plan cannot be trusted. An independent review that rebaselines scope, schedule and cost gives the board a reliable footing before more money is committed. Tranche funding is a good control, but tying it to milestones set by the same leadership builds gates on an unvalidated plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving more money on industry norms ignores the evidence that the current plan and leadership are failing.
wrong_explanations.B: Canceling ends the integration before anyone has assessed whether it can recover, and the deal's rationale still depends on combining the two firms.
wrong_explanations.C: Gated funding helps, but gates based on an unvalidated plan from the same leadership cannot restore the board's confidence.

tips: Eliminate: A funds a failing plan without testing why it slipped, and B ends the integration before any assessment shows it cannot recover.
Final two: D beats C because an independent rebaseline must come before gates; gates built on an unvalidated plan add little assurance.
Exam cue: when a project is far off track and confidence is lost, an independent review and an approved rebaseline come before new funding.

questions.question: Few recommendations from two years of post-implementation reviews were implemented, and no one can say who was meant to act on them. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Repeat each review a year later to see what has changed
options.B: Assign each recommendation an owner and date, tracked to closure
options.C: Record a target date for each recommendation in the report
options.D: Make the PMO accountable for closing open recommendations

questions.key_concept: Review recommendations get implemented when each has a named owner, a due date and status tracked to closure.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the recommendations stalled. Then pick the option that makes someone answerable for each one.
questions.correct_explanation: Recommendations stall when no one is accountable. Giving each one a named owner and due date, with status tracked to closure and reported to governance, creates accountability and evidence of action. Making the PMO accountable is the tempting option: it creates one point of follow-up, but the PMO cannot change the business processes concerned, so each recommendation needs an owner in the area that must act.

wrong_explanations.A: A second review would confirm the backlog again. It adds cost without making anyone responsible for acting.
wrong_explanations.C: A target date sets a deadline, but with no named owner and no tracking, nobody is answerable when it passes.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would welcome the PMO as tracker and chaser, but follow-up is a service and ownership a duty; only duties close findings.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats the review without creating accountability, and C adds a date with no one named to meet it and no tracking to notice a miss.
Final two: B beats D because accountability must sit with whoever can act; the PMO can follow up but cannot change the business processes involved.
Exam cue: for findings that never get fixed, look for named owners, due dates and tracking to closure.

questions.question: Management proposes insourcing 60% of outsourced application development over 24 months after vendor delays and a 28% price rise. Which input is MOST important to the IS auditor's assessment of the decision?

options.A: A multi-year business case comparing both delivery models
options.B: The regulator's stated concern about third-party concentration risk
options.C: The in-house team's current skills and hiring capacity
options.D: The vendor's exit terms and its transition assistance obligations

questions.key_concept: Insourcing decisions rest on a multi-year business case comparing the total cost of each option, made before any exit commitment.
questions.pre_read: Ask which input answers whether to insource at all, and which matters only once that is settled.
questions.correct_explanation: A sourcing change is a major investment with execution risk, so the decision must rest on a multi-year business case comparing the total cost of insourcing, including capability build-up and transition, with staying outsourced. The vendor's exit terms are the tempting input because leaving depends on them, but they inform how to exit, not whether insourcing beats staying outsourced.

wrong_explanations.B: Concentration risk is one reason to act, but it does not show whether insourcing is affordable or achievable.
wrong_explanations.C: Skills and hiring capacity are a key feasibility and risk input, but one factor the business case weighs; alone they do not show whether insourcing beats staying outsourced.
wrong_explanations.D: Exit terms shape transition cost and risk, but they matter once the business case shows insourcing is the better option.

tips: Eliminate: B is a regulator's concern that does not test whether insourcing is affordable, and C is one input the business case weighs (cost, time and execution risk), not the comparison itself.
Final two: A beats D because the decision rests on comparing both models; exit terms matter once leaving is justified.
Exam cue: for a sourcing change, settle whether to change before how; the business case comparing both models comes before exit terms.

questions.question: Legacy supplier data contains many duplicates and outdated addresses ahead of conversion to a new procurement system. Which approach should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Load the data unchanged and cleanse it after go-live
options.B: Let conversion scripts drop any record that fails validation
options.C: Cleanse before loading, with changes approved by the data owner
options.D: Have the system owner approve developer fixes after the data is loaded

questions.key_concept: Cleanse data before loading it into the new system, with the data owner authorizing each change.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether known bad data should ever enter production, and who may authorize changing it.
questions.correct_explanation: Cleansing before loading means the new system starts with accurate data and its controls are not undermined by known errors, and data owner approval ensures each change is authorized and recorded. Loading as is and cleansing later comes closest: it protects the schedule, but known bad data enters production, and cleanup after go-live is often deprioritized and harder to control.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would tolerate deferred cleanup of descriptive fields on a tracked plan, but defects are cheapest to fix before production.
wrong_explanations.B: Silently dropping failed records loses data and hides the problem. Rejected records need review, not deletion.
wrong_explanations.D: Fixing after loading lets known errors enter production first, and the system owner is not the data owner who answers for the records' meaning.

tips: Eliminate: B silently loses records, and D fixes errors after loading, approved by the system owner rather than the data owner.
Final two: C beats A because known errors should be fixed and approved before they enter production.
Exam cue: known defects are fixed before they enter production, not deferred; changes to business data need the data owner's approval.

questions.question: Management leans toward canceling a paused program that is $22M over budget, though three business units already use its delivered modules. Which risk should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Retraining costs for the three units returning to old processes
options.B: Loss of the vendor's specialist knowledge of the delivered modules
options.C: Write-off of the $22M already spent
options.D: Disruption to live processes relying on the partial system

questions.key_concept: Cancellation decisions must weigh exit complexity, especially disruption to processes already relying on delivered components, above bounded contractual costs.
questions.pre_read: Notice that business units already use parts of the program. Ask what stopping it would do to them.
questions.correct_explanation: Canceling is a management decision, but it must account for exit complexity. Three business units already run live processes on the delivered modules, so stopping without a transition plan could halt operations, a larger and less reversible impact than any one-off cost. Retraining the three units is a real cost to weigh, but it is bounded and plannable, unlike disruption to the business.

wrong_explanations.A: Before leaving a program, protect what already runs. Retraining is a cost any exit must fund, yet live operations come first in every exit plan.
wrong_explanations.B: Knowledge loss matters for future support, but it can be handled through transition terms; it is not the immediate exposure of live operations.
wrong_explanations.C: Spend already made is sunk; it is lost whichever way management decides, so it is not a risk created by canceling.

tips: Eliminate: B is a support issue manageable through transition terms, and C is sunk cost, lost whichever way management decides.
Final two: D beats A because disruption to live operations outweighs a bounded, plannable retraining cost.
Exam cue: when stopping a system others rely on, weigh business continuity and exit complexity before cost.

questions.subtopic: Distributed Agile Teams Across Time Zones
questions.question: Across six time zones, an IS auditor finds decisions made in US hours are not recorded, and developers merge code without review to avoid 18-hour waits. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Record decisions in a shared log and review merges after the fact
options.B: Appoint one lead per time zone to relay decisions to their team
options.C: Record decisions and block merges until a US-based reviewer approves
options.D: Document decisions and assign reviewers in every time zone

questions.key_concept: Distributed teams need written decisions and review capacity in each time zone, so controls fit the way the work is spread.
questions.pre_read: Notice two findings and what drives them. Ask which option removes the cause rather than only enforcing the control.
questions.correct_explanation: Both findings come from a process built around one time zone: decisions live in US meetings and reviews wait for US reviewers, so developers bypass them. Written decisions give every site the same record, and reviewers in each time zone remove the wait that drives the bypass. Recording decisions and blocking merges for US approval is the tempting option: it covers both findings but keeps the 18-hour wait.

wrong_explanations.A: A shared log fixes the record, but reviewing merges after the fact lets unreviewed code into the main branch; review belongs before the merge.
wrong_explanations.B: Relayed decisions are still unrecorded and depend on one person, and the review delay that drives the bypass is untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Recording decisions fixes one finding and blocking merges enforces review, but the 18-hour wait remains, so the pressure to work around it stays.

tips: Eliminate: A reviews merges only after the code is in, which detects rather than prevents, and B relays decisions without recording them or touching the review delay.
Final two: D beats C because it removes the wait that drives the bypass; blocking merges for US approval enforces review but keeps the 18-hour delay.
Exam cue: when people bypass a control, fix the process gap that drives the bypass rather than only tightening enforcement.

questions.question: Eight product teams deploy independently to shared production, and six recent incidents came from one team's change breaking another's feature. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST control?

options.A: Coordinate releases by risk tier, backed by interface contracts
options.B: Joint risk, test and rollback sign-off by eight teams on every release
options.C: Give each team its own separate production environment
options.D: Cut each team's release frequency to once a month

questions.key_concept: Multi-team release coordination should be risk-tiered, with interface contracts catching cross-team breaks before release.
questions.pre_read: Notice the incidents come from interactions between teams. Ask which option targets those changes without slowing all others.
questions.correct_explanation: Cross-team incidents come from changes to shared interfaces. Risk-tiered coordination, as COBIT BAI06 expects, focuses review on changes that can affect others, while interface contracts and contract tests catch breaks before release. A joint review by all teams sounds thorough, but it adds delay to every low-risk change and gives teams a reason to bypass the process.

wrong_explanations.B: Change control scales only when scrutiny follows impact. Joint sign-off does involve every affected team, yet attention spread evenly starves the few risky changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Separate production environments do not reflect how shared services interact, and the integration risk returns when they connect.
wrong_explanations.D: Fewer, larger releases bundle more changes together, which raises the risk of each release rather than lowering it.

tips: Eliminate: C separates environments although the services must still interact in production, and D makes each release larger and riskier.
Final two: A beats B because risk-based coordination targets the changes that matter, while universal review adds delay without focus.
Exam cue: for change control at scale, prefer risk-tiered controls over uniform heavy review of every change.

questions.question: In week 14 of a 20-week release, executives have added 16 features; velocity fell 28% and QA tests cover only the original scope. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add QA testers so testing keeps pace with the additions
options.B: Freeze further additions and defer the 16 to the next release
options.C: Put each addition through formal change control and rebaseline
options.D: Extend the test plan to cover the added features

questions.key_concept: Scope creep is controlled by formal change control and rebaselining, so management decides each addition on its impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word FIRST. Ask whether to fix the cause, uncontrolled scope, or one of its symptoms.
questions.correct_explanation: The root problem is scope entering without assessment of cost, schedule and quality impact. Routing each addition through formal change control and rebaselining the release lets management decide which features to keep, defer or fund with more time. Extending the test plan is needed, but done first it accepts every addition as given and leaves scope uncontrolled.

wrong_explanations.A: More testers treat a resourcing symptom; additions still enter without any assessment of their cost, schedule or quality impact.
wrong_explanations.B: A freeze stops new additions, but deferring all 16 without assessing their value or impact is a blanket call; management should decide each through change control.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing the added features is necessary, but it accepts the uncontrolled scope rather than deciding what should stay.

tips: Eliminate: A adds resources to absorb uncontrolled scope, and B defers every addition unassessed, a call management should make after impact analysis.
Final two: C beats D because controlling scope comes first; extending tests accepts every addition without assessment.
Exam cue: for scope creep, formal change control and rebaselining come before work that absorbs the extra scope.

questions.question: A new CTO proposes merging 47 microservices into about 10, citing tripled operating cost and slower delivery, although reliability has improved 25%. Which decision basis should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: Aggregate cost, speed and reliability trends since the migration
options.B: Service-by-service analysis of value, coupling, cost and ownership
options.C: The original architect's view that reliability gains justify the cost
options.D: Industry benchmarks of how many services similar firms run

questions.key_concept: Architecture reversal decisions need per-service evidence on value, coupling, cost and ownership, not aggregate trends or advocacy.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence points both ways. Ask which option breaks the problem down to where the costs and benefits arise.
questions.correct_explanation: Aggregate figures hide which services earn their cost. Analyzing each service for the value it delivers, how tightly it is coupled to others, what it costs to run and who owns it shows where consolidation helps and where separation keeps the reliability gains. Platform-wide cost and speed trends are real evidence, but they cannot say which services to merge.

wrong_explanations.A: Platform-wide trends show a problem exists but cannot identify which services to merge, risking the reliability gains.
wrong_explanations.C: One stakeholder's view based on one metric ignores the tripled cost and slower delivery the firm is facing.
wrong_explanations.D: Benchmarks describe other firms' platforms, not which of these services earn their cost or carry the reliability gains.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on one person's view of one metric, and D relies on other firms' figures rather than this platform's.
Final two: B beats A because per-service analysis shows where to consolidate, while aggregate trends cannot.
Exam cue: for architecture reversal decisions, prefer granular evidence over aggregate metrics or advocates' positions.

questions.subtopic: Database Technology Selection. SQL vs NoSQL Trade-off
questions.question: A fleet-tracking application must ingest 1.6 million telemetry writes per second and also support relational queries. Which evidence is MOST important for the IS auditor to see before the database is selected?

options.A: Reference calls with customers already running the leading candidate engine
options.B: Vendor benchmark results showing similar write volumes per second
options.C: An assessment of the team's experience with each candidate engine
options.D: Proof-of-concept results for this system's workloads on each design

questions.key_concept: Technology selection should rest on evidence from tests against every documented workload before a choice is made, not on vendor claims or familiarity.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose workloads and whose configuration each kind of evidence reflects.
questions.correct_explanation: The strongest evidence is a proof of concept that runs this system's own workloads, the 1.6 million writes per second and the relational queries, against each candidate design before commitment. Vendor benchmarks are the tempting option: they show write capacity, but the vendor chose the configuration and the test, and they say nothing about the relational queries this system also needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Reference customers run different workloads and configurations; their satisfaction does not show fit for this system's write and query mix.
wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would treat vendor benchmarks as a reasonable shortlisting input, but a decision is tested against its own requirements, not someone else's showcase.
wrong_explanations.C: Team experience affects delivery risk, but it cannot show that any engine meets 1.6 million writes per second.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on other customers' different workloads, and C measures the team's skills, not whether an engine meets the stated workloads.
Final two: D beats B because evidence from this system's own workloads outranks vendor-run tests that cover only writes.
Exam cue: for a selection decision, prefer evidence produced against your own requirements before commitment over vendor or third-party claims.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a cloud migration plan covering strategic, stable utility and soon-to-retire applications. Which migration approach is BEST?

options.A: Refactor every application as cloud-native for one consistent architecture
options.B: Match each application's migration path to its business value
options.C: Let each app team pick rehost, replatform, refactor or retire
options.D: Rehost every application first, then refactor strategic ones after cutover

questions.key_concept: Cloud migration paths are matched to each application's business value at portfolio level, not applied uniformly or left to team preference.
questions.pre_read: Notice the portfolio mixes strategic, stable and retiring applications. Ask which approach respects those differences.
questions.correct_explanation: A mixed portfolio needs a migration path matched to each application's business value and lifespan: refactor what is strategic, replatform what is stable, rehost commodity systems and retire what is ending. Rehosting everything first sounds pragmatic, but it spends effort moving applications due for retirement and moves strategic ones twice, so the investment is not aligned to value.

wrong_explanations.A: Refactoring everything spends the most expensive treatment on stable and retiring applications that return little value from it.
wrong_explanations.C: Listing every path does not make the choice value-based; team preference replaces a portfolio decision, so costly treatments may go where value is low.
wrong_explanations.D: Rehosting first holds up only when a deadline, such as a data center exit, forces everyone out at once; otherwise each application's path follows its value.

tips: Eliminate: A applies the costliest treatment uniformly, and C leaves each path to team preference instead of business value.
Final two: B beats D because each application's path should follow its business value, not a uniform first step.
Exam cue: when a portfolio is mixed, prefer the option that differentiates by business value over any one-size-fits-all approach.

questions.question: A firm will migrate 40 applications, some of which exchange data in real time, to a new data center in waves. What should the IS auditor expect the migration team to do FIRST?

options.A: Move the applications by business unit, one unit per wave
options.B: Move the least critical applications first to gain experience
options.C: Map application and data dependencies to define the waves
options.D: Size the target data center for each wave's capacity

questions.key_concept: Map application, data and interface dependencies before sequencing migration waves, so tightly coupled systems move together.
questions.pre_read: Ask what breaks if one application moves without the systems it calls.
questions.correct_explanation: When applications exchange data, moving one without the systems it calls can break interfaces and batch flows, so the team must first map application, data and interface dependencies and group tightly coupled systems into the same wave. Starting with low-criticality applications is the tempting option: it is a sound sequencing principle, but it can be applied safely only once dependencies are known.

wrong_explanations.A: Business-unit waves are easy to organize, but units do not match technical dependencies, so tightly coupled systems can be split across waves.
wrong_explanations.B: Starting with less critical systems is sensible, but without a dependency map a minor application may still break critical ones.
wrong_explanations.D: Capacity sizing matters, but the waves must be defined first; sizing for waves drawn without dependencies plans around the wrong groups.

tips: Eliminate: A groups waves by business unit rather than by dependencies, and D sizes capacity for waves that have not yet been defined.
Final two: C beats B because sequencing by criticality works only once dependencies are known.
Exam cue: in migrations, map dependencies before deciding what moves when.

questions.question: A project manager has drawn down most of a project's management reserve, with no record of who authorized each drawdown. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Sponsor approval of each drawdown, with its reason documented
options.B: Monthly notice to the sponsor of the reserve balance
options.C: PMO review of reserve drawdowns at each stage gate
options.D: Project manager logging of each drawdown with its reason

questions.key_concept: Management reserve sits outside the cost baseline, so each drawdown needs sponsor or steering committee approval, with the reason recorded.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the issue is how much money there is, or who decides when it is used.
questions.correct_explanation: A management reserve covers unforeseen risks outside the cost baseline, so releasing it is a governance decision. Requiring sponsor approval for each drawdown, with the reason documented, keeps the accountable sponsor in control before money is spent. A project manager's log of each drawdown is the tempting option: it creates the missing record, but the manager still decides alone, so the log documents spending no one authorized.

wrong_explanations.B: The sponsor learns the balance only after the money is spent; the notice detects use of the reserve but does not authorize it.
wrong_explanations.C: The PMO does not own the reserve, and stage-gate reviews come after drawdowns; neither authorizes the spend.
wrong_explanations.D: A log records each drawdown and why, but the project manager still authorizes their own use of the reserve; release belongs to the sponsor.

tips: Eliminate: B tells the sponsor the balance only after the money is spent, and C hands review to the PMO, which does not own the reserve, at later stage gates.
Final two: A beats D because a log records drawdowns but leaves the manager authorizing their own; releasing the reserve is the sponsor's decision.
Exam cue: management reserve is released by the sponsor or steering committee; contingency for planned risk responses is managed within the project.

questions.question: After a successful cutover to a new ERP system, management wants to shut down the legacy system next week. What should the IS auditor confirm FIRST?

options.A: That the legacy hardware has a buyer or a disposal contract
options.B: That business users have stopped logging in to the legacy system
options.C: That legacy user accounts have been disabled
options.D: That reconciliation is signed off and legacy data is archived

questions.key_concept: Decommission a legacy system only after final reconciliation is signed off and its records are archived in an accessible form.
questions.pre_read: Ask what you lose for good when the old system is switched off.
questions.correct_explanation: Shutting down the legacy system removes the last way to check or recover converted data. The auditor should first confirm that the business has signed off final reconciliation and that legacy data needed for retention or inquiry is archived in an accessible form. Users having stopped logging in is the closest choice: it shows adoption, but not that the data is complete or preserved.

wrong_explanations.A: Disposal arrangements come later. Selling hardware before data is preserved could lose records permanently.
wrong_explanations.B: Users leaving the legacy system shows adoption. It does not prove converted data is complete or that records are retained.
wrong_explanations.C: Disabling accounts is a routine deprovisioning step, but shutdown ends access anyway; what cannot be undone is losing data no one reconciled or archived.

tips: Eliminate: A is commercial clean-up that can wait until the data questions are settled, and C removes access that the shutdown itself will end.
Final two: D beats B because sign-off and archiving protect the data; users leaving the old system shows adoption, not completeness.
Exam cue: never retire the old system until the new data is reconciled and the old records are preserved.

questions.question: A federal contractor's contract requires a minimum software supply-chain (SLSA) level; the CISO wants the top level, costing about $8M over 18 months. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Commit now to the top level as the lowest-risk position
options.B: Meet the mandated level first, then raise levels by risk
options.C: Pick a mid level matching what peer contractors report
options.D: Reach the mandated level on new releases first, legacy later

questions.key_concept: Assurance targets are set by risk: meet mandatory requirements, then invest in higher maturity where risk reduction justifies the cost, with reassessment gates.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the contract requires now from what risk might justify later.
questions.correct_explanation: A maturity target should first meet the level the contract requires, then rise in phases where the risk reduction justifies the cost, with gates to reassess as requirements evolve. Committing to the top level appears thorough, but it fixes an $8M spend before the firm knows which risks justify it, and it may delay meeting the contract's requirement while the full program is built.

wrong_explanations.A: The top level is a legitimate long-term aim, but compliance sets the floor and risk prices each step above it.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying peers ignores the firm's own contractual floor and risk profile, so the target is neither compliance-based nor risk-based.
wrong_explanations.D: Phasing by release leaves legacy software delivered under the contract below the required level; the contractual minimum applies to every covered product.

tips: Eliminate: C copies peers instead of using the firm's own requirements and risk, and D phases by release, leaving legacy software below the contract's minimum.
Final two: B beats A because investment should follow risk and required compliance, not maximum maturity for its own sake.
Exam cue: contractual requirements set the floor for every covered product; risk then decides where to invest beyond it.
