questions.question: After a loan-system conversion, auditors cannot link converted balances to the source records they came from. Which conversion control would MOST directly have prevented this?

options.A: A retained cross-reference of legacy keys to new keys
options.B: Record counts and totals reconciled to the legacy system
options.C: User acceptance testing of the new loan screens
options.D: Field mappings for legacy account numbers, approved by the data owner

questions.key_concept: Conversion traceability needs a retained cross-reference from each legacy key to its new key, plus conversion logs.
questions.pre_read: Separate completeness (did everything arrive?) from traceability (where did this record come from?).
questions.correct_explanation: Traceability needs a retained record linking each legacy account key to its new key, together with conversion logs, so any converted balance can be followed back to its source. Reconciled record counts come closest: they show that totals and volumes match, which supports completeness, but they cannot show which legacy account produced a given new record.

wrong_explanations.B: Reconciled counts do prove nothing was lost in bulk, yet a total vouches for the whole and never for any one of its parts.
wrong_explanations.C: Screen testing checks that functions work for users. It does not create a link between old and new records.
wrong_explanations.D: A field mapping defines how each legacy field converts, but it does not link each converted record to the legacy account it came from.

tips: Eliminate: C tests functions, not data lineage, and D maps fields, which defines how data converts but does not link individual records.
Final two: A beats B because a key cross-reference traces each record, while counts confirm only that totals match.
Exam cue: completeness asks whether everything arrived; traceability asks where each item came from. Match the control to the objective.

questions.question: A post-implementation review must confirm that a new warehouse system cut order-picking errors by 40%. Which evidence should the IS auditor consider MOST reliable?

options.A: A survey measuring supervisors' view of the change in error levels
options.B: The vendor's case study of results at similar warehouses
options.C: Measured error rates compared with the pre-project baseline
options.D: The project closure report stating the target was achieved

questions.key_concept: Benefit claims are best supported by objective measured data compared with a pre-project baseline, not by assertions or opinion.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how independent and objective each source is, then ask which one actually measures the 40%.
questions.correct_explanation: Measured error rates from operational records, compared with the pre-project baseline, are objective, complete and independent of anyone's view of the project, so they directly test the claimed 40% reduction. The project closure report is the strongest alternative: it is formal, but it is the project's own assertion of success, and an auditor should verify such claims against underlying data rather than accept them.

wrong_explanations.A: A survey measures opinion, not errors; supervisors' impressions may reflect bias and cannot confirm a 40% reduction.
wrong_explanations.B: Results at other warehouses describe someone else's operation. They are not evidence of what happened here.
wrong_explanations.D: Evidence outranks assertion. A closure report usefully records what the project believes it achieved, yet a claim is a lead to test.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on opinion, and B describes results from other organizations.
Final two: C beats D because measured data independently tests the claim, while a closure report merely asserts it.
Exam cue: for benefit claims, the most reliable evidence is objective measured data against a baseline, not assertions or surveys.

questions.question: Two weeks before quarter close, three critical finance reports depend on rebuilt ETL jobs on a new data warehouse that are not yet validated. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Cut over the finance reports to the new warehouse on schedule
options.B: Seek a filing extension while the new ETL jobs are validated
options.C: Run quarter close on the old warehouse and halt the migration
options.D: Parallel-run and reconcile the three reports to the old warehouse

questions.key_concept: Before relying on a migrated system for financial reporting, a parallel run and reconciliation provide the evidence that outputs are complete and accurate.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly three reports are unvalidated and two weeks remain. Ask which option produces evidence for a decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Parallel running the three affected reports and reconciling them to the old warehouse produces evidence on whether the rebuilt jobs are accurate, while the old platform stays available as a fallback. Management can then decide with facts. Running close on the old warehouse and halting the migration is safe for this quarter, but it stops the whole program over three reports that may reconcile cleanly.

wrong_explanations.A: Relying on unvalidated ETL jobs for public financial reporting risks misstatement and certification exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Extensions exist for genuine emergencies, but seeking one to finish a migration signals reporting weakness to regulators and markets when validation can be completed before the fixed deadline.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing on the old warehouse does protect this quarter, but a fallback is a safety net under a decision, not a substitute for one.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because A relies on unvalidated jobs, and B moves a fixed filing deadline to suit the migration.
Final two: D beats C because reconciliation produces evidence for the decision, while halting stops the program without it.
Exam cue: before cutover of financial data, look for parallel run and reconciliation as the deciding evidence.

questions.question: A post-implementation review cannot confirm a promised 30% cut in claims processing time because nobody recorded processing times before the project. Which IS auditor recommendation BEST addresses the underlying weakness?

options.A: Reconstruct the baseline from legacy system transaction logs
options.B: Make a measured starting point a condition of business case approval
options.C: Measure processing times in the new system's reports from now on
options.D: Estimate the baseline from a sample of the archived claim files

questions.key_concept: Benefits can only be proven against a measured starting point, so business cases should record baselines before approval.
questions.pre_read: Separate fixing this one review from fixing the process that let the gap happen.
questions.correct_explanation: The underlying weakness is that the business case was approved without a measured starting point, so no later review can prove the benefit. Making a measured baseline, with an owner and method, a condition of approval fixes this for every future project. Reconstructing the baseline from legacy logs is the tempting option: it may give solid evidence for this review, but it leaves the approval gap in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Legacy logs may rebuild this one baseline, but the approval process that skipped it stays unchanged, so the gap recurs.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring processing time from now on shows the result, but without a recorded before-figure the 30% cut still cannot be shown, and future projects repeat the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: An estimate from sampled files patches this one review with weaker evidence than full logs, and the approval process that skipped the baseline stays unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: C measures only the after state, so no before-figure exists, and D estimates this one baseline from a sample, leaving the approval gap that caused it.
Final two: B beats A because it fixes the approval process that caused the gap; reconstructing the baseline only patches this one review.
Exam cue: when asked for the fix to an underlying weakness, choose the process change that prevents recurrence, not the one-off workaround.

questions.question: A post-implementation review finds finance staff approve vendor payments in spreadsheets because the new system lacks its designed approval workflow. How should the IS auditor BEST report this?

options.A: As a risk-rated control gap for management to remediate
options.B: As a training issue to be fixed through refresher sessions
options.C: As an enhancement request for the next scheduled release
options.D: As a workaround, with spreadsheets locked, versioned and logged

questions.key_concept: User workarounds for a missing designed control are a control gap: report the risk so management assigns an owner and a fix date.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the approval step was a designed control. If it was, its absence is a risk, not a feature request.
questions.correct_explanation: The approval workflow was a designed control, so its absence is a control gap: payments now rely on spreadsheets that can be changed without trace. The auditor should report it with a risk rating so management assigns an owner and a remediation date. An enhancement request nearly wins: it may be the eventual fix, but filing it as routine change hides the risk and lets it wait for release planning.

wrong_explanations.B: Staff are not misusing the system. The designed control is missing, so training cannot close the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Change requests are the normal channel for fixes; a finding's label, though, decides who answers for it, so missing controls are labeled as risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Locking and logging spreadsheets makes the workaround more traceable, but it replaces a designed system control with a manual one management never accepted.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a missing control as a user skill gap, and D hardens a manual workaround instead of restoring the designed control.
Final two: A beats C because a missing designed control is a risk to report and fix; treating it as an enhancement hides it.
Exam cue: user workarounds found in a review usually signal a control gap; report the risk and let management own the fix.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a newly formed project management office (PMO) decides which projects receive funding and priority. What is the MOST significant concern?

options.A: The PMO also manages project delivery staff
options.B: The PMO has not yet issued standard project methods and templates
options.C: Funding choices are made outside the steering committee
options.D: The PMO ranks projects without published scoring criteria

questions.key_concept: A PMO enables project delivery through standards, methods, support and consolidated reporting; funding and priority decisions sit with portfolio governance.
questions.pre_read: Separate what a PMO normally does from what governance bodies decide. Ask which finding puts a decision with the wrong body.
questions.correct_explanation: A PMO enables delivery through standards, support and consolidated reporting, while decisions on which projects get funded belong to the steering committee or portfolio board that is accountable for investment. Unpublished scoring criteria are the tempting concern: criteria would make the ranking transparent, but the deeper issue is that the PMO is making the decision at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Directive PMOs often manage delivery staff; that is a recognized PMO model, not a governance concern.
wrong_explanations.B: A new PMO still building its methods has a maturity gap it can close; decision rights over investment are the governance issue.
wrong_explanations.D: Published criteria would make the ranking consistent, but the larger issue is who decides; funding priority belongs to the steering committee, not the PMO.

tips: Eliminate: A describes a recognized directive PMO model, and B is a maturity gap a new PMO can close.
Final two: C beats D because published criteria would make the PMO's ranking transparent, but the decision belongs to the accountable steering committee.
Exam cue: distinguish who supports delivery (PMO) from who approves investment (steering committee or portfolio board).

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews management's choice of prototyping to build a new claims system. Which project condition MOST supports that choice?

options.A: Requirements are stable and fully documented at project start
options.B: Users want to see screens early, though requirements are signed off
options.C: The system must meet strict performance targets from day one
options.D: Users struggle to describe their needs in the abstract

questions.key_concept: Prototyping suits uncertain or evolving requirements that users refine by interacting with a working model; stable requirements favor a planned sequential approach.
questions.pre_read: Focus on how certain the requirements are. Ask where interacting with a model adds the most value.
questions.correct_explanation: Prototyping earns its cost when requirements are unclear and users can only define them by trying a working model; each iteration turns feedback into firmer requirements. Users wanting early screens is the tempting option, but the requirements are already agreed, so a prototype adds review effort without resolving any real uncertainty, and the auditor would question the choice.

wrong_explanations.A: Stable, documented requirements fit a planned sequential method; prototyping adds iterations without reducing uncertainty.
wrong_explanations.B: With requirements signed off, early screens are a presentation preference rather than a reason to change method.
wrong_explanations.C: Prototypes are built for feedback, not production performance; strict day-one targets call for engineered, performance-tested design.

tips: Eliminate: A has stable requirements that suit a sequential method, and C needs production-grade performance that prototypes are not built to prove.
Final two: D beats B because prototyping resolves requirements uncertainty, and B has none left to resolve.
Exam cue: match the method to requirements certainty: uncertain favors prototyping or iteration, stable favors sequential.

questions.question: A development team adopts a code generator to produce application modules. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Treat generated code as source under review and testing
options.B: Validate the generator's templates, settings and sample output once
options.C: Ban generators and require developers to hand-write the code
options.D: Accept the vendor's assurance that generated output is secure

questions.key_concept: Generated code is source code: it goes through the same review, testing and configuration management as hand-written code before reaching production.
questions.pre_read: Think about what actually reaches production. Ask which control examines that output every time.
questions.correct_explanation: What reaches production is the generated code, and its quality depends on inputs, templates and configuration that change over time. Treating it as source under peer review, testing and version control checks every output. Validating the generator before first use is a sensible step, but a one-time approval of the tool cannot catch defects in later outputs.

wrong_explanations.B: Validating templates, settings and samples once checks the tool at one point; later outputs from changed inputs and templates are never examined.
wrong_explanations.C: Banning generators gives up productivity without addressing risk; the issue is control over output, not the tool.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor assurance covers the tool generally, not the specific code produced for this application.

tips: Eliminate: C gives up the generator's productivity when review and testing can control its output, and D relies on a vendor claim about generic output.
Final two: A beats B because ongoing control of each output outranks a one-time approval of the tool.
Exam cue: whatever produces code, the code itself must pass the same SDLC controls before production.

questions.question: A bank's regulated payments platform has passed independent control certification, and the CIO wants to skip formal accreditation (authorization) to protect the timeline. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Release now, relying on the certification results as approval
options.B: Have the authorizing official accept residual risk before deployment
options.C: Treat passing development tests as sufficient evidence for release
options.D: Authorize the platform after go-live using production feedback

questions.key_concept: Authorization (accreditation) is a management decision: an authorized official accepts residual risk, based on certification evidence, before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the decision to accept risk on a regulated system, and when it must happen.
questions.correct_explanation: Accreditation, called authorization in current NIST guidance, is the formal management decision in which the authorizing official reviews certification evidence and accepts the residual risk before the system operates, keeping accountability with management. Releasing on the certification results sounds rigorous, but certification only evaluates whether controls work; it is evidence for the decision, not the decision, so the accountable risk acceptance would be skipped.

wrong_explanations.A: Certification shows the controls work, but it is evidence, not approval. No authorizing official has accepted the residual risk, so no one is accountable.
wrong_explanations.C: Development testing shows functions work but does not document control evidence or formal risk acceptance.
wrong_explanations.D: Authorization is a pre-deployment gate; doing it after go-live leaves customers exposed to risk nobody has accepted.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses testing with authorization, and D moves the gate to after go-live.
Final two: B beats A because certification supplies evidence, while authorization is management's accountable acceptance of residual risk.
Exam cue: certification evaluates controls; authorization (accreditation) is management formally accepting the remaining risk before go-live.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that, to meet a regulatory date, a waterfall project plans to deploy to production before system testing is complete. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Defects found after release will cost more to fix in production
options.B: Test documentation will be finished after the system goes live
options.C: The release will go live without a rehearsed rollback
options.D: Unverified code will process live transactions from day one

questions.key_concept: In a waterfall life cycle, system testing gates deployment so unverified code does not reach production and process live transactions.
questions.pre_read: Find which phase gate the plan removes. Ask what that gate exists to prevent.
questions.correct_explanation: In a waterfall life cycle, system testing is the gate that stops unverified code reaching production. Deploying before testing ends removes that gate, so live transactions run on code whose defects have not been found, risking errors in business records. Higher fix costs are the tempting option: they are real, but they are a consequence for IT; the greater risk is to the business processing that relies on the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Late defects do cost more to fix, but that is a cost consequence; the greater risk is untested code processing live business data.
wrong_explanations.B: Late documentation weakens the audit trail, but it does not expose business transactions to undetected defects.
wrong_explanations.C: An unrehearsed rollback weakens recovery, but it matters only after a failure; untested code processing live transactions is the exposure itself.

tips: Eliminate: B is a documentation lag and C weakens recovery after a failure; neither is the exposure the missing test gate creates.
Final two: D beats A because removing the testing gate exposes live business processing; higher fix costs are a consequence for IT.
Exam cue: testing gates deployment; when a plan releases before testing ends, the greatest risk is unverified code in production.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a Scrum team has stopped holding sprint retrospectives to save time. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Stakeholders lose their regular view of the completed increment
options.B: Daily progress toward the sprint goal goes uninspected
options.C: Recurring process problems go unexamined and uncorrected
options.D: No record of lessons learned is kept as audit evidence

questions.key_concept: Scrum's events are built-in controls: the Sprint Retrospective inspects how the team works so process problems are found and corrected.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each Scrum event inspects. Then ask what goes unchecked when this one is dropped.
questions.correct_explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is the event where the team inspects how it works and agrees improvements; it is Scrum's built-in control over its own process. Without it, the same delays and defects recur. The missing record of lessons is the tempting option, but documentation is secondary: the risk is that the process never improves, whether or not anyone writes it down.

wrong_explanations.A: Stakeholders see the increment at the Sprint Review, which still takes place; the retrospective inspects the team's own process.
wrong_explanations.B: Daily progress is inspected at the Daily Scrum, which the team still holds; dropping the retrospective does not remove it.
wrong_explanations.D: A record helps, but the greater loss is the inspection itself; process problems recur whether or not lessons are written down.

tips: Eliminate: A belongs to the Sprint Review and B to the Daily Scrum, events the team still holds.
Final two: C beats D because the retrospective exists to improve the process; a missing record is secondary to losing the inspection.
Exam cue: each Scrum event is a control; ask what that event inspects, and the risk is losing that inspection.

questions.subtopic: CI/CD. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
questions.question: A continuous deployment pipeline sends every passing build to production with no manual approval. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Enforced automated test gates and peer review before each merge
options.B: Production monitoring with automatic rollback when error rates rise
options.C: A weekly report of deployments sent to the change board
options.D: A canary release to a small share of users before full rollout

questions.key_concept: Continuous deployment releases passing builds without manual approval, so enforced automated gates and pre-merge review must replace the human release decision.
questions.pre_read: Ask which control the removed approval used to provide, and where it must now sit.
questions.correct_explanation: With continuous deployment the human release approval is gone, so prevention must move into the pipeline: tests that block failing builds and independent review before code merges ensure only verified, reviewed changes can deploy. Monitoring with automatic rollback is the tempting option, and it is valuable, but it reacts after a defect has already reached customers.

wrong_explanations.B: Rollback limits damage after release, but it is corrective; customers meet the defect before it triggers.
wrong_explanations.C: A weekly report tells the change board what already happened; it cannot stop an unverified change from deploying.
wrong_explanations.D: A canary limits how many customers meet a defect, but it still releases unverified code; it detects problems rather than preventing them.

tips: Eliminate: C reports deployments after they happen, and D still releases an unverified change to some customers; neither verifies a change before it deploys.
Final two: A beats B because the removed human approval must be replaced by preventive gates; rollback acts after customers meet the defect.
Exam cue: when automation removes a manual approval, look for the preventive control that moves into the pipeline.

questions.subtopic: User Acceptance Testing. Purpose and Timing
questions.question: To save three weeks, a billing system's project plan runs user acceptance testing (UAT) in parallel with system testing. What is the GREATEST risk for the IS auditor to raise?

options.A: Business users stay tied up in testing longer than planned
options.B: Users find technical defects that system testers should catch
options.C: System test fixes are not regression-tested before UAT
options.D: Acceptance is signed on a build that later changes

questions.key_concept: UAT follows successful system testing and precedes cutover, with business users testing in a production-like environment.
questions.pre_read: Place UAT in the test sequence. Ask what must be stable before business users can accept the system.
questions.correct_explanation: UAT is the business's acceptance gate, so it must rest on a stable build that system testing has already cleared. Running both together means users may sign off a version that changes afterward as system-test defects are fixed, so the acceptance no longer covers what goes live. Users finding technical defects is the tempting option: it wastes their time, but it does not invalidate acceptance.

wrong_explanations.A: Longer user involvement is a resourcing cost the plan can absorb; it does not undermine the acceptance itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Users finding technical defects wastes effort, but the greater risk is that their sign-off covers a build that later changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Regression gaps can be closed by retesting before go-live; the greater risk is that sign-off covers a build that then changes.

tips: Eliminate: A is a resourcing cost and C a retesting gap that can be closed before go-live; neither voids the acceptance itself.
Final two: D beats B because acceptance must rest on a stable, system-tested build; wasted user effort is the lesser cost.
Exam cue: an acceptance or approval only covers the version it was given; when a plan lets the build change after sign-off, that is the greatest risk.

questions.subtopic: Go-Live Readiness. Evidence for the Decision
questions.question: A steering committee must decide whether a new billing system is ready to go live next week. Which evidence should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: The vendor's statement that the system is ready for production
options.B: A signed readiness checklist with open exceptions listed
options.C: The project schedule, signed off by its owner, showing tasks complete
options.D: A count of defects fixed during the final test cycle

questions.key_concept: Go-live decisions rest on readiness criteria signed off by accountable owners, with open exceptions visible and formally accepted.
questions.pre_read: Separate evidence of activity (tasks done) from evidence of outcomes (criteria met).
questions.correct_explanation: Readiness depends on more than finished tasks: testing results, data conversion, training, support and rollback must each meet agreed criteria. A checklist signed by the accountable owners, with open exceptions listed and risk-accepted, gives the committee a basis to decide. A schedule showing tasks complete is the closest choice: tasks can be done while their outcomes still fall short of the criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: The vendor has an interest in go-live and is not accountable for the organization's readiness. It is not independent evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Completed tasks show activity, not outcomes, even with the owner's sign-off. Testing can finish with critical defects still open.
wrong_explanations.D: Fixed defects show progress but not what remains open, or whether users, data and support are ready.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on an interested vendor, and D counts progress without showing what remains.
Final two: B beats C because readiness is judged by outcomes against criteria, signed by owners; task completion shows activity.
Exam cue: go-live decisions rest on agreed readiness criteria signed off by accountable owners, with exceptions visible.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a firm's source code escrow agreement for critical software from a small vendor. Which control BEST assures the deposit would be usable if released?

options.A: The vendor's own annual written confirmation that deposits are current
options.B: Contract terms defining release triggers such as vendor insolvency
options.C: Annual agent verification that the deposit builds the live version
options.D: Deposits held by an independent escrow agent under a signed agreement

questions.key_concept: Escrow assurance requires independent, periodic verification that the deposit is complete, current and builds the production version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens if the vendor fails tomorrow and the deposit is outdated.
questions.correct_explanation: Escrow only protects the licensee if the deposited material can actually rebuild the software in use. Periodic verification by the escrow agent, compiling the deposit and comparing it with the live version, provides that evidence. Clear release triggers are essential, but they only determine when the code is handed over, not whether what is handed over will work.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's own confirmation is self-assertion; it does not show the deposit is complete or will build.
wrong_explanations.B: Triggers decide when code is released, but a stale or incomplete deposit is useless when it arrives.
wrong_explanations.D: Independent custody protects access, but nobody has shown the deposit is complete or builds the version in use.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on vendor self-assertion, and D secures independent custody without testing what is held.
Final two: C beats B because triggers govern when code is released, while verification proves it will work.
Exam cue: for escrow assurance, an independent periodic test build beats any vendor assertion, however often it is made.

questions.subtopic: Scheduling and the Critical Path. Estimating Uncertain Durations
questions.question: A project plan uses single-point duration estimates for a first-of-its-kind data migration whose effort is highly uncertain. Which estimating approach should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: A flat 20% buffer on design, build and test tasks
options.B: Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations weighted per task
options.C: Monte Carlo simulation of the schedule from single-point inputs
options.D: Analogous estimates from the last ERP migration, scaled for data volume

questions.key_concept: Three-point estimating, as in the program evaluation and review technique (PERT), weights optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations for each uncertain task.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the plan can show a range of possible durations instead of one guess per task.
questions.correct_explanation: Three-point estimating, used in the program evaluation and review technique (PERT), weights optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations as (O + 4M + P) / 6, so each task's estimate reflects its own uncertainty and the spread shows schedule risk. A flat 20% buffer is the most tempting alternative: it adds contingency, but the amount is arbitrary and spread evenly instead of where the uncertainty lies.

wrong_explanations.A: A flat buffer serves repeat work whose variance history is known; where no history exists, the estimate itself must carry the uncertainty.
wrong_explanations.C: Simulation needs a range for each task; fed single points, it repeats them and shows no spread of possible durations.
wrong_explanations.D: Scaling helps only when the past project is comparable; this migration is the first of its kind, so the analogy carries little weight.

tips: Eliminate: C simulates without ranges to sample from, and D borrows from a past project that is not comparable to a first-of-its-kind migration.
Final two: B beats A because task-level ranges place contingency where uncertainty lies, while a flat buffer is arbitrary.
Exam cue: when task durations are uncertain, look for three-point estimates rather than single figures or blanket padding.

questions.subtopic: Scheduling and the Critical Path. Slippage on a Chain with Slack
questions.question: An IS auditor finds critical-path tasks on schedule, but the data conversion chain, which had five days of total float before go-live, has slipped eight days. What is the MOST LIKELY effect on go-live?

options.A: Go-live holds, because data conversion sits outside the critical path
options.B: Go-live slips eight days, matching the full delay to conversion
options.C: Go-live slips about three days, since conversion now drives the end
options.D: Go-live holds if extra staff join the original critical-path tasks

questions.key_concept: A chain that slips beyond its slack becomes the critical path and moves the end date by the excess.
questions.pre_read: Compare the slip with the slack the chain had before it started to slip.
questions.correct_explanation: Slack, or total float, is how far a chain can slip without moving the end date. The conversion chain had five days, so an eight-day slip uses all of it and adds three more, making conversion the new critical path. Concluding that go-live holds because conversion was not critical comes closest, yet a chain stays non-critical only while its delay stays within its slack.

wrong_explanations.A: Conversion was off the critical path only while its delay stayed within five days of slack; at eight days it drives the end date.
wrong_explanations.B: Five of the eight days are absorbed by the chain's slack, so only the excess three days move go-live.
wrong_explanations.D: The original critical-path tasks are on schedule and no longer the longest chain, so adding staff there cannot pull go-live back.

tips: Eliminate: B counts the full delay although five days of float absorb part of it, and D adds staff to tasks that no longer set the end date.
Final two: C beats A because slack protects a chain only until it is used up; after that, the chain is critical.
Exam cue: subtract the slack from the slip; any excess moves the end date and makes that chain critical.

questions.subtopic: Scheduling and the Critical Path. Reading Aggregate Progress
questions.question: A steering committee report shows 80% of planned work complete, mostly training and reporting tasks that had ample slack and finished early. Which indicator should the IS auditor treat as MOST reliable for go-live risk?

options.A: Forecast finish of the critical-path tasks against the baseline
options.B: Earned value schedule performance index for the whole project
options.C: Share of the approved project budget spent to date
options.D: Count of tasks completed ahead of their baseline dates

questions.key_concept: Aggregate progress measures, including the schedule performance index, can hide critical-path delays; only critical-path forecasts show end-date risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask which tasks actually decide the finish date, and whether the indicator looks at them.
questions.correct_explanation: Only critical-path tasks have zero slack, so their forecast finish decides whether go-live holds. Early work on non-critical training and reporting tasks inflates aggregate progress. The schedule performance index nearly wins: it values work done instead of counting tasks, but it still sums all work, so early non-critical progress can offset, and hide, late critical-path tasks.

wrong_explanations.B: The index aggregates earned value across all tasks, so early non-critical work can offset a late critical path and show a healthy figure.
wrong_explanations.C: Budget spent measures cost consumption, not whether the tasks that drive the end date are on time.
wrong_explanations.D: Counting early tasks treats every task alike and ignores which ones actually determine the finish date.

tips: Eliminate: C measures cost rather than schedule, and D counts tasks without regard to which ones drive the end date.
Final two: A beats B because an aggregate index lets early non-critical work mask late critical-path tasks.
Exam cue: to judge whether a project will finish on time, look at the critical path, not totals or averages of all work.

questions.subtopic: Application Input Controls. Keyed Account Numbers
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that transposition errors in account numbers keyed by clerks sometimes post customer payments to another valid customer. Which missing control MOST LIKELY explains this?

options.A: An existence check that each account number is on file
options.B: A batch total of payment amounts agreed before posting
options.C: A daily posting report reviewed by a supervisor
options.D: A check digit verified on every account number at entry

questions.key_concept: A check digit tests an identification number's internal consistency at entry, catching transpositions that an existence check misses.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a mistyped account number could still match a real customer.
questions.correct_explanation: A check digit is calculated from the other digits of the account number, so most transpositions produce a number that fails the calculation and is rejected at entry, before posting. An existence check comes closest: it is a sound input edit, but a transposed number that belongs to another real customer is on file and passes it.

wrong_explanations.A: Match the edit to the error: existence checks catch numbers never issued, while keying errors need a test of the number's own structure.
wrong_explanations.B: The amounts are keyed correctly, so the batch total still agrees even though payments reach the wrong customers.
wrong_explanations.C: A report reviewed after posting is detective, and a supervisor is unlikely to spot a swapped pair of digits.

tips: Eliminate: B checks amounts, which are correct, and C reviews postings only after the damage is done.
Final two: D beats A because a transposed number can still belong to a real customer; only a check digit tests the number itself.
Exam cue: transposition or keying errors in identification numbers point to a check digit.

questions.subtopic: Application Processing Controls. Records Lost Between Steps
questions.question: A nightly billing run passes records through three processing steps, and a failed step silently dropped 400 records last month. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as the PRIMARY means of detection?

options.A: Control totals carried forward and reconciled at each step
options.B: Monthly reconciliation of billed revenue to the general ledger
options.C: Range checks on billing amounts when charges are entered
options.D: Restricted distribution of printed invoices to authorized staff

questions.key_concept: Run-to-run control totals prove completeness across each processing step and show where records were lost.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the records went missing and which control watches that point.
questions.correct_explanation: Run-to-run control totals carry a record count or amount from one processing step to the next, so a step that drops records is caught the same night, and the failing step is identified. Reconciling billed revenue to the general ledger is the strongest alternative: it also tests completeness, but only monthly and in aggregate, so missing records surface weeks later and are hard to trace.

wrong_explanations.B: Revenue-to-ledger reconciliation is a core financial close control, but detection belongs at the stage where records are lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Range checks test values at input; they cannot notice records lost later during processing.
wrong_explanations.D: Controlling who receives invoices protects output; it does nothing to show that records went missing earlier.

tips: Eliminate: C acts at input, and D protects output distribution; neither watches what happens between processing steps.
Final two: A beats B because step-by-step totals catch a loss the same night, while a monthly ledger check finds it late and in aggregate.
Exam cue: records lost between processing steps point to run-to-run totals, the processing-stage completeness control.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS06.02 (Control the processing of information); COBIT 2019 DSS06.04 (Manage errors and exceptions)

All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: COBIT 2019 DSS06.

questions.subtopic: Machine Learning Release. Weekly Retraining by the Builders
questions.question: An airline's data scientists retrain its fare-pricing model weekly and deploy each version themselves, arguing that retraining changes no code. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Retrain monthly instead of weekly to cut the number of releases
options.B: Freeze the model until an annual independent review
options.C: Release each new version through validation and change control
options.D: Have the data scientists log each retraining run and its results

questions.key_concept: A retrained machine learning model is a production change and needs validation, approval and controlled release with a way back.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether new model behavior counts as a change, even when no code changes.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrained model changes system behavior just as new code does, so each version needs validation, approval and deployment through change control, with a way back to the prior version. Having the data scientists log each run nearly wins: it creates a record, but the builders still release their own changes with no independent check before customers see the new fares.

wrong_explanations.A: Fewer releases reduce volume, but each one still reaches production without validation or approval.
wrong_explanations.B: Freezing the model lets it fall out of step with demand for a year; the aim is controlled change, not no change.
wrong_explanations.D: A retraining log does give the model the audit trail it needs, yet a record of a change is never its authorization.

tips: Eliminate: A only slows the release rate, and B stops needed retraining instead of controlling it.
Final two: C beats D because a log records changes after the fact, while change control validates and approves them before release.
Exam cue: a retrained model is a production change; expect validation, approval and controlled release, whatever the team calls it.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 5338:2023 (AI System Life Cycle Processes); COBIT 2019 BAI06.01 (Evaluate, prioritize and authorize change requests)

Distinct from d3_038 (drift monitoring and model ownership), d4_231 (rolling back a biased model version) and d1_029 (agile audit of a retrained model): tests that each retrained model is a change needing validation, approval and controlled release. All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: ISO/IEC 5338:2023; COBIT 2019 BAI06.

questions.question: A bank's data science team has built and tested a model that flags transactions for anti-money-laundering review. Before release, what should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: A second project data scientist reviewing the team's test results
options.B: Independent testing of the model's accuracy, bias and limits
options.C: Business owner sign-off based on the builders' own test results
options.D: Drift, bias and accuracy alerts set for live performance

questions.key_concept: Before release, a model needs validation independent of its builders; business acceptance should rest on that evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has checked the builders' work, and whether they are independent of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Model validation must be independent of the builders, who tend to test their own assumptions. Independent testing of accuracy, unfair bias and known limits gives the business owner a sound basis for acceptance. Owner sign-off comes closest: the owner should accept the model, but signing off on the builders' own results adds accountability without independent evidence, so validation comes first.

wrong_explanations.A: A colleague on the same project shares the team's assumptions and incentives, so the review is not independent.
wrong_explanations.C: Owner sign-off and independent testing both gate the model's release, though acceptance is a decision, and decisions rest on evidence someone has challenged.
wrong_explanations.D: Live alerts watch the model after release; they cannot show it is sound before it starts flagging transactions.

tips: Eliminate: A stays inside the project team, and D monitors the model only after it is live.
Final two: B beats C because owner sign-off needs independent evidence first; approving the builders' own results adds no challenge.
Exam cue: before a model is released, look for validation by someone other than its builders, then business acceptance.
questions.framework_ref: Federal Reserve SR 11-7 (Model Risk Management); NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

questions.subtopic: Machine Learning Release. Disputed Automated Decisions
questions.question: A lender's model, updated several times a year, automatically declines loan applications, and complaints staff cannot tell which version declined an applicant. Which control should the IS auditor recommend to MOST directly address this?

options.A: Archive each released model version in a controlled repository
options.B: Explain disputed declines by rerunning them through the current model
options.C: Update the model less often to limit the number of versions
options.D: Record the model version and inputs with each automated decision

questions.key_concept: Automated decisions are traceable only if each one records the model version and inputs that produced it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what links one past decision to the exact model that made it.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing a decision requires a record, made at the time, of which model version and which inputs produced it. With that record, the lender can rebuild and explain any disputed decline. Archiving every version is the closest choice: it keeps the models, but without a link from each decision to its version, staff still cannot tell which archived model declined a given applicant.

wrong_explanations.A: Archived versions are needed, but without the version recorded on each decision, nobody knows which archived model to examine.
wrong_explanations.B: The current model may differ from the one that made the decision, so its output proves nothing about past declines.
wrong_explanations.C: Fewer updates mean fewer versions, but decisions would still carry no record of which version made them.

tips: Eliminate: B uses a model that may not have made the decision, and C reduces versions without linking any of them to decisions.
Final two: D beats A because keeping versions helps only once each decision records which version made it.
Exam cue: to explain automated decisions later, look for a per-decision record of the model version and inputs.

questions.subtopic: Reverse Engineering. Decompiling Licensed Vendor Software
questions.question: The vendor of a licensed claims-processing engine will not share its design, so developers propose decompiling the engine to build new interfaces. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have legal counsel confirm the decompiling is lawfully permitted
options.B: Request the engine's source code from the software escrow agent
options.C: Carry out the decompiling in an isolated, logged test environment
options.D: Plan integration testing of the new interfaces before go-live

questions.key_concept: A license grants use, not ownership; reverse engineering vendor software needs legal confirmation that the license permits it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the license actually lets the organization do with the vendor's code.
questions.correct_explanation: A software license grants the right to use the product, not rights to its code. Many licenses forbid decompiling, and many jurisdictions allow it only in narrow cases, such as interoperability, so legal review must come before any work starts. An isolated, logged environment is the strongest alternative: it controls technical risk, such as harm to production, but it does nothing to make the decompiling lawful.

wrong_explanations.B: Escrow releases code only on defined events such as vendor failure; refusing to share design is not one.
wrong_explanations.C: Isolation contains technical risk, but the decompiling itself may breach the license wherever it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Interface testing is needed later, but it assumes the work behind the interfaces is permitted in the first place.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on escrow, which a design refusal does not trigger, and D is a later step that assumes the work is allowed.
Final two: A beats C because isolation controls technical risk, while the larger risk is legal and arises the moment decompiling starts.
Exam cue: before reverse engineering vendor software, look for legal review of the license terms first.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.32 (Intellectual Property Rights); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance with External Requirements)

Tests that legal review of license terms comes before reverse engineering vendor code. All scenario specifics invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Component-Based Development. Reusing a Proven Component
questions.question: A team will reuse a tax-calculation component, proven in the retail system, inside a new wholesale system with different pricing data. What should the IS auditor consider the PRIMARY testing need?

options.A: Rerunning the retail unit tests inside the wholesale build
options.B: Integration testing in the wholesale build with wholesale transactions
options.C: Relying on the retail system's earlier production results for the component
options.D: Reviewing the component's source code for secure coding flaws

questions.key_concept: Reused components must be tested in each new system, with its data and interfaces; earlier success elsewhere is not evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what is different about the new system the component will serve.
questions.correct_explanation: A component that worked in one system can fail in another that sends it different data or calls it differently. Testing it inside the wholesale system, with wholesale pricing data and interfaces, shows whether it works in its new setting. Rerunning the original unit tests comes closest: it confirms the component is unchanged, but those cases reflect retail data, not wholesale use.

wrong_explanations.A: Rerunning unit tests also exercises the component inside the wholesale build, but tests prove only the conditions they were written for.
wrong_explanations.C: Retail results show the component works in retail; the wholesale system will use it with different data.
wrong_explanations.D: Secure coding review looks for vulnerabilities, not whether tax is calculated correctly on wholesale data.

tips: Eliminate: C counts operating history as test evidence, though no test was designed or run for this system, and D checks for security flaws rather than correct calculation.
Final two: B beats A because old unit tests confirm the component is unchanged, not that it works with new data.
Exam cue: reused components need integration testing in each new system, however well they worked before.

questions.subtopic: Audit Trails. Investigating Changed Bank Details
questions.question: After a salary diversion, the payroll audit trail showed who edited bank details and when, but investigators could not tell which accounts received the pay. Which improvement should the IS auditor give the GREATEST priority?

options.A: Sending payroll logs to a central store that payroll staff cannot alter
options.B: Keeping payroll logs for seven years instead of one year
options.C: Recording the prior and new values of each changed field
options.D: Having payroll managers review the logs every week

questions.key_concept: Audit trails for sensitive data changes must capture prior and new values, not just who and when, to support investigation.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of who, what and when the audit trail is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap is content: the trail shows who changed bank details but not what changed, so the diverted account numbers cannot be traced or reversed from it. Recording prior and new values closes that gap. Central, protected storage nearly wins: it makes logs trustworthy, but protecting a record that lacks the changed values still leaves investigators without the evidence they need.

wrong_explanations.A: Protection keeps logs from being altered, but a protected log that omits the changed values still cannot show where pay was redirected.
wrong_explanations.B: Longer retention keeps the same incomplete records for longer; it adds none of the missing detail.
wrong_explanations.D: Weekly review of logs that lack the changed values cannot show whether a new account is legitimate or which account to restore.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps incomplete records longer, and D reviews records that still lack the changed values.
Final two: C beats A because protection secures the log, but the gap here is what the log captures.
Exam cue: an audit trail needs who, what, when and the before-and-after values; fix the missing element first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); COBIT 2019 DSS06.05 (Ensure traceability and accountability for information events)

All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-3; COBIT 2019 DSS06.

questions.question: Requirements for a new loan-origination system specify logging of technical errors only, and the project team plans to add business-event logging after go-live. What should the IS auditor consider the GREATEST risk of this plan?

options.A: Adding the logging after go-live will cost more than building it now
options.B: Technical error logs will fill the available storage before testing ends
options.C: Performance tests will not reflect the load of later logging
options.D: Early loan approvals and rate exceptions will have no audit trail

questions.key_concept: Business events must be defined for logging in requirements, because actions taken before logging exists leave no evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to accountability for actions taken before the logging is added.
questions.correct_explanation: Business events such as loan approvals and rate exceptions are the evidence of who did what. If they are not logged from go-live, any error or fraud in the early months leaves no trail, and that history can never be recreated. Higher retrofit cost is the closest concern: building controls in early is cheaper, but cost can be absorbed, while missing evidence is lost for good.

wrong_explanations.A: Retrofitting costs more, but the extra cost can be funded later; months of approvals with no record cannot be recovered.
wrong_explanations.B: Storage capacity is a routine operational matter, and nothing suggests error logs will exhaust it.
wrong_explanations.C: The added load can be performance-tested when the logging is added; that is a manageable testing gap, not lost evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B is a routine capacity concern, and C is a testing gap that can be closed when the logging is added.
Final two: D beats A because extra cost can be absorbed, while approvals made without a record leave an evidence gap that can never be filled.
Exam cue: decide which business events to log during design; evidence not captured from day one is gone for good.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); OWASP ASVS 5.0 V16 (Security Logging and Error Handling)

questions.subtopic: Test Environments and Test Data. Proposal to Test in Production
questions.question: With no test environment that matches production, a retailer's project team proposes running user acceptance testing (UAT) in the live order system using test customer accounts. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Allow testing in production, then reverse every test transaction afterward
options.B: Run the tests in the development environment the programmers use
options.C: Build a separate environment configured like production for the testing
options.D: Restrict testing in production to inquiry transactions that change nothing

questions.key_concept: User acceptance testing belongs in a separate, production-like environment; only controlled audit techniques, such as an integrated test facility, run test data in live systems.
questions.pre_read: Ask what test transactions could set off in a live system before anyone reverses them.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing belongs in a separate environment that mirrors production in configuration and versions, so results are reliable without putting live data or service at risk. Building one fixes the real gap. Testing live and reversing transactions afterward is the most tempting alternative: test orders can still trigger shipments, postings and interface messages, and reversals may miss some, so live data and service stay exposed.

wrong_explanations.A: Reversals are a standard cleanup for test postings, but isolating tests from live assets beats repairing what they touched afterward.
wrong_explanations.B: A development environment is controlled by programmers and rarely matches production, so results would be unreliable and testing would lack independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Inquiry-only testing cannot exercise order entry, pricing or posting, so the functions users must accept would go untested.

tips: Eliminate: B uses a programmer-controlled environment unlike production, and D leaves the order-processing functions untested.
Final two: C beats A because reversing test transactions cannot undo shipments, postings and interface messages already triggered in the live system.
Exam cue: project testing belongs in a separate, production-like environment; live-system testing is reserved for tightly controlled audit techniques such as an integrated test facility.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.31 (Separation of Development, Test and Production Environments); COBIT 2019 BAI07.04 (Establish a test environment)

questions.subtopic: Test Environments and Test Data. Cases Missing from Production
questions.question: A pension fund must test benefit rules for rare cases, such as members with three overlapping claims, that appear in no production record. Which test data should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: A masked extract of the full production member history
options.B: Test member records created in production and flagged as test
options.C: Unmasked production records copied to test, then edited into the cases
options.D: Synthetic records generated to cover each specified scenario

questions.key_concept: Synthetic data fits early testing and edge cases that real records lack, and it carries no personal data.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether any copy of production data, masked or not, could contain these cases.
questions.correct_explanation: Synthetic data suits cases that real data does not contain: records generated to the specified scenarios exercise the rare rules and hold no personal data. A masked production extract nearly wins because masking is the right way to use real data in test, but no extract, however large, contains cases that appear in no production record.

wrong_explanations.A: Masking protects real data, but these cases appear in no production record, so no extract can supply them.
wrong_explanations.B: Flagged test accounts in production are a common shortcut, but they mix test activity with live member data and risk test runs reaching real payments or reports.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying unmasked records into test exposes real personal data in a less controlled environment before any edit is made.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because B stages test cases inside the live production system, and C puts unmasked personal data into test.
Final two: D beats A because a masked extract still holds only real cases, and these rare cases exist in no production record.
Exam cue: mask real data when realistic patterns matter; generate synthetic data for early tests and cases production lacks.

questions.subtopic: Performance and Specialized Testing. New System on a Shared Cluster
questions.question: A new warehouse system passed functional and load tests run in isolation but will share production's database cluster with order entry. What should the IS auditor recommend as the PRIMARY focus of further testing?

options.A: Both systems tested together under combined peak load
options.B: Stress testing the warehouse system beyond its expected peak volume
options.C: Beta testing by selected warehouse staff at two sites
options.D: Unit testing of the warehouse database queries by developers

questions.key_concept: Sociability testing confirms a new system can share production resources without harming, or being harmed by, existing systems.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risk remains when each system has only ever been tested on its own.
questions.correct_explanation: Sociability testing runs the new system alongside the systems it will share production with, revealing contention for database locks, memory or connections that neither shows alone. That is the untested risk here. Stress testing is the strongest alternative: finding the warehouse system's breaking point is useful, but done in isolation it still cannot show whether the two systems harm each other.

wrong_explanations.B: Stress testing finds the warehouse system's breaking point, but run alone it cannot reveal contention with order entry on the shared cluster.
wrong_explanations.C: Beta testing checks fit with real users' work; it does not create the combined load that reveals conflicts between systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Unit tests check individual queries in isolation, so they cannot show how two systems compete for one database cluster.

tips: Eliminate: C checks user fit rather than shared resources, and D is developer unit testing, a build-stage check of query logic rather than of load.
Final two: A beats B because a stress test of the warehouse system alone still misses conflicts with order entry on the shared cluster.
Exam cue: when a new system shares infrastructure, test sociability by running it with its neighbors under production-like conditions.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity); ISO/IEC 25010:2023 (Product Quality Model)

All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: COBIT 2019 BAI04; ISO/IEC 25010:2023 compatibility (co-existence).

questions.subtopic: Performance and Specialized Testing. Targets Set After the First Results
questions.question: A call-center system's performance test report shows every test passed, but the IS auditor learns the test team set the response-time targets after seeing the first results. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The test environment may not match production data volumes
options.B: The passing thresholds may not reflect what the business requires
options.C: The test team may lack tools to simulate peak call volumes
options.D: The tests may have run too briefly to expose gradual slowdowns

questions.key_concept: Performance targets come from business needs and are fixed before testing, or a pass proves nothing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a pass means when the bar was set after seeing the score.
questions.correct_explanation: Performance targets must come from business needs and be fixed before testing. Targets set after seeing results can simply be moved to whatever the system achieves, so every pass proves little. A production-like environment comes closest: it also matters for valid results, but nothing suggests it is missing, while the moved targets are a known flaw that undermines every result.

wrong_explanations.A: Environment fidelity matters, but nothing in the report suggests a mismatch; the known flaw is that targets were fitted to the results.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing suggests the tools fell short, and better load tools would not fix targets that were set to match the results.
wrong_explanations.D: Test duration matters for endurance risks, but longer runs measured against moved targets would still prove little.

tips: Eliminate: C speculates about tools with no supporting fact, and D raises an endurance gap that moved targets would still undermine.
Final two: B beats A because the environment is not in doubt, while targets set after the results make every pass meaningless.
Exam cue: a pass means nothing unless the target came from business needs and was fixed before testing began.
questions.framework_ref: ISTQB Certified Tester Performance Testing (CT-PT) Syllabus; COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity)

questions.subtopic: Test Types and Techniques. Retesting Only Changed Modules
questions.question: To shorten two-week release cycles, a claims team reruns tests only for changed modules. Which defect should the IS auditor consider MOST LIKELY to slip through?

options.A: A coding error inside one of the modules the release altered
options.B: A slowdown that appears when peak claim volumes hit the new release
options.C: A known flaw in an outdated third-party library the system uses
options.D: A failure in an unchanged function that depends on altered modules

questions.key_concept: Regression testing confirms unchanged functions still work after a change, so its scope follows dependencies, not just changed code.
questions.pre_read: Ask which parts of the system this practice never exercises after a release.
questions.correct_explanation: Regression testing exists because a change can break functions that were never touched, such as a claims calculation that calls a modified module. Rerunning only the changed modules' tests skips exactly those dependents. An error inside a changed module is the closest choice, but those modules are the ones being retested, so their defects are the most likely to be caught.

wrong_explanations.A: Changed modules do breed most new defects, yet a defect slips through only where testing stops, so judge escape risk by coverage, not by origin.
wrong_explanations.B: Peak-volume slowdowns call for performance testing, which a functional regression suite, full or partial, does not provide.
wrong_explanations.C: Outdated library flaws are found by software composition analysis, not by choosing which functional tests to rerun.

tips: Eliminate: B needs performance testing and C needs composition analysis; neither depends on which functional tests are rerun.
Final two: D beats A because the changed modules are retested, while the untouched functions that depend on them are not.
Exam cue: regression testing protects what did not change; set its scope by tracing what depends on the changed code.
questions.framework_ref: ISTQB Foundation Level Syllabus; COBIT 2019 BAI03.08 (Execute solution testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Test Types and Techniques. Retesting Only Changed Modules'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 3B1.2 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q14: thin subtopic). Distinct from d3_065 (test pyramid composition), d3_050 (risk-based test strategy) and d4_119 (vendor patch applied without testing): tests that regression scope limited to changed modules misses failures in dependent unchanged functions. All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: ISTQB Foundation Level Syllabus; COBIT 2019 BAI03.08.

questions.subtopic: Financial Measures and Investment Decisions. Ranking Two Approved Projects
questions.question: Management will pick one of two projects by internal rate of return: $0.3 million at 45%, or $6 million at 20%, both above the hurdle rate. Which advice from the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Compare each project's net present value at the required rate
options.B: Choose the smaller project, because its rate of return is higher
options.C: Rank them by present value returned per dollar invested
options.D: Choose the larger project, because it returns more total cash

questions.key_concept: Internal rate of return can mislead between projects of very different sizes; net present value shows the value each adds.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a high percentage on a small sum beats a lower percentage on a large one.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal rate of return is a percentage, so it can mislead when options differ greatly in size: 45% on $0.3 million may add far less value than 20% on $6 million. Net present value at the required rate shows which project adds more value in today's money. Choosing by the higher rate nearly wins: it ranks return per dollar invested, not the total value created.

wrong_explanations.B: A higher rate on a much smaller investment can create less total value; rates alone mislead when project sizes differ greatly.
wrong_explanations.C: Value per dollar invested is a ratio, so like the rate of return it can rank the smaller project first while hiding the total value each adds.
wrong_explanations.D: Total cash ignores when the returns arrive; scale matters, but only value discounted at the required rate compares the projects fairly.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks by a ratio, which shares the rate's blindness to scale, and D adds up cash without discounting it for timing.
Final two: A beats B because a percentage return hides scale, while net present value shows which project adds more value.
Exam cue: when options differ greatly in size, rank them by net present value, not by internal rate of return.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Financial Measures and Investment Decisions. Ranking Two Approved Projects'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 3A2.3 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q14: thin subtopic). Distinct from d3_006 (net present value versus payback for late benefits) and d3_100/d3_105 (sunk cost in continue-or-stop decisions): tests that internal rate of return misleads between projects of very different sizes. All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: ISACA Val IT Framework; COBIT 2019 APO05. Difficulty upgrade (Oct 2026, owner's rule: two options eliminable only by CISA knowledge, a hard final two): replaced 'raise the hurdle rate until one clears' with undiscounted scale reasoning (the larger project returns more total cash). Round 2 (Oct 2026, quality-gate fixes from the standards audit, pedagogy check and strong and weak blind tests): self-check after the weak blind test: C (payback) was an easy cut; C is now a value-per-dollar ratio that repeats the rate's scale problem. Round 3 (Oct 2026, concept check, blind tests and wording-cue balance): concept check (precision): W-C says the ratio 'can' favor the small project; the framework reference is COBIT 2019.

questions.subtopic: Financial Measures and Investment Decisions. Lender's Recovery Condition
questions.question: Under a cash-preservation plan agreed with its lender, a manufacturer will fund only systems whose cash returns cover their outlay within 18 months. Which measure should the IS auditor expect as the PRIMARY screen?

options.A: The net present value of each proposed system
options.B: The payback period each proposed system is forecast to achieve
options.C: The total cost of owning each system over its life
options.D: The internal rate of return forecast for each proposed system

questions.key_concept: Choose the financial measure that fits the decision: payback when quick recovery of cost is the binding constraint.
questions.pre_read: Ask which question the 18-month rule forces management to answer first.
questions.correct_explanation: Measures answer different questions, and the plan agreed with the lender makes speed of recovery the binding constraint: a system that pays back in 30 months fails it, however valuable it is. Payback period answers exactly that question, so it is the primary screen. Net present value comes closest: it best shows whole-life value and can rank the proposals that pass, but it does not show when cost is recovered.

wrong_explanations.A: Net present value shows whole-life value, but a high-value proposal may still take too long to recover its cost under the 18-month rule.
wrong_explanations.C: Total cost of ownership counts costs only; without benefits and their timing it cannot show whether cost is recovered in time.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal rate of return gives a whole-life percentage return, not whether cost is recovered within 18 months.

tips: Eliminate: C counts costs without benefits, and D gives a whole-life percentage return rather than a recovery time.
Final two: B beats A because the 18-month rule makes speed of recovery the deciding constraint, which payback measures and net present value does not.
Exam cue: match the measure to the question; when cash or a recovery deadline binds, payback comes first.

questions.subtopic: Acquiring Software from Vendors. Award to the Lowest Bid
questions.question: Four proposals for transit fare-collection software meet the minimum requirements, and procurement wants the lowest bid to win, though the request for proposal set cost at 30%. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate recommendation?

options.A: Accept the lowest bid, since each proposal meets the requirements
options.B: Seek best and final offers from the two cheapest bidders
options.C: Select the vendor ranking highest across the stated criteria
options.D: Rescore the four proposals using new weights agreed with operations staff

questions.key_concept: Select vendors on weighted criteria fixed before proposals arrive; meeting minimum requirements only makes a bid eligible.
questions.pre_read: Ask how much the request for proposal said price should decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Vendors should be selected against criteria and weights fixed before proposals arrive. The request for proposal gave cost 30%, so fit, support and stability carry the rest, and meeting minimum requirements makes a proposal eligible, not equal. Rescoring with new weights is the strongest alternative: input from operations staff sounds sensible, but changing weights after seeing the bids invites bias toward a favored vendor.

wrong_explanations.A: Meeting minimum requirements makes a proposal eligible, not equal; awarding on price alone ignores the 70% of the score set for other criteria.
wrong_explanations.B: Best and final offers still decide on price and pass over vendors that may score highest on fit, support and stability.
wrong_explanations.D: Weights changed after proposals arrive can be tilted toward a favored vendor; operations staff's views belong in the criteria before proposals are requested.

tips: Eliminate: A treats eligibility as equality, and B still lets price alone decide.
Final two: C beats D because weights changed after bids arrive invite bias, while the stated criteria keep the selection fair.
Exam cue: fix weighted criteria before proposals arrive, then select on the full score; meeting minimums only earns a place.

questions.subtopic: Acquiring Software from Vendors. Proposal Request Before Requirements
questions.question: Facing a funding deadline, a county will issue a request for proposal (RFP) for a permitting system before documenting user requirements. What should the IS auditor consider the GREATEST risk of issuing the RFP now?

options.A: Proposals cannot be scored against what the county needs
options.B: The chosen vendor may charge heavily for later change requests
options.C: Fewer vendors may respond within a shortened bidding period
options.D: Vendors may send the county many clarification questions

questions.key_concept: Document requirements before issuing a request for proposal, because they are the basis for evaluating every proposal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the evaluation team would score the proposals against.
questions.correct_explanation: Requirements come first because they are the yardstick for scoring proposals. Without them, the county cannot tell which proposal fits its permitting process and may commit funds to a system that does not meet business needs. Costly change requests come closest: they are a likely consequence, but they are a symptom of that root problem rather than the problem itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Change-request costs are likely, but they are a symptom of the root problem: selecting a system without defined needs to judge it by.
wrong_explanations.C: A shorter bidding window may reduce responses, but more proposals would not help with no requirements to judge them against.
wrong_explanations.D: A vague request does draw more questions, but answering them is routine bidding work; it gives the county no yardstick for judging which proposal fits its needs.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because both are bidding-process concerns the procurement team can manage, not the business risk of buying without defined needs.
Final two: A beats B because change-request costs follow from the root flaw: no defined needs to judge proposals against.
Exam cue: in acquisition, requirements come before the request for proposal; without them, no proposal can be scored fairly.
