questions.subtopic: Project Roles and Accountability. When the IS Auditor Joins
questions.question: To protect audit independence, a bank's project office plans to involve the IS auditor in a new lending system only after system testing ends. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Agreement with the plan, because independence outweighs early advisory input
options.B: A voting seat on the steering committee from project start
options.C: Reliance on quality assurance reviews in place of audit input
options.D: Advisory input from requirements onward, without design or approval duties

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor advises from requirements onward; independence comes from not designing, building or approving, not from staying away.
questions.pre_read: Ask when controls are cheapest to add, and which roles would impair independence.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls are cheapest to build in at requirements and design, so the IS auditor should take part from the start in an advisory role. Independence comes from agreed advisory terms and from not designing, building or approving the system, not from staying away. A voting steering committee seat nearly wins: it gives early involvement, but voting makes the IS auditor share management's project decisions, which impairs independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Advisory input under agreed terms keeps independence; waiting until testing ends means missing controls are found when they are costliest to add.
wrong_explanations.B: No one audits objectively a decision they helped make. A steering seat does give early sight, yet auditors influence projects by advice, never by vote.
wrong_explanations.C: Quality assurance checks deliverables against standards; it does not replace the IS auditor's independent view of control requirements.

tips: Eliminate: A delays input until controls are costliest to add, and C swaps audit's control view for a standards check.
Final two: D beats B because voting on project decisions makes the IS auditor part of management, while advisory input keeps independence.
Exam cue: the IS auditor joins early and advises under agreed terms, but never designs, builds, approves or votes on project decisions.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity); COBIT 2019 BAI11 (Managed Projects)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Project Roles and Accountability. When the IS Auditor Joins'. questions.subtopic: Project Roles and Accountability. Business Staff Withheld from Requirements
questions.question: Business managers will not release staff for requirements workshops on a new claims system, so IT analysts are writing the requirements alone. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Proceed, and rely on user acceptance testing to find any gaps
options.B: Escalate to the steering committee to commit knowledgeable users
options.C: Hire external consultants to stand in for the business users
options.D: Have business managers formally sign off the analysts' requirements

questions.key_concept: User management owns requirements and must supply knowledgeable staff; the steering committee resolves gaps in business participation.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can commit business people to the project, and why their input matters.
questions.correct_explanation: User management owns the new system and must supply people who know the work, because requirements written by IT alone often miss how claims are really handled. The steering committee can commit those people, so escalating is the first step. Formal sign-off by business managers is the closest choice: it records ownership, but approving a document they did not help write rarely catches missing needs.

wrong_explanations.A: User acceptance testing finds gaps late, when fixing them means rework; missing needs should be caught while requirements are written.
wrong_explanations.C: Consultants may know the industry but not this organization's claims process, and they cannot take on the business's ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: Sign-off would close the loop if users had helped write the requirements; approval cannot add knowledge that was never gathered.

tips: Eliminate: A finds gaps only after the system is built, and C substitutes outsiders for the business's own knowledge.
Final two: B beats D because sign-off of a document the business did not help write records ownership without supplying its knowledge.
Exam cue: when the business will not take part, escalate; requirements need user ownership, not just user signatures.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI02 (Managed Requirements Definition); COBIT 2019 BAI11 (Managed Projects)

questions.subtopic: Purpose and Timing of the Review. Scheduling the First Review
questions.question: A ski resort's new booking system went live in May, and its business case promised faster bookings during the December-to-March season. Which timing for the post-implementation review should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Three months after go-live, as the usual settling interval
options.B: One week after go-live, while the project team is still assembled
options.C: Soon after the first December-to-March period has ended
options.D: After two full booking periods, once planned enhancements are finished

questions.key_concept: Schedule the post-implementation review once the system has run under conditions that let the promised benefits be measured.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the benefit promised in the business case can first be observed.
questions.correct_explanation: A review must wait until the system has run long enough, under representative conditions, to measure the promised benefits. Here the benefit is faster bookings from December to March, so the review belongs soon after the first such period ends, while fixes are still practical. Three months after go-live is the strongest alternative: it is a common settling period, but August data shows off-season volumes and cannot confirm the peak-season benefit.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would accept a usual settling interval as a default, but a seasonal promise can only be judged in its season.
wrong_explanations.B: One week after go-live shows start-up problems and the learning curve, not the normal or peak results the review must measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Two booking periods later, context is lost and changes have piled up, so findings come too late to correct cheaply.

tips: Eliminate: B is too early to show anything but start-up issues, and D is too late to act on findings cheaply.
Final two: C beats A because the promised benefit appears only at peak volume, which off-season data cannot show.
Exam cue: time the review for when the promised benefit can actually be measured, not by a fixed number of months.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Val IT Framework; COBIT 2019 BAI07.08 (Perform a post-implementation review)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Purpose and Timing of the Review. Scheduling the First Review'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 3B4.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q14: thin subtopic). Distinct from d3_066 (review one week after go-live), d3_016 (benefits as the primary focus) and d3_097 (risk-based selection of reviews): tests timing the review to the period when the promised benefit can be measured. All scenario specifics invented for this question. Public sources: ISACA Val IT Framework; COBIT 2019 BAI07.08.

questions.subtopic: Release Control. Who Signs Off a Release
questions.question: A product team wants an independent sign-off on each production release and asks the IS auditor to provide it from the attached test and scan results. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: The change authority approves releases on the attached test evidence
options.B: The IS auditor approves releases on the attached test evidence
options.C: The developer approves each release once an independent peer review passes
options.D: The change advisory board approves and deploys each release

questions.key_concept: Release approval is a management control: the change authority approves on attached evidence, and the IS auditor later tests that approvals were evidence-based.
questions.pre_read: Compare who performs the approval in each option, not only what evidence the approval uses.
questions.correct_explanation: The change authority, a management role independent of the developers, approves each release on the attached test and scan evidence; the IS auditor can later test that approvals were evidence-based. The IS auditor approving releases is the most tempting alternative. It uses the same evidence, but it makes the IS auditor operate a production control that the IS auditor must later audit, a self-review threat.

wrong_explanations.B: Both approvers would rely on identical test results, but independence is lost by what an auditor does, not by what an auditor reads.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer review helps, but the author still approves the author's own release, so the separation between writing and approving code is lost.
wrong_explanations.D: A board that both approves and deploys merges authorizing with doing; deployment should run through the pipeline or operations staff, separate from approval.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because authors must not approve their own changes, and the body that approves a release should not also deploy it.
Final two: A beats B because a management role should operate the approval; the IS auditor using the same evidence would audit its own control later.
Exam cue: if two options differ only in who acts, choose the one where management runs the control and the IS auditor tests it.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Change Enablement practice; COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Release Control. Who Signs Off a Release'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 3B2.2 (batch Q18: practice for principles with under ten tagged questions; principle recommend-dont-implement). Key and runner-up use the same evidence and differ only in who approves: management versus the IS auditor. questions.subtopic: Project Closure. Order of Closing Steps
questions.question: A new billing system went live last week, and the project manager plans to close the project and release the team on Friday. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Hold a lessons-learned review while the team is still together
options.B: Release the team on Friday, since the system runs in production
options.C: Confirm the business owner's formal sign-off on the deliverables
options.D: Begin the post-implementation review of the business benefits realized

questions.key_concept: Project closure starts with the business owner's formal acceptance; releasing resources, financial closeout and lessons learned follow it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which closing step decides whether the others can happen at all.
questions.correct_explanation: Closure starts by confirming the business owner's formal acceptance of the deliverables against the agreed criteria, because go-live is not acceptance. If acceptance reveals gaps, the team is still needed, so acceptance decides whether the project can close at all. The lessons-learned review comes closest. It is valuable, but it can be held after acceptance, and it does not decide whether closure may proceed.

wrong_explanations.A: Lessons matter, but they can be captured after acceptance; they do not decide whether the project may close or the team may go.
wrong_explanations.B: Deployment is not acceptance; releasing the team before the owner signs off leaves no one to fix gaps that acceptance finds.
wrong_explanations.D: A post-implementation review measures benefits months after go-live; it is not a closure step and would come far too early here.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because going live is not acceptance, and the benefits review comes months later, not at closure.
Final two: C beats A because confirmed acceptance decides whether the project can close and the team can go; lessons can be captured after it.
Exam cue: between two good FIRST steps, choose the one that decides whether the plan in the stem can go ahead; here, acceptance decides closure.
questions.framework_ref: PMBOK Guide 6th Edition, Section 4.7 (Close Project or Phase); COBIT 2019 BAI11 (Managed Projects)
